questions.q: About anatomical position and directional terminology:

items.text: In the standard anatomical position, the palms face anteriorly.
items.explain: The body is erect, the head and eyes face forward, the upper limbs are at the sides, and the forearms are supinated so the palms face forward.

items.text: The anatomical terms right and left refer to the observer facing the patient.
items.explain: Right and left are always the subject's own right and left, not the observer's.

items.text: The term proximal describes a structure nearer to the trunk or point of origin of a limb.
items.explain: Proximal and distal describe relative distance along a limb or structure from its attachment or origin.

items.text: A structure described as medial lies farther from the body's midline than a lateral structure.
items.explain: Medial means nearer the median plane; lateral means farther from it.

items.text: The median plane divides the body into equal right and left halves.
items.explain: The median (midsagittal) plane is the vertical plane through the midline; other sagittal planes are parallel to it but need not divide the body equally.

items.text: A coronal plane divides the body into anterior and posterior parts.
items.explain: Coronal (frontal) planes are vertical and separate front from back.

items.text: A transverse plane is always parallel to the long axis of the body.
items.explain: A transverse (horizontal) plane is perpendicular to the long axis and separates superior from inferior parts.

items.text: The term superficial describes a structure nearer the body surface than another structure.
items.explain: Superficial and deep express relative distance from the external surface.

items.text: It usually arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus.
items.explain: The musculocutaneous nerve is the terminal branch of the lateral cord and commonly carries C5–C7 fibres.

items.text: It pierces coracobrachialis.
items.explain: It typically enters and supplies coracobrachialis before passing between biceps brachii and brachialis.

items.text: It supplies biceps brachii and most of brachialis.
items.explain: It supplies the anterior compartment of the arm; the lateral part of brachialis may receive radial nerve contribution.

items.text: It provides cutaneous sensation to the medial side of the forearm.
items.explain: Its continuation as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm supplies skin on the lateral forearm.

items.text: It arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.
items.explain: The axillary nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord, usually carrying C5–C6 fibres.

items.text: It passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral vessels.
items.explain: The nerve and vessels wind around the surgical neck of the humerus through the quadrangular space.

items.text: It supplies deltoid and teres minor.
items.explain: These muscles are key motor targets; deltoid is important for shoulder abduction after the initial phase.

items.text: It supplies cutaneous sensation to the medial side of the forearm.
items.explain: The axillary nerve supplies the regimental-badge area over the upper lateral arm. The medial forearm is supplied by the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve.

items.text: The sodium-potassium ATPase moves three sodium ions out of the cell for every two potassium ions moved in.
items.explain: The pump hydrolyses ATP to maintain the sodium and potassium gradients and is electrogenic because there is a net outward movement of positive charge.

items.text: Facilitated diffusion moves a solute down its electrochemical gradient without directly using ATP.
items.explain: Channels and carrier proteins can mediate facilitated diffusion, but the transported substance still moves down its gradient.

items.text: Primary active transport obtains its energy directly from ATP hydrolysis or another direct energy source.
items.explain: The sodium-potassium ATPase and calcium ATPase are examples of primary active transport.

items.text: Osmosis requires direct ATP hydrolysis to move water across a selectively permeable membrane.
items.explain: Osmosis is passive net water movement down a water-potential gradient; it does not directly consume ATP.

items.text: In many excitable cells, resting membrane potential is closer to the potassium equilibrium potential than to the sodium equilibrium potential.
items.explain: At rest, membrane permeability to potassium is relatively high, so potassium conductance strongly influences the resting potential.

items.text: The sodium-potassium ATPase is the sole cause of the rapid upstroke of a neuronal action potential.
items.explain: The rapid upstroke is primarily caused by opening of voltage-gated sodium channels and inward sodium current; the pump maintains gradients over time.

items.text: A rise in extracellular potassium concentration generally makes the resting membrane potential less negative.
items.explain: Increasing extracellular potassium reduces the outward potassium gradient, tending to depolarise the cell.

items.text: The absolute refractory period occurs while voltage-gated sodium channels are inactivated.
items.explain: During this period, another action potential cannot be initiated regardless of stimulus strength because many sodium channels have not recovered.

items.text: Calcium binds to troponin C during skeletal muscle contraction.
items.explain: Calcium binding changes the troponin complex and moves tropomyosin away from myosin-binding sites on actin.

items.text: Tropomyosin normally covers myosin-binding sites on actin when the resting muscle fibre has low cytosolic calcium.
items.explain: This prevents strong cross-bridge formation until calcium rises and the regulatory proteins change position.

items.text: ATP binding to myosin is required for myosin to detach from actin.
items.explain: ATP binding reduces myosin's affinity for actin; ATP hydrolysis then re-cocks the myosin head for another cycle.

items.text: SERCA pumps calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol to initiate relaxation.
items.explain: SERCA uses ATP to pump calcium from the cytosol back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, lowering cytosolic calcium and promoting relaxation.

items.text: Phosphocreatine can rapidly donate a phosphate group to ADP to regenerate ATP.
items.explain: Creatine kinase catalyses this rapid buffer reaction, helping maintain ATP during the first seconds of intense activity.

items.text: Anaerobic glycolysis can provide ATP when oxygen delivery is insufficient for the rate of ATP demand.
items.explain: It produces ATP rapidly from glucose or glycogen and converts pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺.

items.text: A motor unit consists of one motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it innervates.
items.explain: All fibres in a motor unit are activated when that motor neuron discharges.

items.text: Recruitment of additional motor units generally decreases the force produced by a whole muscle.
items.explain: Recruiting more motor units increases the number of active fibres and generally increases muscle force.

questions.q: About body-fluid compartments in a typical healthy adult:

items.text: Total body water is often approximated as about 60% of body mass in a young adult man.
items.explain: This is a teaching approximation; age, sex and body-fat proportion alter the actual fraction.

items.text: Intracellular fluid accounts for approximately two-thirds of total body water.
items.explain: The remaining one-third is extracellular fluid, which includes interstitial fluid and plasma.

items.text: Plasma is the largest component of extracellular fluid.
items.explain: Interstitial fluid is the larger extracellular compartment; plasma is the smaller intravascular component.

items.text: Potassium is the major cation of intracellular fluid, while sodium is the major cation of extracellular fluid.
items.explain: These concentration differences are maintained largely by membrane transport systems including the sodium-potassium ATPase.

items.text: An isotonic saline infusion expands extracellular fluid volume without causing a major sustained shift of water into cells.
items.explain: Sodium and chloride remain mainly extracellular, so isotonic saline expands the extracellular compartment.

items.text: A sufficiently hypotonic extracellular fluid causes water to move into cells.
items.explain: Water moves toward the compartment with the higher effective osmotic concentration, so cells swell.

items.text: A hypertonic extracellular fluid causes cells to gain water and swell.
items.explain: Water leaves cells toward the more concentrated extracellular fluid, causing cells to shrink.

items.text: The osmolality of plasma is determined mainly by sodium salts and their accompanying anions.
items.explain: Sodium and its associated anions are the major contributors to extracellular-fluid osmolality under usual conditions.

items.text: Enzymes lower the activation energy of a reaction.
items.explain: They provide an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation-energy barrier, increasing reaction rate.

items.text: An enzyme changes the equilibrium constant of the reaction it catalyses.
items.explain: Enzymes accelerate the approach to equilibrium but do not change the reaction's equilibrium constant or overall free-energy change.

items.text: In classical competitive inhibition, apparent Km increases while Vmax is unchanged when sufficient substrate is available.
items.explain: Substrate can outcompete a reversible competitive inhibitor at the active site, so the same Vmax can be reached at higher substrate concentration.

items.text: A pure noncompetitive inhibitor decreases Vmax without changing Km in the classical model.
items.explain: It reduces the fraction of functional enzyme without changing substrate affinity in the pure noncompetitive case.

items.text: Most enzymes are proteins, although some RNA molecules also have catalytic activity.
items.explain: Catalytic RNA molecules are called ribozymes; they are important exceptions to the usual protein nature of enzymes.

items.text: Enzymes are consumed stoichiometrically during the reactions they catalyse.
items.explain: Enzymes participate in catalytic cycles and are regenerated rather than consumed as reactants.

items.text: Many enzymes require cofactors such as metal ions or coenzymes for full activity.
items.explain: A cofactor may be an inorganic ion or an organic coenzyme, often derived from a vitamin.

items.text: The activity of every enzyme increases indefinitely as temperature rises.
items.explain: Activity usually rises toward an optimum, but excessive heat can disrupt protein structure and reduce catalytic activity.

items.text: Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol.
items.explain: The pathway converts glucose to pyruvate (or lactate under anaerobic conditions) through cytosolic reactions.

items.text: The net yield of glycolysis from one molecule of glucose to two pyruvate molecules is two ATP.
items.explain: Four ATP are generated and two are consumed, giving a net yield of two ATP per glucose.

items.text: Gluconeogenesis occurs exclusively in skeletal muscle.
items.explain: The liver is the principal site; the kidney cortex also contributes, especially during prolonged fasting.

items.text: Insulin generally promotes glycogen synthesis in liver and skeletal muscle.
items.explain: Insulin favours storage pathways and suppresses hepatic glucose output in the fed state.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose-1-phosphate from glycogen by phosphorolysis.
items.explain: It cleaves α-1,4 glycosidic bonds at non-reducing ends, releasing glucose-1-phosphate.

items.text: The glycogen branching enzyme creates α-1,6 linkages.
items.explain: Branching increases the number of non-reducing ends and permits rapid synthesis and breakdown.

items.text: Skeletal muscle can directly release substantial free glucose into the blood because it contains glucose-6-phosphatase.
items.explain: Skeletal muscle lacks significant glucose-6-phosphatase activity; its glycogen is used locally to support muscle metabolism.

items.text: Glucagon stimulates glycogen breakdown in skeletal muscle as its principal direct target.
items.explain: Glucagon acts mainly on the liver; skeletal-muscle glycogenolysis is stimulated chiefly by epinephrine and contraction-related signals.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: At physiological pH, many free amino acids exist predominantly as zwitterions.
items.explain: Their amino group is protonated and their carboxyl group is deprotonated, giving both positive and negative charges.

items.text: All amino acids used in human proteins have an identical side chain.
items.explain: The side chain (R group) differs and determines much of each amino acid's chemical behaviour.

items.text: Essential amino acids must be obtained from the diet in amounts adequate for the body's needs.
items.explain: Humans cannot synthesise the carbon skeletons of essential amino acids in sufficient amounts.

items.text: Cysteine residues can form disulfide bonds after oxidation of their sulfhydryl groups.
items.explain: Disulfide bonds can stabilise the tertiary or quaternary structure of proteins.

items.text: The peptide bond has partial double-bond character and is relatively planar.
items.explain: Resonance restricts rotation around the peptide C–N bond, contributing to the geometry of the polypeptide backbone.

items.text: Primary protein structure refers to the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
items.explain: It is the linear amino-acid sequence, including the positions of covalent links such as disulfide bonds in some conventions.

items.text: Alpha helices and beta sheets are examples of secondary protein structure.
items.explain: They are stabilised mainly by hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl and amide groups.

items.text: Denaturation always hydrolyses all peptide bonds in a protein.
items.explain: Denaturation disrupts higher-order structure without necessarily breaking the covalent peptide backbone.

items.text: Flexion generally decreases the angle between articulating bones.
items.explain: Flexion is a bending movement that usually reduces the angle at a joint.

items.text: Abduction of a limb moves it away from the median plane.
items.explain: Abduction is movement away from the body's midline; adduction moves toward it.

items.text: Pronation of the forearm turns the palm anteriorly in the standard anatomical position.
items.explain: Pronation rotates the radius over the ulna and turns the palm posteriorly from the anatomical position.

items.text: Dorsiflexion raises the dorsum of the foot toward the anterior leg.
items.explain: Dorsiflexion occurs at the ankle and brings the dorsum of the foot closer to the shin.

questions.q: About the median nerve in the upper limb:

items.text: The median nerve is formed by contributions from the lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus.
items.explain: Its lateral and medial roots unite anterior to the third part of the axillary artery.

items.text: The median nerve normally supplies flexor carpi ulnaris.
items.explain: Flexor carpi ulnaris is supplied by the ulnar nerve; most forearm flexors receive median or anterior interosseous innervation.

items.text: The recurrent branch of the median nerve supplies several thenar muscles.
items.explain: It supplies key thenar muscles involved in opposition and abduction of the thumb.

items.text: A lesion at the wrist can impair opposition of the thumb.
items.explain: Median nerve injury at the wrist may weaken thenar function and produce difficulty opposing the thumb.

items.text: The rotator cuff is formed by supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis.
items.explain: These four muscles blend with the shoulder joint capsule and help stabilise the glenohumeral joint.

items.text: Supraspinatus initiates the first part of arm abduction.
items.explain: Supraspinatus is especially important in initiating abduction; the deltoid becomes the major abductor through much of the range.

items.text: The subscapularis inserts on the greater tubercle of the humerus.
items.explain: Subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle; the other three cuff muscles insert on facets of the greater tubercle.

items.text: The rotator cuff helps hold the humeral head against the glenoid cavity during movement.
items.explain: Dynamic stabilisation by the cuff counters translation generated by larger shoulder muscles.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The main intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove along the inferior border of a rib.
items.explain: The vein, artery and nerve are arranged from superior to inferior in the groove, commonly remembered as VAN.

items.text: A needle inserted just inferior to a rib is generally less likely to injure the main intercostal neurovascular bundle than one inserted just superior to it.
items.explain: The main bundle lies in the costal groove along the inferior border of the rib above. A procedural approach just superior to a rib is generally chosen to reduce risk, while collateral branches mean care is still required.

items.text: The external intercostal muscles are replaced by an external intercostal membrane anteriorly near the sternum.
items.explain: The external intercostals extend from the vertebral region to the costochondral junction and continue anteriorly as a membrane.

items.text: The intercostal nerve is a branch of the anterior ramus of a thoracic spinal nerve.
items.explain: The anterior rami of most thoracic spinal nerves form the intercostal nerves.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The visceral pleura is normally insensitive to pain from ordinary somatic sensory nerves.
items.explain: Visceral pleura receives autonomic afferents and is relatively insensitive to pain, whereas parietal pleura is pain-sensitive.

items.text: The costal part of parietal pleura is supplied by intercostal nerves.
items.explain: Intercostal nerves carry somatic sensory fibres from the costal and peripheral diaphragmatic pleura.

items.text: The mediastinal pleura is supplied by the phrenic nerve.
items.explain: The mediastinal pleura and central diaphragmatic pleura receive sensory innervation from the phrenic nerve.

items.text: The pleural cavity normally contains a large volume of air.
items.explain: The pleural cavity is a potential space containing a thin film of lubricating fluid; air in it constitutes pneumothorax.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Simple diffusion occurs down a concentration or electrochemical gradient.
items.explain: Net movement is from higher to lower chemical potential and does not require a carrier or direct ATP input.

items.text: Facilitated diffusion can show saturation because it depends on a finite number of carrier proteins.
items.explain: Carrier-mediated transport has a transport maximum when available carriers are occupied.

items.text: Simple diffusion across a cell membrane requires a specific carrier protein to bind the transported molecule.
items.explain: Simple diffusion occurs directly through the lipid bilayer for suitable substances. Transport through channels or carriers is classified as facilitated diffusion.

items.text: Secondary active transport uses energy stored in an ion gradient established by primary active transport.
items.explain: The downhill movement of one solute can drive uphill transport of another, as in sodium-glucose cotransport.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The rising phase of a typical neuronal action potential is associated with increased sodium permeability.
items.explain: Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels causes rapid sodium entry and depolarisation.

items.text: The falling phase is associated in part with increased potassium conductance.
items.explain: Delayed opening of voltage-gated potassium channels promotes potassium efflux and repolarisation.

items.text: The amplitude of a typical action potential increases in direct proportion to stimulus strength once threshold is reached.
items.explain: Action potentials are all-or-none; stronger stimuli generally increase firing frequency or recruit more fibres rather than increasing individual action-potential amplitude.

items.text: Myelin increases conduction velocity by allowing saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier.
items.explain: Action potentials are regenerated at nodes, so current spreads rapidly beneath myelin between nodes.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: During an isometric contraction, muscle tension changes while muscle length remains approximately constant.
items.explain: The muscle develops force without appreciable shortening, such as holding a load steady.

items.text: During a concentric isotonic contraction, the active muscle shortens while producing force.
items.explain: Concentric contraction occurs when muscle force exceeds the opposing load.

items.text: During an eccentric contraction, the active muscle lengthens while resisting a load.
items.explain: Eccentric activity controls movement, for example when lowering a weight slowly.

items.text: An isometric contraction necessarily produces joint movement through a large range.
items.explain: Because muscle length is held approximately constant, an isometric contraction does not produce the corresponding joint movement.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The filtration barrier includes fenestrated glomerular capillary endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragms.
items.explain: These layers provide size- and charge-selective filtration between plasma and Bowman's space.

items.text: Healthy glomeruli normally allow large quantities of albumin to pass freely into Bowman's space.
items.explain: The filtration barrier restricts albumin passage; persistent albuminuria suggests glomerular or other renal pathology.

items.text: Podocyte foot processes interdigitate to form filtration slits.
items.explain: Slit diaphragms between adjacent foot processes form the final cellular component of the filtration barrier.

items.text: The glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure favours filtration into Bowman's space.
items.explain: It is the main pressure promoting filtration, opposed by plasma colloid osmotic pressure and Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure.

items.text: The proximal tubule reabsorbs the majority of filtered sodium and water.
items.explain: Bulk reabsorption occurs in the proximal tubule, with water following solute approximately iso-osmotically.

items.text: Under normal conditions, nearly all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.
items.explain: Sodium-glucose cotransporters reclaim filtered glucose until transport capacity is exceeded.

items.text: The loop of Henle reabsorbs all filtered plasma proteins.
items.explain: Most plasma proteins are retained in the circulation by the filtration barrier; small filtered proteins may be reclaimed by proximal tubular cells.

items.text: Tubular secretion moves substances from peritubular blood or tubular cells into the tubular lumen.
items.explain: Secretion contributes to potassium, hydrogen ion and organic ion handling and to elimination of selected drugs.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Radiation can transfer heat between the body and surrounding surfaces without direct contact.
items.explain: Infrared radiation exchanges heat between surfaces according to their temperatures.

items.text: Conduction is heat transfer through direct contact between objects.
items.explain: Heat flows from the warmer object to the cooler one when they are in contact.

items.text: Evaporation of sweat removes heat from the body.
items.explain: Conversion of liquid sweat to vapour requires latent heat, which is drawn from the skin.

items.text: Vasoconstriction of cutaneous blood vessels generally increases heat loss from the skin.
items.explain: Cutaneous vasoconstriction reduces warm blood flow to the skin and conserves core heat.

items.text: An increase in capillary hydrostatic pressure can favour movement of fluid from capillaries into the interstitial space.
items.explain: Raised venous pressure, for example, can increase filtration and contribute to oedema.

items.text: A reduction in plasma colloid osmotic pressure can promote interstitial oedema.
items.explain: Low plasma albumin reduces the force retaining water within capillaries.

items.text: Lymphatic obstruction usually reduces interstitial fluid volume.
items.explain: Impaired lymph drainage causes protein-rich fluid to accumulate in the interstitium and can produce lymphoedema.

items.text: Increased capillary permeability can contribute to oedema during inflammation.
items.explain: Inflammatory mediators increase endothelial permeability, allowing protein and fluid to enter the interstitial space.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Allosteric regulators bind at a site distinct from the active site and can alter enzyme activity.
items.explain: Binding can change enzyme conformation and increase or decrease catalytic activity.

items.text: Feedback inhibition commonly involves a pathway's end product inhibiting an earlier enzyme.
items.explain: This helps match pathway flux to cellular demand and limits unnecessary product formation.

items.text: A competitive inhibitor permanently destroys the active site of every enzyme molecule it encounters.
items.explain: Reversible competitive inhibitors bind non-covalently and can dissociate; irreversible inhibitors are a different category.

items.text: Covalent modification such as phosphorylation can regulate the activity of some enzymes.
items.explain: Phosphorylation can alter enzyme conformation, interactions and activity, depending on the enzyme.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: In eukaryotic cells, most reactions of the TCA cycle occur in the mitochondrial matrix.
items.explain: The cycle is located in the matrix, although succinate dehydrogenase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

items.text: Each turn of the TCA cycle releases two molecules of carbon dioxide.
items.explain: Two decarboxylation reactions occur per turn. The carbon atoms released in a given turn are not necessarily the same two carbons that entered as acetyl-CoA in that turn.

items.text: The TCA cycle directly consumes molecular oxygen at one of its enzyme-catalysed steps.
items.explain: Oxygen is not a direct substrate of the cycle; it is required by the respiratory chain to reoxidise NADH and FADH2.

items.text: One turn of the cycle generates reduced coenzymes that transfer electrons to the respiratory chain.
items.explain: NADH and FADH2 carry high-energy electrons for oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Gluconeogenesis synthesises glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors such as lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids.
items.explain: It helps maintain blood glucose during fasting when dietary glucose is unavailable.

items.text: The liver is a major site of gluconeogenesis.
items.explain: The kidney cortex also contributes, particularly during prolonged fasting and acidosis.

items.text: Gluconeogenesis is simply the reversal of glycolysis using exactly the same enzymes in reverse order.
items.explain: Several glycolytic steps are essentially irreversible and are bypassed by distinct gluconeogenic enzymes.

items.text: The conversion of pyruvate to phosphoenolpyruvate in gluconeogenesis involves pyruvate carboxylase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase.
items.explain: Pyruvate carboxylase forms oxaloacetate, which is then converted to phosphoenolpyruvate by PEP carboxykinase.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Transamination transfers an amino group from an amino acid to an alpha-keto acid.
items.explain: Aminotransferases commonly transfer amino groups to alpha-ketoglutarate, forming glutamate.

items.text: Many aminotransferases require pyridoxal phosphate, derived from vitamin B6.
items.explain: PLP acts as a coenzyme in amino-group transfer reactions.

items.text: The urea cycle is a major pathway for disposal of nitrogen derived from amino acid catabolism.
items.explain: The liver converts toxic ammonia nitrogen into urea for excretion by the kidneys.

items.text: The urea cycle occurs entirely in the cytosol.
items.explain: The first two reactions occur in mitochondria and the remaining reactions occur in the cytosol.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Pepsin begins protein digestion in the stomach.
items.explain: Pepsin is activated from pepsinogen in the acidic gastric environment and cleaves peptide bonds.

items.text: Pancreatic proteases are secreted in active form to maximise digestion immediately after release.
items.explain: Several pancreatic proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens, reducing the risk of autodigestion.

items.text: Enteropeptidase at the small-intestinal brush border activates trypsinogen to trypsin.
items.explain: Trypsin then activates several other pancreatic zymogens.

items.text: Amino acids and small peptides are absorbed by enterocytes using specific transport systems.
items.explain: Free amino acids and di-/tripeptides use distinct transporters; intracellular peptidases hydrolyse many absorbed small peptides.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Thiamine is the precursor of thiamine pyrophosphate, a coenzyme in oxidative decarboxylation reactions.
items.explain: Thiamine pyrophosphate is required by enzymes such as pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

items.text: Riboflavin is the precursor of FMN and FAD.
items.explain: These flavin coenzymes participate in oxidation-reduction reactions.

items.text: Niacin is the precursor of NAD+ and NADP+.
items.explain: Nicotinamide-containing coenzymes transfer electrons in many metabolic pathways.

items.text: Vitamin C is the direct precursor of coenzyme A.
items.explain: Coenzyme A contains a pantothenate (vitamin B5) component; vitamin C has other roles, including collagen hydroxylation.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: DNA contains deoxyribose, whereas RNA contains ribose.
items.explain: Ribose has a 2′ hydroxyl group that deoxyribose lacks.

items.text: In standard double-stranded DNA, adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds.
items.explain: A–T base pairs form two hydrogen bonds, while G–C pairs form three.

items.text: Uracil is the usual pyrimidine base in DNA.
items.explain: DNA normally contains thymine; uracil is used in RNA.

items.text: The two strands of a typical DNA double helix run antiparallel to one another.
items.explain: One strand runs 5′ to 3′ and the complementary strand runs 3′ to 5′.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: DNA polymerases extend a new DNA strand by adding nucleotides to a free 3′ hydroxyl group.
items.explain: DNA synthesis proceeds in the 5′ to 3′ direction because each incoming nucleotide is added to the 3′ end.

items.text: The leading strand is synthesised continuously in the direction of replication fork movement.
items.explain: Its template is oriented so DNA polymerase can synthesise continuously toward the advancing fork.

items.text: Okazaki fragments are formed on the leading strand.
items.explain: Okazaki fragments are short DNA segments synthesised discontinuously on the lagging strand.

items.text: DNA ligase joins adjacent DNA fragments by sealing phosphodiester backbone breaks.
items.explain: Ligase seals nicks after primer removal and replacement during lagging-strand synthesis.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding protein structure, all the following statements are true except:

items.text: The primary structure of a protein is its amino-acid sequence.
items.explain: Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino-acid residues joined by peptide bonds.

items.text: Alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets are forms of secondary structure.
items.explain: These regular local folding patterns are stabilised mainly by hydrogen bonds involving peptide-backbone groups.

items.text: Tertiary structure describes the overall three-dimensional conformation of a single polypeptide chain.
items.explain: Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of one polypeptide, involving side-chain interactions and other stabilising forces.

items.text: Ordinary denaturation necessarily hydrolyses peptide bonds and destroys the primary structure.
items.explain: Denaturation disrupts higher-order structure and biological activity but usually does not cleave the covalent peptide bonds of the primary sequence.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding amino acids, all the following statements are false except:

items.text: Glycine is the only standard amino acid whose alpha carbon is not chiral.
items.explain: Glycine has two hydrogen atoms attached to its alpha carbon, so that carbon is not an asymmetric centre.

items.text: All amino acids have an aromatic side chain.
items.explain: Only a subset, including phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan, have aromatic side chains.

items.text: Humans can synthesise every amino acid in quantities sufficient for all physiological needs.
items.explain: Several amino acids are essential and must be supplied by the diet in adequate amounts.

items.text: The peptide bond freely rotates because it is a simple single bond.
items.explain: Resonance gives the peptide C–N bond partial double-bond character, restricting rotation and favouring a planar arrangement.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: During quiet inspiration, contraction of the diaphragm increases the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity.
items.explain: The diaphragm contracts and descends during quiet inspiration, increasing the vertical thoracic dimension and helping lower intrathoracic pressure.

items.text: Quiet expiration normally requires active contraction of the internal intercostal muscles.
items.explain: Quiet expiration is usually passive. Relaxation of inspiratory muscles and elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall reduce thoracic volume; internal intercostals are recruited during forced expiration.

items.text: Intrapleural pressure is normally subatmospheric at the end of a quiet expiration.
items.explain: At functional residual capacity, opposing recoil forces of the lungs inward and chest wall outward maintain a normally negative intrapleural pressure.

items.text: Pulmonary surfactant increases alveolar surface tension and makes the lungs harder to expand.
items.explain: Surfactant reduces surface tension at the air–liquid interface, increases lung compliance and helps prevent alveolar collapse, especially at low lung volumes.

items.text: Most oxygen in arterial blood is transported bound to haemoglobin.
items.explain: The great majority of blood oxygen is reversibly bound to haemoglobin inside erythrocytes; only a small fraction is physically dissolved in plasma.

items.text: An increase in temperature and a decrease in pH shift the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the left.
items.explain: Increased temperature and decreased pH reduce haemoglobin's oxygen affinity and shift the curve to the right, promoting oxygen unloading in metabolically active tissues.

items.text: Carbon monoxide can impair tissue oxygen delivery by binding haemoglobin with high affinity.
items.explain: Carbon monoxide forms carboxyhaemoglobin, reducing available oxygen-binding sites and increasing the affinity of remaining sites, which impairs oxygen unloading.

items.text: A rightward shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve means haemoglobin has increased affinity for oxygen.
items.explain: A right shift means decreased oxygen affinity and a higher P50, facilitating oxygen release to tissues.

questions.q: About primary haemostasis and platelet function:

items.text: Platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial structures is facilitated by von Willebrand factor.
items.explain: Von Willebrand factor binds exposed subendothelial collagen and platelet GPIb, helping platelets adhere at sites of vascular injury.

items.text: Platelet aggregation is mediated in part by fibrinogen binding to activated platelet GPIIb/IIIa receptors.
items.explain: Activated GPIIb/IIIa receptors bind fibrinogen, which bridges adjacent platelets and supports aggregation.

items.text: Thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin during coagulation.
items.explain: Thrombin cleaves fibrinopeptides from fibrinogen, producing fibrin monomers that polymerise and are subsequently stabilised by factor XIIIa.

items.text: Aspirin promotes platelet aggregation by irreversibly activating cyclo-oxygenase-1.
items.explain: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, reducing thromboxane A2 synthesis and thereby inhibiting platelet activation and aggregation.

items.text: The first heart sound is associated mainly with closure of the atrioventricular valves.
items.explain: S1 occurs at the onset of ventricular systole and is associated with closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves.

items.text: During isovolumetric ventricular contraction, both the atrioventricular and semilunar valves are closed.
items.explain: Ventricular pressure rises after AV valve closure but before aortic and pulmonary valve opening, so all four valves are closed and ventricular volume is unchanged.

items.text: The aortic valve opens when left ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure.
items.explain: The aortic valve opens when left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure during systole, allowing ventricular ejection.

items.text: The T wave on a normal ECG represents ventricular depolarisation.
items.explain: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation. The T wave represents ventricular repolarisation.

questions.sub: Red blood cells and oxygen delivery
questions.q: About red blood cells and oxygen delivery:

items.text: Mature human erythrocytes lack mitochondria.
items.explain: Mature erythrocytes lose their mitochondria during maturation, so they generate ATP mainly through anaerobic glycolysis and do not consume the oxygen they transport.

items.text: Erythropoietin is produced mainly by renal peritubular interstitial cells in adults.
items.explain: In adults, renal peritubular interstitial cells are the principal source of erythropoietin in response to reduced tissue oxygen availability.

items.text: A low haemoglobin concentration can reduce arterial oxygen content even when arterial oxygen saturation is normal.
items.explain: Oxygen content depends strongly on haemoglobin concentration as well as saturation; normal saturation does not compensate fully for a markedly reduced haemoglobin level.

items.text: Pulse oximetry directly measures the total oxygen content of blood.
items.explain: Pulse oximetry estimates peripheral arterial haemoglobin oxygen saturation. It does not directly measure haemoglobin concentration or total arterial oxygen content.

questions.q: About early development of the central nervous system:

items.text: The neural tube develops from ectoderm.
items.explain: The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate, which folds and closes to create the neural tube.

items.text: The neural tube gives rise to the brain and spinal cord.
items.explain: The neural tube is the embryonic precursor of the central nervous system, including the brain and spinal cord.

items.text: The neural crest contributes to structures of the peripheral nervous system.
items.explain: Neural crest cells migrate extensively and contribute to peripheral ganglia, Schwann cells and several other tissues.

items.text: Failure of cranial neuropore closure is classically associated with spina bifida.
items.explain: Failure of cranial neuropore closure is associated with severe cranial neural tube defects such as anencephaly; caudal neuropore closure failure is associated with spina bifida.

questions.q: Regarding embryological development of the heart:

items.text: The primitive heart begins to beat during the fourth week of development.
items.explain: The embryonic heart begins rhythmic activity around day 22, during the fourth week when age is expressed in gestational weeks.

items.text: The paired endocardial heart tubes fuse to form a single primitive heart tube.
items.explain: The paired endocardial tubes approach and fuse in the midline, forming the primitive heart tube.

items.text: The primitive heart tube develops from ectoderm.
items.explain: The heart develops primarily from splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm within the cardiogenic region, not ectoderm.

items.text: The primitive heart tube undergoes looping as it develops into the four-chambered heart.
items.explain: Cardiac looping establishes the spatial arrangement of the primitive chambers and outflow tract and is an essential step in later septation and alignment.

items.text: The glycolytic pathway converts one six-carbon glucose molecule into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules.
items.explain: The ten reactions of glycolysis split one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules; the pathway occurs in the cytosol.

items.text: The net yield of glycolysis per molecule of glucose is two ATP.
items.explain: Four ATP are generated and two ATP are consumed in the preparatory steps, giving a net yield of two ATP per glucose.

items.text: Glycolysis can proceed in the absence of oxygen.
items.explain: Glycolysis itself does not directly require oxygen. Under anaerobic conditions, pyruvate can be reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD+.

items.text: The conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase directly produces ATP.
items.explain: Hexokinase transfers a phosphate group from ATP to glucose, consuming ATP and forming glucose-6-phosphate.

items.text: Gluconeogenesis produces glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors.
items.explain: Gluconeogenesis synthesises glucose from precursors such as lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids, particularly during fasting.

items.text: During fasting, hepatic gluconeogenesis helps maintain the circulating glucose concentration.
items.explain: As fasting progresses and hepatic glycogen becomes depleted, the liver synthesises glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors to support glucose-dependent tissues.

items.text: Even-chain fatty acids are a major net source of glucose carbon in humans.
items.explain: Even-chain fatty acids yield acetyl-CoA, which cannot provide net glucose in humans because the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible and acetyl-CoA carbons are lost in the TCA cycle.

items.text: Pyruvate carboxylase catalyses the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate.
items.explain: Mitochondrial pyruvate carboxylase uses ATP and bicarbonate to convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate, the first bypass step in gluconeogenesis.

items.text: The oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway generates NADPH.
items.explain: The oxidative phase converts glucose-6-phosphate toward ribulose-5-phosphate and generates NADPH, which supports reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defence.

items.text: The pathway is an important source of ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis.
items.explain: Ribose-5-phosphate produced by the pathway provides the pentose sugar required for nucleotide and nucleic acid synthesis.

items.text: The pentose phosphate pathway directly generates ATP as one of its principal products.
items.explain: The pathway's main products are NADPH and pentose phosphates; it is not an ATP-generating pathway.

items.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase catalyses the first and rate-limiting step of the oxidative phase.
items.explain: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase catalyses the first oxidative reaction and is a major regulatory step, producing NADPH.

items.text: Gastrin is secreted by G cells, principally in the gastric antrum.
items.explain: G cells in the gastric antrum are the principal source of gastrin; the hormone promotes gastric acid secretion and supports gastric mucosal growth.

items.text: Secretin is released from duodenal S cells in response to acidic chyme entering the duodenum.
items.explain: Acid in the duodenal lumen stimulates S cells to release secretin, which promotes bicarbonate-rich pancreatic and biliary secretion.

items.text: Cholecystokinin is released mainly in response to fatty acids and amino acids in the small intestine.
items.explain: CCK is released from I cells in the duodenum and jejunum when digestion products, particularly fatty acids and amino acids, enter the lumen.

items.text: Gastrin is the principal hormone that stimulates gallbladder contraction after a fatty meal.
items.explain: CCK is the principal gut hormone that contracts the gallbladder and promotes delivery of bile after a meal; gastrin's major actions are on gastric secretion and mucosal growth.

items.text: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
items.explain: Gastric parietal cells produce hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, which is required for normal vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

items.text: Chief cells are the principal source of pepsinogen.
items.explain: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, which is converted to active pepsin in the acidic gastric lumen.

items.text: The stomach has only two layers of smooth muscle in its muscularis externa.
items.explain: The stomach has three muscular layers: inner oblique, middle circular and outer longitudinal; the oblique layer assists mixing and churning.

items.text: Fat entering the duodenum tends to slow gastric emptying.
items.explain: Duodenal fat stimulates feedback mechanisms, including CCK release and enterogastric neural reflexes, that slow gastric emptying and regulate nutrient delivery.

items.text: Insulin is secreted by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets.
items.explain: Pancreatic islet beta cells synthesise and secrete insulin in response to increased blood glucose and other nutrient signals.

items.text: Glucagon is secreted by pancreatic alpha cells and acts importantly on the liver.
items.explain: Alpha cells release glucagon, which acts predominantly on hepatocytes to promote glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

items.text: Insulin secretion is stimulated when ATP-sensitive potassium channels in beta cells open.
items.explain: Glucose metabolism raises beta-cell ATP, which closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels; membrane depolarisation then opens voltage-gated calcium channels and promotes insulin exocytosis.

items.text: C-peptide is released together with endogenous insulin when proinsulin is processed.
items.explain: Cleavage of proinsulin produces insulin and C-peptide, which are released in approximately equimolar amounts and make C-peptide useful as a marker of endogenous insulin secretion.

items.text: The adrenal cortex has three zones: zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata and zona reticularis.
items.explain: From outer to inner, the adrenal cortex is arranged into zona glomerulosa, fasciculata and reticularis.

items.text: Aldosterone is produced mainly by the zona glomerulosa.
items.explain: The zona glomerulosa synthesises mineralocorticoids, principally aldosterone, under regulation mainly by angiotensin II and plasma potassium.

items.text: Cortisol is produced mainly by the zona fasciculata.
items.explain: The zona fasciculata is the major glucocorticoid-producing zone and secretes cortisol under ACTH influence.

items.text: The adrenal medulla is derived from mesoderm and secretes aldosterone.
items.explain: The adrenal medulla is derived from neural crest cells and secretes catecholamines, principally epinephrine and norepinephrine; aldosterone is made in the cortical zona glomerulosa.

items.text: Beta-oxidation of most fatty acids occurs mainly in the mitochondrial matrix.
items.explain: For most short-, medium- and long-chain fatty acids, beta-oxidation occurs in mitochondria; very-long-chain fatty acids are initially shortened in peroxisomes.

items.text: Long-chain fatty acyl groups enter the mitochondrial matrix using the carnitine shuttle.
items.explain: The carnitine shuttle transfers long-chain acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane using CPT-I, carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase and CPT-II.

items.text: Each complete cycle of beta-oxidation of an even-chain fatty acyl-CoA yields one acetyl-CoA, one NADH and one FADH2.
items.explain: A typical beta-oxidation cycle produces one FADH2, one NADH and one acetyl-CoA; the final cleavage of an even-chain substrate yields two acetyl-CoA molecules.

items.text: Malonyl-CoA activates CPT-I and therefore accelerates mitochondrial entry of long-chain fatty acids.
items.explain: Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, limiting mitochondrial import of long-chain fatty acyl groups when fatty acid synthesis is active.

items.text: Ketogenesis occurs mainly in the mitochondria of liver cells.
items.explain: Hepatic mitochondria contain the enzymes that convert excess acetyl-CoA into the ketone bodies acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate.

items.text: The principal ketone bodies are acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone.
items.explain: Acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are the main circulating ketone bodies; acetone is formed from acetoacetate and is largely exhaled.

items.text: The liver can use ketone bodies as its own major fuel because it contains abundant thiophorase.
items.explain: The liver lacks succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase/SCOT), so it exports ketone bodies rather than oxidising them for its own energy.

items.text: During prolonged fasting, the brain can increase its use of ketone bodies as an energy source.
items.explain: Ketone bodies cross the blood-brain barrier and become an important alternative cerebral fuel during prolonged fasting, reducing but not eliminating the brain's glucose requirement.

items.text: The inguinal canal lies immediately superior to the medial part of the inguinal ligament.
items.explain: The inguinal canal is an oblique passage through the lower anterior abdominal wall, situated just above the inguinal ligament.

items.text: The anterior wall is formed mainly by the external oblique aponeurosis and is reinforced laterally by internal oblique fibres.
items.explain: The external oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall; laterally, internal oblique fibres provide additional reinforcement.

items.text: The posterior wall is formed mainly by transversalis fascia and is reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.
items.explain: The transversalis fascia forms the principal posterior wall, with medial reinforcement from the conjoint tendon in the usual anatomical description.

items.text: The deep inguinal ring lies medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
items.explain: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in transversalis fascia lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; an indirect inguinal hernia enters through it.

items.text: The inguinal ligament forms its superior boundary.
items.explain: The femoral triangle is bounded superiorly by the inguinal ligament, medially by adductor longus and laterally by sartorius.

items.text: The sartorius forms its medial boundary.
items.explain: Sartorius forms the lateral boundary; adductor longus forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle.

items.text: From lateral to medial, the principal contents are femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein and lymphatics.
items.explain: The familiar lateral-to-medial arrangement is nerve, artery, vein and lymphatics (NAVEL); the femoral nerve lies outside the femoral sheath.

items.text: The femoral nerve is enclosed within the femoral sheath alongside the femoral artery and vein.
items.explain: The femoral sheath encloses the femoral artery, femoral vein and femoral canal/lymphatics; the femoral nerve lies lateral to and outside the sheath.

items.text: Epithelial cells are usually closely packed, with relatively little intercellular matrix.
items.explain: Epithelia form continuous sheets of closely apposed cells, so the extracellular matrix between neighbouring epithelial cells is limited.

items.text: A typical epithelium contains blood vessels running between its epithelial cells.
items.explain: Epithelial tissue is avascular. It receives nutrients by diffusion from vessels in the underlying connective tissue across the basement membrane.

items.text: The basal surface of an epithelium is associated with a basement membrane.
items.explain: The basement membrane supports and anchors the epithelium and separates it from the underlying connective tissue.

items.text: Simple squamous epithelium is well suited to rapid diffusion across thin surfaces.
items.explain: Its single layer of flattened cells provides a short diffusion distance, as seen in alveoli and the endothelial lining of blood vessels.

items.text: Connective tissue generally contains cells embedded in an extracellular matrix.
items.explain: A defining feature of connective tissue is its extracellular matrix, composed of ground substance and fibres produced by resident cells.

items.text: Collagen fibres provide high tensile strength to many connective tissues.
items.explain: Collagen fibres resist stretching forces and contribute substantially to the tensile strength of tendons, ligaments, dermis and other connective tissues.

items.text: Mature cartilage is normally supplied directly by blood vessels within its matrix.
items.explain: Cartilage is avascular. Nutrients diffuse through its matrix from the perichondrium or, in articular cartilage, from synovial fluid.

items.text: Adipose tissue is a specialised form of connective tissue.
items.explain: Adipose tissue consists predominantly of adipocytes within a supporting connective-tissue framework and functions in energy storage, insulation and signalling.

questions.q: About the histology of blood vessels and the heart:

items.text: The tunica intima is the innermost layer of a typical blood vessel.
items.explain: The tunica intima lines the vascular lumen and includes endothelium with a thin supporting subendothelial layer.

items.text: The tunica media contains smooth muscle and may contain elastic fibres.
items.explain: The tunica media is composed chiefly of smooth muscle and elastic tissue, with its relative thickness varying among vessel types.

items.text: Veins generally have thicker tunica media than accompanying arteries of similar size.
items.explain: Arteries generally have a thicker tunica media to withstand and regulate higher pulsatile pressures; veins have thinner walls and larger lumens.

items.text: Cardiac muscle fibres are joined end-to-end by intercalated discs.
items.explain: Intercalated discs connect cardiomyocytes mechanically and electrically, helping the myocardium contract as a coordinated functional syncytium.

items.text: The first pharyngeal arch contributes to the maxilla and mandible through its maxillary and mandibular prominences.
items.explain: The first arch divides into maxillary and mandibular prominences, which contribute to much of the upper and lower jaw regions.

items.text: The muscles of mastication are derived from the first pharyngeal arch.
items.explain: First-arch mesenchyme gives rise to the muscles of mastication, supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

items.text: The facial nerve is the principal nerve of the second pharyngeal arch.
items.explain: The second arch is associated with the facial nerve (CN VII), which supplies its derivative muscles including muscles of facial expression.

items.text: The third pharyngeal arch is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.
items.explain: The third pharyngeal arch is associated with the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX); the hypoglossal nerve supplies most tongue muscles and is not the third-arch nerve.

items.text: Primary oocytes begin meiosis before birth and remain arrested in prophase I until maturation resumes.
items.explain: Oogonia enter meiosis during fetal life; primary oocytes remain arrested in prophase I, with selected oocytes resuming meiosis after puberty.

items.text: A secondary oocyte is normally ovulated while arrested in metaphase II.
items.explain: The LH surge leads to completion of meiosis I; the secondary oocyte begins meiosis II and is ovulated while arrested at metaphase II.

items.text: Spermatogenesis normally begins during fetal life and is completed before birth.
items.explain: Spermatogonial development begins before birth, but active spermatogenesis begins at puberty and continues through adult reproductive life.

items.text: Fertilisation usually occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube.
items.explain: The ampulla is the usual site of fertilisation, where sperm and the ovulated secondary oocyte commonly meet.

questions.q: Regarding renal regulation of acid-base balance:

items.text: The kidneys contribute to acid-base regulation by reabsorbing filtered bicarbonate.
items.explain: Reclaiming filtered bicarbonate prevents loss of this major extracellular buffer and is an important renal contribution to pH homeostasis.

items.text: Type A intercalated cells in the collecting duct can secrete hydrogen ions.
items.explain: Type A (alpha) intercalated cells secrete H+ into tubular fluid and return newly generated bicarbonate to the blood during acidosis.

items.text: The kidneys normally excrete most of the daily acid load as free hydrogen ions at very low urine pH.
items.explain: Because free H+ excretion is limited by the minimum achievable urine pH, most net acid is excreted buffered as ammonium and titratable acid.

items.text: Ammoniagenesis in the proximal tubule helps the kidney excrete acid as ammonium.
items.explain: Proximal tubular metabolism of glutamine generates ammonium for urinary excretion and new bicarbonate that can be returned to the circulation.

items.text: The detrusor muscle forms the muscular wall of the urinary bladder.
items.explain: The detrusor is the smooth muscle layer of the bladder wall and contracts to expel urine during voiding.

items.text: Parasympathetic outflow from sacral spinal segments promotes detrusor contraction.
items.explain: Pelvic parasympathetic nerves from S2–S4 activate muscarinic pathways that contract the detrusor during micturition.

items.text: The external urethral sphincter is composed of smooth muscle under involuntary control only.
items.explain: The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle under somatic control, allowing voluntary modulation of continence.

items.text: The pontine micturition centre coordinates bladder contraction with relaxation of the outlet.
items.explain: The pontine micturition centre coordinates detrusor activation and urethral sphincter relaxation so that bladder emptying is appropriately synchronised.

questions.q: Regarding the hypothalamus and pituitary gland:

items.text: The anterior pituitary is connected functionally to the hypothalamus through the hypophyseal portal circulation.
items.explain: Hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones reach the anterior pituitary through portal vessels in the pituitary stalk.

items.text: The posterior pituitary synthesises oxytocin and vasopressin in its own endocrine cells.
items.explain: Oxytocin and vasopressin are synthesised in hypothalamic neurons and transported down their axons for storage and release from the posterior pituitary.

items.text: Prolactin secretion is under tonic inhibitory control by hypothalamic dopamine.
items.explain: Dopamine from hypothalamic tuberoinfundibular neurons inhibits lactotrophs; reduced dopaminergic inhibition can therefore increase prolactin secretion.

items.text: Growth hormone secretion is stimulated by hypothalamic growth hormone-releasing hormone.
items.explain: GHRH stimulates anterior pituitary somatotrophs to release growth hormone, while somatostatin inhibits GH secretion.

items.text: The rapid depolarising phase of a typical neuronal action potential is mainly due to sodium influx through voltage-gated sodium channels.
items.explain: At threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium enters down its electrochemical gradient, producing the rapid upstroke.

items.text: The falling phase of a typical neuronal action potential is mainly associated with potassium efflux.
items.explain: Delayed opening of voltage-gated potassium channels permits K+ to leave the cell, driving repolarisation toward the resting potential.

items.text: The absolute refractory period occurs because all voltage-gated potassium channels are permanently closed.
items.explain: The absolute refractory period is primarily due to inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels, which must recover before another action potential can be initiated.

items.text: A stronger suprathreshold stimulus normally produces a larger-amplitude action potential in the same axon.
items.explain: Action potentials are all-or-none once threshold is reached; stimulus strength is generally encoded by firing frequency and recruitment rather than increased spike amplitude.

items.text: Arrival of an action potential at a presynaptic terminal can open voltage-gated calcium channels.
items.explain: Depolarisation of the presynaptic terminal opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, allowing calcium to enter the terminal.

items.text: Calcium entry into the presynaptic terminal helps trigger synaptic vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release.
items.explain: The local rise in presynaptic calcium activates the vesicle fusion machinery, leading to exocytosis of neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft.

items.text: Neurotransmitters cross the synaptic cleft mainly by travelling through a continuous cytoplasmic bridge between neurons.
items.explain: At a typical chemical synapse, the presynaptic and postsynaptic cells are separated by a synaptic cleft; neurotransmitter diffuses across this extracellular gap.

items.text: An inhibitory postsynaptic potential always results from sodium entering the postsynaptic cell.
items.explain: Inhibitory postsynaptic potentials commonly involve chloride entry or potassium exit, moving the membrane potential away from threshold or increasing membrane conductance.

items.text: DNA replication is described as semiconservative.
items.explain: Each daughter DNA molecule contains one parental strand and one newly synthesised strand, which is the defining semiconservative pattern.

items.text: DNA helicase helps separate the two strands of the parental DNA double helix.
items.explain: Helicase unwinds the parental double helix by disrupting the hydrogen bonding between complementary bases at the replication fork.

items.text: DNA polymerases generally synthesise a new DNA strand in the 3′ to 5′ direction.
items.explain: DNA polymerases add nucleotides to the 3′ hydroxyl end, so new DNA is synthesised in the 5′ to 3′ direction.

items.text: DNA ligase helps join adjacent DNA fragments by sealing breaks in the sugar-phosphate backbone.
items.explain: DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds that seal nicks between adjacent DNA fragments, including Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.

questions.q: Regarding vitamin B12 and folate metabolism:

items.text: Intrinsic factor is required for efficient absorption of dietary vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum.
items.explain: Vitamin B12 binds intrinsic factor in the upper gastrointestinal tract; the complex is recognised by receptors in the terminal ileum for absorption.

items.text: Vitamin B12 is required for methionine synthase activity.
items.explain: Methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin as a cofactor to transfer a methyl group from 5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, forming methionine.

items.text: Folate deficiency typically causes a raised methylmalonic acid concentration.
items.explain: Methylmalonic acid rises characteristically in vitamin B12 deficiency, not isolated folate deficiency; both deficiencies can raise homocysteine.

items.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause neurological abnormalities as well as megaloblastic anaemia.
items.explain: Cobalamin deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and can disrupt myelin maintenance, producing megaloblastic anaemia with potentially serious neurological manifestations.

items.text: Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells responsible for bone resorption.
items.explain: Osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells derived from the monocyte-macrophage lineage; they resorb mineralised bone using acid and proteolytic enzymes.

items.text: Osteoblasts produce osteoid, the unmineralised organic component of bone matrix.
items.explain: Osteoblasts synthesise osteoid, which is rich in type I collagen and other matrix proteins and subsequently undergoes mineralisation.

items.text: Osteocytes are mature bone cells located in lacunae within the mineralised matrix.
items.explain: Osteocytes are former osteoblasts enclosed within lacunae; their processes extend through canaliculi and help coordinate bone maintenance and mechanosensing.

items.text: The epiphyseal growth plate is composed mainly of fibrocartilage.
items.explain: The epiphyseal plate is hyaline cartilage organised into zones of chondrocyte proliferation, hypertrophy and matrix calcification before replacement by bone.

questions.q: About the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid:

items.text: The dura mater is the outermost meningeal covering of the brain.
items.explain: The cranial meninges are arranged from superficial to deep as dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater.

items.text: The subarachnoid space contains cerebrospinal fluid and major cerebral blood vessels.
items.explain: The subarachnoid space lies between arachnoid and pia and contains CSF, arteries and veins travelling over the surface of the brain.

items.text: Cerebrospinal fluid is produced mainly by the arachnoid granulations.
items.explain: Most CSF is produced by the choroid plexuses in the ventricles; arachnoid granulations are important sites for CSF absorption into dural venous sinuses.

items.text: The cerebral aqueduct connects the third and fourth ventricles.
items.explain: The cerebral aqueduct passes through the midbrain and connects the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle.

items.text: Type I pneumocytes form most of the thin alveolar surface across which gas exchange occurs.
items.explain: Type I alveolar cells are extremely thin squamous cells covering most of the alveolar surface and forming a major part of the air-blood barrier.

items.text: Type II pneumocytes secrete pulmonary surfactant.
items.explain: Type II pneumocytes produce and release surfactant, which reduces surface tension and helps prevent alveolar collapse.

items.text: Alveolar macrophages contribute to pulmonary defence by phagocytosing inhaled particles and microbes.
items.explain: Alveolar macrophages patrol the alveolar spaces and remove particles and microorganisms by phagocytosis.

items.text: The conducting portion of the respiratory tract is the principal site of oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.
items.explain: The conducting airways transport, warm, humidify and filter air; significant gas exchange occurs in the respiratory portion, especially alveoli.

items.text: Intramembranous ossification forms bone directly from mesenchymal tissue.
items.explain: In intramembranous ossification, mesenchymal cells differentiate into osteoblasts and lay down bone without a pre-existing cartilage model.

items.text: Endochondral ossification involves replacement of a hyaline cartilage model by bone.
items.explain: Most long bones develop by endochondral ossification, in which a cartilage template is progressively replaced by bone.

items.text: The clavicle develops entirely by endochondral ossification.
items.explain: The clavicle is unusual because most of it develops by intramembranous ossification, although its ends have endochondral contributions.

items.text: The primary ossification centre of a typical long bone appears in its diaphysis.
items.explain: The primary ossification centre usually develops in the shaft (diaphysis), while secondary centres commonly develop later in the epiphyses.

items.text: The P wave represents atrial depolarisation.
items.explain: The P wave reflects depolarisation spreading through the atrial myocardium before atrial contraction.

items.text: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation.
items.explain: The QRS complex records ventricular depolarisation; atrial repolarisation occurs at approximately the same time and is usually obscured.

items.text: The T wave represents ventricular repolarisation.
items.explain: The T wave reflects the process of ventricular myocardial repolarisation.

items.text: The PR interval is measured from the beginning of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave.
items.explain: The PR interval extends from the onset of the P wave to the onset of the QRS complex and reflects atrial-to-ventricular conduction time.

items.text: Cardiac output is the product of heart rate and stroke volume.
items.explain: Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by one ventricle per minute and is calculated as heart rate multiplied by stroke volume.

items.text: An increase in venous return can increase stroke volume through the Frank-Starling mechanism.
items.explain: Within physiological limits, greater ventricular filling stretches myocardial fibres and increases the force of contraction, raising stroke volume.

items.text: Ejection fraction is the proportion of end-diastolic volume ejected with each beat.
items.explain: Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, usually expressed as a percentage.

items.text: A rise in afterload always increases stroke volume in an otherwise unchanged ventricle.
items.explain: An acute increase in afterload tends to reduce stroke volume if contractility and preload are unchanged, because the ventricle must eject against a higher pressure.

questions.q: Regarding the ABO and Rh blood group systems:

items.text: Group A red cells express A antigen on their surface.
items.explain: Individuals with group A blood express A antigen on their red blood cells and usually have anti-B antibodies in plasma.

items.text: Group O red cells lack both A and B antigens.
items.explain: Group O erythrocytes lack A and B antigens, although the plasma normally contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.

items.text: An RhD-negative person has the D antigen on their red blood cells.
items.explain: RhD-negative individuals lack the D antigen; exposure to RhD-positive red cells can lead to anti-D alloimmunisation.

items.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin can help prevent RhD-negative mothers from becoming sensitised to fetal RhD-positive red cells.
items.explain: Prophylactic anti-D binds fetal RhD-positive red cells entering maternal circulation and reduces the risk of maternal immune sensitisation.

items.text: Leydig cells in the testes produce testosterone in response to luteinising hormone.
items.explain: LH acts on Leydig cells to stimulate testosterone synthesis; FSH acts mainly on Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules.

items.text: Sertoli cells support developing germ cells and respond to follicle-stimulating hormone.
items.explain: Sertoli cells provide structural and metabolic support to spermatogenic cells and respond to FSH; they also produce inhibin B.

items.text: Inhibin from the gonads selectively suppresses pituitary FSH secretion.
items.explain: Inhibin provides negative feedback that preferentially reduces FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary.

items.text: Testosterone is produced mainly by Sertoli cells in response to FSH.
items.explain: Testosterone is produced mainly by Leydig cells under LH stimulation; Sertoli cells support spermatogenesis and secrete inhibin and androgen-binding protein.

items.text: Adult haemoglobin A is composed of two alpha and two beta globin chains.
items.explain: HbA, the predominant adult haemoglobin, is an alpha-2 beta-2 tetramer, with each globin chain carrying a haem group.

items.text: Each haem group contains an iron atom in the ferrous (Fe2+) state when binding oxygen normally.
items.explain: Functional haemoglobin contains ferrous iron, Fe2+, which reversibly binds oxygen; oxidation to Fe3+ produces methaemoglobin.

items.text: Heme degradation in macrophages produces biliverdin, which is then converted to bilirubin.
items.explain: Reticuloendothelial macrophages degrade haem to biliverdin through haem oxygenase; biliverdin reductase then forms unconjugated bilirubin.

items.text: Unconjugated bilirubin is freely water-soluble and is excreted directly in urine under normal conditions.
items.explain: Unconjugated bilirubin is poorly water-soluble and circulates bound to albumin; after hepatic conjugation, bilirubin becomes more water-soluble and is secreted into bile.

items.text: The phospholipid bilayer forms the basic structural framework of most cell membranes.
items.explain: Amphipathic phospholipids arrange into a bilayer with hydrophilic heads facing aqueous environments and hydrophobic tails directed inward.

items.text: Cholesterol can influence membrane fluidity and permeability.
items.explain: Cholesterol intercalates between phospholipids and modulates membrane fluidity and permeability in a temperature-dependent manner.

items.text: Integral membrane proteins can be removed from the lipid bilayer simply by changing the ionic strength of the surrounding solution.
items.explain: Integral membrane proteins are embedded in or span the hydrophobic bilayer and usually require detergents or other disruptive methods for extraction; peripheral proteins are more readily removed by changing ionic conditions.

items.text: The plasma membrane is selectively permeable rather than freely permeable to all dissolved substances.
items.explain: The lipid bilayer and its transport proteins regulate movement of ions and molecules, allowing selective exchange between the cell and its environment.

items.text: Platelets adhere to exposed subendothelial structures during primary haemostasis.
items.explain: Vascular injury exposes subendothelial matrix; von Willebrand factor helps platelets adhere, initiating platelet activation and aggregation.

items.text: Thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin.
items.explain: Thrombin cleaves fibrinopeptides from fibrinogen, allowing fibrin monomers to polymerise and form the clot framework.

items.text: Vitamin K is required for gamma-carboxylation of several coagulation factors.
items.explain: Vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation enables factors II, VII, IX and X, as well as proteins C and S, to bind calcium and function on phospholipid surfaces.

items.text: Heparin produces anticoagulation mainly by directly dissolving an already formed fibrin clot.
items.explain: Heparin potentiates antithrombin and inhibits activated coagulation factors, especially thrombin and factor Xa; it is an anticoagulant, not a fibrinolytic drug.

items.text: Negative feedback generally opposes a change in a regulated variable.
items.explain: Negative feedback responses act to reduce deviations from a regulated set point or operating range, helping maintain internal stability.

items.text: In a typical homeostatic control system, receptors detect changes in the regulated variable.
items.explain: Receptors or sensors detect a stimulus and send information to an integrating centre, which coordinates an appropriate effector response.

items.text: Positive feedback is the usual mechanism for maintaining most physiological variables within a stable range.
items.explain: Most routine homeostatic regulation relies on negative feedback; positive feedback amplifies a change and is used in specific processes such as labour and blood clotting.

items.text: The hypothalamus participates in regulation of body temperature.
items.explain: The hypothalamus integrates thermal information and coordinates autonomic, endocrine and behavioural responses that help regulate body temperature.

items.text: Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of individual cells.
items.explain: Hypertrophy increases cell size and therefore can enlarge an organ without increasing cell number.

items.text: Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells in a tissue.
items.explain: Hyperplasia results from increased cell proliferation and may occur physiologically or pathologically.

items.text: Metaplasia is always an irreversible change and inevitably progresses to cancer.
items.explain: Metaplasia is an adaptive, potentially reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another; persistent stimuli may increase neoplastic risk but progression is not inevitable.

items.text: Atrophy may involve reduced cell size and, in some tissues, reduced cell number.
items.explain: Atrophy can result from decreased workload, denervation, reduced blood supply, inadequate nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation or ageing.

items.text: Coagulative necrosis is commonly associated with ischaemic infarction in solid organs, except the brain.
items.explain: Ischaemia in most solid organs produces coagulative necrosis; cerebral infarction typically produces liquefactive necrosis.

items.text: Liquefactive necrosis is characterised by enzymatic digestion of dead cells into a liquid mass.
items.explain: Hydrolytic enzymes digest the tissue, classically in bacterial or fungal infections and in brain infarction.

items.text: Apoptosis typically causes marked inflammation in surrounding tissue.
items.explain: Apoptotic cells are usually packaged into membrane-bound bodies and rapidly cleared, generally provoking little inflammation.

items.text: Necrosis commonly involves loss of plasma-membrane integrity and leakage of intracellular contents.
items.explain: Membrane damage releases cellular contents and can trigger an inflammatory response in surrounding tissue.

items.text: Vasodilation contributes to increased blood flow at an acutely inflamed site.
items.explain: Vascular changes increase local blood flow and contribute to redness and heat.

items.text: Increased vascular permeability allows protein-rich fluid to enter the extravascular tissue.
