items.explain: Endothelial gaps and other permeability changes permit plasma proteins and fluid to escape, producing an exudate.

items.text: Neutrophils are commonly prominent early cellular responders in acute inflammation.
items.explain: Neutrophils are rapidly recruited from the circulation and are typical early effector cells in acute inflammation.

items.text: Histamine generally causes sustained arteriolar vasoconstriction at the site of acute inflammation.
items.explain: Histamine is an important mediator of vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, not sustained arteriolar vasoconstriction.

items.text: A benign neoplasm generally remains localised and does not metastasise.
items.explain: Benign tumours may cause harm by compression or hormone production, but by definition they do not metastasise.

items.text: Malignant neoplasms have the capacity to invade surrounding tissues.
items.explain: Invasion into adjacent tissue is a defining feature of malignancy.

items.text: All malignant tumours arise from epithelial tissue and are therefore carcinomas.
items.explain: Malignant tumours may arise from epithelial, mesenchymal, haematolymphoid and other cell lineages; carcinoma refers specifically to malignant epithelial neoplasms.

items.text: Metastasis is the development of tumour deposits discontinuous with the primary tumour.
items.explain: Metastasis describes spread to anatomically discontinuous sites, through lymphatic, haematogenous or other routes.

items.text: Pharmacokinetics describes the absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion of drugs.
items.explain: These four processes are commonly summarised as ADME and describe how the body handles a drug.

items.text: Bioavailability is the fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged.
items.explain: For an intravenous dose, bioavailability is conventionally 100%; oral bioavailability may be reduced by incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism.

items.text: The oral route completely avoids first-pass metabolism by the liver.
items.explain: Many orally absorbed drugs pass through the portal circulation and liver before reaching systemic circulation, where presystemic metabolism may occur.

items.text: A drug's volume of distribution is a proportionality term relating the amount of drug in the body to its plasma concentration.
items.explain: Apparent volume of distribution is calculated as the amount of drug in the body divided by plasma drug concentration; it is not necessarily an anatomical fluid volume.

items.text: Pharmacodynamics concerns the effects of drugs on the body and their mechanisms of action.
items.explain: It includes receptor interactions, mechanisms, dose-response relationships and the resulting biological effects.

items.text: A full agonist can produce the maximal response of a system under the conditions studied.
items.explain: A full agonist has sufficient efficacy to produce the system's maximal response in the assay or physiological system.

items.text: In the classical model, a reversible competitive antagonist shifts the agonist dose-response curve to the right without reducing the maximum response when sufficient agonist is given.
items.explain: A reversible competitive antagonist competes with agonist at the same receptor site. Increasing agonist concentration can overcome the antagonism in the classical equilibrium model, increasing the concentration needed for a given response while preserving Emax.

items.text: Potency and efficacy describe the same pharmacological property.
items.explain: Potency concerns the dose or concentration needed for an effect, whereas efficacy concerns the maximum effect a drug can produce.

items.text: For a drug following first-order elimination, a constant fraction of the drug is eliminated per unit time.
items.explain: First-order elimination rate is proportional to drug concentration, so the fraction eliminated per unit time is constant.

items.text: For a drug with first-order kinetics, the elimination half-life is generally independent of concentration.
items.explain: With linear first-order elimination and constant clearance and distribution volume, half-life remains constant over the relevant concentration range.

items.text: Zero-order elimination removes a constant fraction of the drug per unit time.
items.explain: Zero-order elimination removes a constant amount per unit time when elimination pathways are saturated, rather than a constant fraction.

items.text: Reduced renal function can prolong the elimination of drugs that depend substantially on renal excretion.
items.explain: Lower renal clearance may increase drug exposure and prolong half-life, requiring dose or interval adjustment for some medicines.

questions.q: About adverse drug effects and medicine safety:

items.text: An adverse drug reaction is a harmful or unintended response to a medicine used at normally intended doses.
items.explain: This describes the conventional definition of an adverse drug reaction; harm from overdose or medication error is classified separately in many frameworks.

items.text: A drug with a narrow therapeutic index may require closer monitoring because the effective and toxic concentration ranges are relatively close.
items.explain: Small changes in exposure can cause loss of efficacy or toxicity, so monitoring and careful dose adjustment may be important.

items.text: A side effect is necessarily harmful and always requires discontinuation of the medicine.
items.explain: Side effects may be unwanted but are not invariably serious or a reason to stop treatment; management depends on severity, benefit and alternatives.

items.text: Drug interactions can alter pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics or both.
items.explain: Interactions may affect absorption, metabolism or elimination, or modify effects at receptors and physiological systems.

items.text: Oedema is the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the interstitial tissues or body cavities.
items.explain: Oedema describes excess fluid in the interstitial compartment; fluid accumulation in a body cavity may be termed an effusion.

items.text: Increased hydrostatic pressure in the venous circulation can contribute to oedema.
items.explain: Raised venous pressure increases capillary hydrostatic pressure and favours filtration of fluid into the interstitium.

items.text: Reduced plasma albumin concentration tends to oppose the development of oedema.
items.explain: Albumin is a major contributor to plasma colloid osmotic pressure; hypoalbuminaemia lowers this force and favours movement of fluid out of capillaries.

items.text: Virchow's triad includes endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow and hypercoagulability.
items.explain: These three broad factors promote thrombosis: endothelial injury, stasis or turbulence, and increased tendency of blood to clot.

questions.q: About laboratory assessment of diabetes mellitus:

items.text: A laboratory HbA1c result of 6.5% or higher is one accepted diagnostic criterion for diabetes in nonpregnant adults.
items.explain: An HbA1c at or above 6.5% (48 mmol/mol), measured with an appropriately standardised laboratory method, meets a recognised diagnostic threshold.

items.text: A fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or higher is a diagnostic threshold for diabetes in nonpregnant adults.
items.explain: The fasting threshold is 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) after at least eight hours without caloric intake.

items.text: A random plasma glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or higher establishes diabetes in every asymptomatic person without further confirmation.
items.explain: Random plasma glucose at or above 11.1 mmol/L is diagnostic when accompanied by classic hyperglycaemic symptoms or a hyperglycaemic crisis; in an asymptomatic person, confirmation is generally required.

items.text: A 2-hour plasma glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or higher during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test is a diagnostic criterion.
items.explain: The 2-hour value of at least 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) after a 75-g oral glucose load is an accepted diagnostic threshold.

items.text: Iron deficiency commonly produces a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia when sufficiently established.
items.explain: Reduced haemoglobin synthesis leads to smaller red cells with increased central pallor, although early iron deficiency may not yet be microcytic.

items.text: Serum ferritin is generally reduced in uncomplicated absolute iron deficiency.
items.explain: Ferritin reflects iron stores and is usually low when body iron stores are depleted; inflammation can complicate interpretation because ferritin is an acute-phase reactant.

items.text: Total iron-binding capacity is typically reduced in uncomplicated iron deficiency.
items.explain: Transferrin and total iron-binding capacity are commonly increased in iron deficiency, while serum iron and transferrin saturation fall.

items.text: A normal haemoglobin concentration always excludes iron deficiency.
items.explain: Iron stores can become depleted before haemoglobin falls, so iron deficiency may precede overt anaemia.

items.text: Intravenous administration provides complete systemic bioavailability for the administered dose.
items.explain: An intravenous dose enters systemic circulation directly, so its systemic bioavailability is conventionally 100%.

items.text: Sublingual administration can avoid hepatic first-pass metabolism.
items.explain: Drug absorbed through the oral mucosa drains into systemic venous circulation rather than first entering the hepatic portal circulation.

items.text: Intramuscular administration bypasses the need for absorption before a drug reaches systemic circulation.
items.explain: An intramuscular drug must be absorbed from muscle tissue into the circulation; the rate depends on formulation and local perfusion.

items.text: The oral route is suitable for every patient, including those who are unconscious or unable to swallow safely.
items.explain: Oral administration may be unsafe or impractical in an unconscious patient or one with impaired swallowing and aspiration risk.

items.text: Muscarinic receptor activation can produce bradycardia and increased gastrointestinal motility.
items.explain: Muscarinic receptor effects include slowing of the heart and stimulation of gastrointestinal smooth muscle and secretions.

items.text: Atropine is a muscarinic receptor antagonist.
items.explain: Atropine competitively blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and reduces parasympathetic effects at target organs.

items.text: Neostigmine increases acetylcholine availability by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase.
items.explain: Neostigmine is a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, so acetylcholine persists longer at cholinergic synapses.

items.text: A muscarinic antagonist such as atropine typically causes miosis and increased salivation.
items.explain: Muscarinic blockade commonly causes mydriasis and reduced secretions, including dry mouth.

items.text: Stimulation of beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart increases heart rate and contractility.
items.explain: Cardiac beta-1 receptor activation increases chronotropy and inotropy, raising cardiac work and output.

items.text: Stimulation of beta-2 adrenergic receptors in bronchial smooth muscle promotes bronchodilation.
items.explain: Beta-2 receptor activation relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and is the basis for the bronchodilator action of drugs such as salbutamol.

items.text: Phenylephrine produces its principal decongestant effect through alpha-1 receptor-mediated vasoconstriction.
items.explain: Alpha-1 receptor activation constricts vascular smooth muscle in nasal mucosa, reducing mucosal congestion.

items.text: A non-selective beta blocker such as propranolol selectively blocks beta-1 receptors while sparing beta-2 receptors.
items.explain: Propranolol blocks both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors; beta-2 blockade can provoke bronchoconstriction in susceptible patients.

questions.q: About the pathology of acute myocardial infarction:

items.text: Acute myocardial infarction commonly follows acute coronary thrombosis after rupture or erosion of an atherosclerotic plaque.
items.explain: Plaque disruption exposes thrombogenic material and can trigger thrombus formation that acutely reduces coronary blood flow.

items.text: Prolonged myocardial ischaemia typically produces coagulative necrosis.
items.explain: Ischaemic injury in most solid organs, including myocardium, produces coagulative necrosis; the brain is a notable exception.

items.text: Neutrophils are typically absent from the infarcted myocardium during the first day after infarction.
items.explain: Neutrophilic infiltration is an early histological feature and is commonly seen within the first 12–24 hours.

items.text: The infarcted myocardium is ultimately replaced by a collagenous scar because adult cardiac muscle has very limited regenerative capacity.
items.explain: Necrotic myocardium is cleared and repaired by granulation tissue and collagen deposition rather than meaningful regeneration of contractile cardiomyocytes.

items.text: Furosemide inhibits the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.
items.explain: Loop diuretics inhibit NKCC2 on the luminal membrane of the thick ascending limb, reducing sodium chloride reabsorption.

items.text: Thiazide diuretics inhibit the Na⁺-Cl⁻ cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule.
items.explain: Thiazides inhibit NCC in the distal convoluted tubule, increasing sodium and chloride excretion.

items.text: Thiazide diuretics generally increase urinary calcium excretion more than loop diuretics.
items.explain: Thiazides tend to increase calcium reabsorption and reduce urinary calcium, whereas loop diuretics increase calcium excretion.

items.text: Spironolactone acts by antagonising mineralocorticoid receptors in the distal nephron.
items.explain: Spironolactone competitively blocks aldosterone receptors in principal cells, reducing sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.

items.text: ACE inhibitors reduce the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
items.explain: They inhibit ACE, reducing formation of the potent vasoconstrictor angiotensin II.

items.text: Reduced angiotensin II formation can decrease aldosterone secretion.
items.explain: Lower angiotensin II reduces stimulation of the adrenal zona glomerulosa, lowering aldosterone release.

items.text: ACE inhibitors increase bradykinin degradation.
items.explain: ACE also degrades bradykinin; inhibiting ACE can increase bradykinin concentrations, contributing to cough and angioedema risk.

items.text: Dilation of the renal efferent arteriole can reduce intraglomerular pressure during ACE inhibitor treatment.
items.explain: Reduced angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction lowers intraglomerular pressure and may reduce albuminuria in appropriate patients.

items.text: Beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking by binding penicillin-binding proteins.
items.explain: Their beta-lactam ring acylates transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins), inhibiting the final cross-linking step in peptidoglycan synthesis.

items.text: Beta-lactam antibiotics act primarily by inhibiting bacterial ribosomal protein synthesis.
items.explain: They target cell-wall synthesis, whereas drugs such as tetracyclines and macrolides act on bacterial ribosomes.

items.text: Beta-lactamase production is one mechanism by which bacteria can resist beta-lactam antibiotics.
items.explain: Beta-lactamases hydrolyse the beta-lactam ring and can inactivate susceptible agents.

items.text: Vancomycin is a beta-lactam antibiotic that inhibits penicillin-binding proteins in the same way as penicillin.
items.explain: Vancomycin is a glycopeptide; it binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini of peptidoglycan precursors rather than acting as a beta-lactam PBP acylator.

questions.q: About the tissue changes in acute ischaemic stroke:

items.text: An arterial occlusion can produce an ischaemic core surrounded by potentially salvageable penumbral tissue.
items.explain: Blood flow is most severely reduced in the core; surrounding tissue may be dysfunctional but viable for a limited period.

items.text: ATP depletion during cerebral ischaemia impairs membrane ion pumps.
items.explain: Failure of energy-dependent ion transport causes depolarisation and contributes to cellular swelling.

items.text: Excessive glutamate release and calcium influx contribute to ischaemic neuronal injury.
items.explain: Excitotoxic signalling and intracellular calcium overload promote oxidative stress and cell-death pathways.

items.text: The ischaemic penumbra is already irreversibly necrotic in every patient at the moment symptoms begin.
items.explain: The penumbra is potentially salvageable tissue; its survival depends on residual perfusion, collateral flow and time.

questions.q: About the pathological changes in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease:

items.text: Emphysema involves permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles with destruction of their walls.
items.explain: Loss of alveolar septa reduces elastic recoil and contributes to airflow limitation.

items.text: Chronic bronchitis is associated with increased mucus production and enlargement of bronchial submucosal glands.
items.explain: Goblet-cell metaplasia and submucosal gland hypertrophy contribute to mucus hypersecretion.

items.text: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is associated particularly with panacinar emphysema.
items.explain: Reduced antiprotease protection permits elastase-mediated alveolar destruction, classically with lower-lobe predominance.

items.text: Digital clubbing is a typical defining physical sign of uncomplicated COPD.
items.explain: Clubbing is not typical of COPD; its presence should prompt assessment for another condition such as lung cancer or bronchiectasis.

questions.q: About the pathological consequences of urinary tract obstruction:

items.text: Urinary obstruction can cause back-pressure dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces.
items.explain: Hydronephrosis describes dilatation of the renal collecting system due to impaired urine drainage.

items.text: Persistent obstruction can cause tubular atrophy and loss of functioning nephrons.
items.explain: Sustained increased intrarenal pressure and associated injury can produce progressive parenchymal damage.

items.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is one possible cause of lower urinary tract obstruction.
items.explain: Prostatic enlargement can impede bladder outflow, particularly in older men.

items.text: Relief of a longstanding complete obstruction always restores renal function fully.
items.explain: Recovery depends on duration, severity and underlying damage; prolonged obstruction may leave irreversible renal impairment.

questions.q: About calcium channel blockers used in cardiovascular disease:

items.text: Calcium channel blockers inhibit L-type voltage-gated calcium channels.
items.explain: These drugs reduce calcium entry through L-type channels in vascular smooth muscle and, to varying degrees, cardiac tissue.

items.text: Dihydropyridines such as amlodipine act predominantly as peripheral arteriolar vasodilators at usual doses.
items.explain: Their vascular selectivity reduces systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure.

items.text: Verapamil and diltiazem can slow atrioventricular nodal conduction.
items.explain: Non-dihydropyridines have clinically important effects on SA/AV nodal activity and cardiac contractility.

items.text: Verapamil commonly causes diarrhoea rather than constipation.
items.explain: Constipation is a recognised adverse effect of verapamil; diarrhoea is not its characteristic gastrointestinal effect.

questions.q: About the cellular and tissue features of inflammation:

items.text: Neutrophils commonly predominate in the early cellular infiltrate of acute inflammation.
items.explain: Neutrophils are typically the predominant leukocytes during the first 6–24 hours of an acute inflammatory response.

items.text: Monocytes and macrophages commonly become more prominent after the initial neutrophilic response.
items.explain: Monocytes enter the tissue and differentiate into macrophages, which become more prominent around 24–48 hours and help clear debris.

items.text: Chronic inflammation is characterised exclusively by neutrophils and has no associated tissue repair.
items.explain: Chronic inflammation typically involves macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells, with ongoing tissue injury and attempts at repair such as fibrosis.

items.text: Complete resolution is the inevitable outcome of every episode of acute inflammation.
items.explain: Outcome depends on the extent of injury, tissue regenerative capacity and persistence of the stimulus; fibrosis or progression to chronic inflammation may occur.

questions.q: About the causes and pathology of peptic ulcer disease:

items.text: Helicobacter pylori infection is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease.
items.explain: H. pylori is one of the two major causes of peptic ulcer disease, alongside NSAID-associated mucosal injury.

items.text: NSAIDs can promote gastric ulceration by reducing protective prostaglandin synthesis.
items.explain: Cyclo-oxygenase inhibition reduces prostaglandin-mediated mucus and bicarbonate secretion, mucosal blood flow and epithelial protection.

items.text: H. pylori-associated chronic gastritis can progress through atrophy and intestinal metaplasia to gastric adenocarcinoma.
items.explain: In a subset of patients, chronic active gastritis may progress through atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia before adenocarcinoma.

items.text: A peptic ulcer is limited to superficial epithelial erosion and does not breach the muscularis mucosae.
items.explain: A peptic ulcer is deeper than an erosion: it breaches the muscularis mucosae and extends into the submucosa or deeper tissue.

questions.q: About the renal pathology of diabetic nephropathy:

items.text: Thickening of the glomerular basement membrane is among the characteristic structural changes of diabetic nephropathy.
items.explain: Glomerular basement membrane thickening is an early characteristic lesion and may be present before clinically apparent albuminuria.

items.text: Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules represent nodular glomerulosclerosis.
items.explain: These nodular mesangial lesions are the characteristic light-microscopic feature of class III diabetic nephropathy.

items.text: Arteriolar hyalinosis in diabetic nephropathy is restricted to the efferent arteriole.
items.explain: Hyalinosis may affect both afferent and efferent arterioles; involvement of both is a useful pathological clue.

items.text: The presence of Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules is required for every case of advanced diabetic renal dysfunction.
items.explain: Diabetic kidney disease can progress with diffuse glomerulosclerosis and tubulointerstitial injury; nodules are characteristic but are not required for severe dysfunction.

questions.q: About beta-2 adrenergic agonists used in obstructive airway disease:

items.text: Activation of beta-2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle increases intracellular cyclic AMP.
items.explain: Beta-2 receptor coupling to Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP and promoting smooth-muscle relaxation.

items.text: Salbutamol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used for rapid relief of bronchospasm.
items.explain: Inhaled salbutamol acts rapidly and is commonly used as a short-acting bronchodilator for symptom relief.

items.text: Tremor, tachycardia and hypokalaemia can occur with beta-2 agonist treatment.
items.explain: Systemic beta-adrenergic effects can produce skeletal-muscle tremor, cardiovascular stimulation and intracellular potassium shift.

items.text: Long-acting beta-2 agonists should be used alone for routine asthma control without inhaled corticosteroid therapy.
items.explain: In asthma, LABAs should not be used as monotherapy; they are used with inhaled corticosteroid treatment to address airway inflammation and reduce risk.

questions.q: About artemisinin-based combination therapy for malaria:

items.text: Artemisinin-based combination therapies pair an artemisinin derivative with a partner antimalarial drug.
items.explain: ACTs combine an artemisinin derivative with a partner medicine that has a complementary role in clearing residual parasites.

items.text: The artemisinin component rapidly reduces the parasite biomass during the first few days of treatment.
items.explain: Artemisinin derivatives rapidly reduce circulating parasite numbers, while the partner drug helps eliminate remaining parasites.

items.text: Oral artemisinin derivatives should routinely be prescribed as monotherapy for uncomplicated falciparum malaria.
items.explain: WHO recommends combination treatment; oral artemisinin monotherapy contributes to resistance and is not recommended.

items.text: WHO recommends confirming suspected malaria parasitologically with microscopy or a rapid diagnostic test before treatment whenever testing is available.
items.explain: WHO recommends parasitological confirmation before antimalarial treatment when diagnostic testing is accessible.

questions.q: About the biological behaviour and spread of neoplasms:

items.text: Anaplasia refers to a lack of differentiation in neoplastic cells.
items.explain: Anaplasia is loss of structural and functional differentiation and is a feature of many malignant neoplasms.

items.text: Metastasis is unequivocal evidence that a neoplasm is malignant.
items.explain: A benign tumour does not metastasise; demonstration of metastasis establishes malignant behaviour, although many malignant tumours have not metastasised when first diagnosed.

items.text: Carcinomas usually spread through lymphatic vessels, whereas sarcomas commonly spread haematogenously.
items.explain: This is the usual pattern, although important exceptions occur and either route may be used by malignant tumours.

items.text: A well-differentiated tumour is necessarily benign.
items.explain: Some malignant tumours are well differentiated; differentiation alone does not establish benign behaviour.

questions.q: About thyroid follicular adenomas and carcinomas:

items.text: Follicular thyroid carcinoma is diagnosed by demonstrating capsular and/or vascular invasion.
items.explain: Invasion through the tumour capsule and/or into blood vessels distinguishes follicular carcinoma from follicular adenoma.

items.text: Fine-needle aspiration cytology alone can reliably distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma.
items.explain: Cytology cannot assess capsular or vascular invasion; definitive distinction generally requires histological examination of the excised lesion.

items.text: Papillary thyroid carcinoma commonly shows optically clear nuclei with grooves and intranuclear inclusions.
items.explain: These nuclear features are characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma.

items.text: Papillary thyroid carcinoma typically spreads predominantly by haematogenous dissemination to bone and lung.
items.explain: Papillary thyroid carcinoma commonly spreads through lymphatics to regional cervical lymph nodes; follicular carcinoma more often spreads haematogenously.

questions.q: About the inherited coagulation disorders haemophilia A and B:

items.text: Haemophilia A results from deficiency or dysfunction of coagulation factor VIII.
items.explain: Haemophilia A is caused by pathogenic variants affecting the F8 gene and reduced or dysfunctional factor VIII.

items.text: Haemophilia B is caused by deficiency of coagulation factor IX.
items.explain: Haemophilia B, also called Christmas disease, results from factor IX deficiency or dysfunction.

items.text: Both haemophilia A and haemophilia B usually produce an isolated prolongation of prothrombin time.
items.explain: They affect the intrinsic pathway and typically prolong the activated partial thromboplastin time; prothrombin time is usually normal.

items.text: Haemophilia A and B are commonly inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern.
items.explain: Both are classically X-linked recessive disorders, so affected males and carrier females are typical inheritance patterns.

questions.q: About the anticoagulant drugs heparin and warfarin:

items.text: Unfractionated heparin enhances the activity of antithrombin, particularly against thrombin and factor Xa.
items.explain: Heparin binds antithrombin and accelerates inhibition of activated coagulation factors, especially thrombin and factor Xa.

items.text: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase and reduces the regeneration of active vitamin K.
items.explain: Warfarin inhibits VKORC1, impairing gamma-carboxylation and functional production of factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S.

items.text: The anticoagulant effect of warfarin is routinely monitored using the activated partial thromboplastin time.
items.explain: Warfarin is monitored using the prothrombin time expressed as the international normalised ratio (INR).

items.text: Protamine sulphate can be used to reverse the anticoagulant effect of unfractionated heparin.
items.explain: Protamine forms a stable complex with heparin and neutralises much of its anticoagulant activity.

items.text: Insulin promotes glucose uptake in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue by increasing GLUT4 translocation to the cell membrane.
items.explain: Insulin receptor signalling promotes GLUT4 vesicle translocation in insulin-sensitive skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.

items.text: Insulin stimulates hepatic glycogen synthesis and suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis.
items.explain: Insulin promotes glycogen storage and suppresses hepatic glucose production through effects on metabolic enzymes and gene expression.

items.text: Hypoglycaemia is an important dose-related adverse effect of insulin therapy.
items.explain: Excess insulin relative to food intake, activity or physiological requirements can cause clinically significant hypoglycaemia.

items.text: All insulin preparations are suitable for intravenous administration in the treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis.
items.explain: Regular (soluble) insulin is used intravenously for DKA; long-acting preparations are not interchangeable for IV use.

questions.q: About the mechanisms of hypersensitivity reactions:

items.text: Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by allergen-specific IgE bound to mast cells and basophils.
items.explain: On re-exposure, allergen cross-links cell-bound IgE and triggers mediator release from mast cells and basophils.

items.text: Type II hypersensitivity typically involves antibodies directed against cell-surface or extracellular-matrix antigens.
items.explain: IgG or IgM can cause cell injury, inflammation or altered receptor function by binding to these targets.

items.text: Type III hypersensitivity is caused primarily by antigen-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
items.explain: Type III reactions are driven by deposited antigen-antibody immune complexes; T-cell-mediated injury characterises type IV reactions.

items.text: Type IV hypersensitivity is mediated by sensitised T lymphocytes rather than antibodies.
items.explain: Delayed-type reactions involve T-cell cytokines and/or cytotoxic T-cell activity, typically developing over 48–72 hours.

items.text: HIV is an enveloped retrovirus with an RNA genome.
items.explain: HIV belongs to the retrovirus family and carries two copies of positive-sense single-stranded RNA.

items.text: HIV reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA into DNA after entry into a susceptible cell.
items.explain: The resulting viral DNA can be transported into the nucleus and integrated into host-cell DNA.

items.text: The viral envelope glycoprotein gp120 binds to CD4 and a chemokine co-receptor during cell entry.
items.explain: After CD4 attachment, gp120 engages CCR5 or CXCR4, facilitating the conformational changes required for fusion.

items.text: HIV primarily targets mature erythrocytes because they express abundant CD4 receptors.
items.explain: HIV targets CD4-expressing cells, particularly CD4 T lymphocytes and cells of the monocyte/macrophage lineage; mature erythrocytes lack nuclei and CD4 receptors.

questions.q: About commonly used systemic antifungal drugs:

items.text: Azole antifungals inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase and impair ergosterol synthesis.
items.explain: Inhibition of this cytochrome P450 enzyme disrupts ergosterol production and fungal cell-membrane function.

items.text: Amphotericin B binds ergosterol in fungal membranes and promotes membrane pore formation.
items.explain: Binding to ergosterol increases membrane permeability, causing leakage of intracellular contents.

items.text: Echinocandins inhibit synthesis of beta-(1,3)-D-glucan in the fungal cell wall.
items.explain: They inhibit the glucan synthase complex, weakening the fungal cell wall.

items.text: Flucytosine acts by directly inhibiting human thymidylate synthase after conversion by human cells.
items.explain: Fungal cells convert flucytosine to fluorinated metabolites, including 5-fluorouracil derivatives, which interfere with fungal RNA and DNA synthesis.

items.text: Valproate can increase central nervous system GABA concentrations.
items.explain: Its antiseizure actions include enhancement of GABAergic inhibition, alongside effects on voltage-gated ion channels.

items.text: Valproate can reduce high-frequency neuronal firing by affecting voltage-gated sodium channels.
items.explain: Use-dependent inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels contributes to its broad-spectrum antiseizure activity.

items.text: Exposure to valproate during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of neural tube defects.
items.explain: Valproate is a significant teratogen; prenatal exposure is associated with neural tube defects and other adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes.

items.text: Valproate is a suitable first-choice antiseizure medicine for every pregnant patient because it has no clinically important fetal risks.
items.explain: Valproate carries substantial fetal risks and should generally be avoided in pregnancy when clinically appropriate alternatives are available.

questions.q: About rational prescribing and the selection of medicines:

items.text: A rational prescription should be based on a clearly defined clinical problem and an appropriate therapeutic objective.
items.explain: The prescriber should identify the patient's problem, define the treatment goal and select a suitable intervention.

items.text: The prescriber's personal formulary or P-drug selection should take account of efficacy, safety, suitability and cost.
items.explain: A P-drug is selected for a defined indication using these practical criteria, then tailored to the individual patient.

items.text: Writing a generic medicine name can reduce ambiguity when equivalent products are available.
items.explain: Generic prescribing identifies the active ingredient and can reduce confusion caused by multiple brand names.

items.text: Once a medicine has been prescribed, checking adherence and monitoring response are unnecessary if the initial diagnosis was correct.
items.explain: Rational prescribing includes follow-up: assess effectiveness, adverse effects, adherence and whether treatment should be continued, changed or stopped.

questions.q: About the structure of the skin:

items.text: The epidermis is derived from surface ectoderm.
items.explain: The epidermis develops from ectoderm; the dermis has region-dependent mesodermal contributions.

items.text: The epidermis is avascular.
items.explain: It receives nutrients by diffusion from vessels in the underlying dermis.

items.text: The hypodermis is always considered part of the skin proper.
items.explain: The subcutaneous tissue lies deep to the dermis and is usually distinguished from skin proper.

items.text: Thick skin of the palms and soles lacks hair follicles and sebaceous glands.
items.explain: Glabrous thick skin has a prominent epidermis and lacks these appendages.

questions.q: About the histological features of muscle tissue:

items.text: Skeletal muscle fibres are multinucleated and have peripherally placed nuclei.
items.explain: Skeletal myoblasts fuse to form multinucleated fibres with peripheral nuclei.

items.text: Cardiac muscle cells are joined end-to-end by intercalated discs.
items.explain: Intercalated discs contain mechanical and electrical junctions.

items.text: Smooth muscle cells typically show prominent cross-striations under light microscopy.
items.explain: Smooth muscle lacks sarcomeric striations and has spindle-shaped cells.

items.text: Cardiac muscle is normally under voluntary somatic motor control.
items.explain: Cardiac muscle is involuntary and modulated by autonomic and intrinsic conduction systems.

questions.q: About the anatomy of the neck:

items.text: The sternocleidomastoid divides each side of the neck into anterior and posterior triangles.
items.explain: It is the principal boundary between the two cervical triangles.

items.text: The posterior triangle is bounded anteriorly by the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid.
items.explain: Its other boundaries are trapezius and the clavicle.

items.text: The external jugular vein usually runs deep to the investing layer of deep cervical fascia throughout its course.
items.explain: It runs superficially in the roof of the posterior triangle, deep to platysma.

items.text: The spinal accessory nerve traverses the posterior triangle and is vulnerable during lymph-node biopsy.
items.explain: It crosses the triangle to supply trapezius and may be injured during procedures.

questions.q: About the histology of the alimentary canal:

items.text: The mucosa consists of epithelium, lamina propria and muscularis mucosae.
items.explain: These three components form the mucosal layer.

items.text: The submucosa commonly contains larger vessels and the submucosal nerve plexus.
items.explain: Meissner's plexus lies in the submucosa.

items.text: The myenteric plexus lies between the circular and longitudinal layers of muscularis externa.
items.explain: Auerbach's plexus is located between these muscle layers and regulates motility.

items.text: The stomach normally has villi projecting from its mucosal surface.
items.explain: The stomach has gastric pits and glands; villi are characteristic of small intestine.

questions.q: About the pre-embryonic period of human development:

items.text: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube.
items.explain: The ampullary region is the usual site of fertilisation.

items.text: Cleavage increases the overall size of the conceptus with each mitotic division.
items.explain: Cleavage partitions the zygote into smaller blastomeres without a corresponding increase in overall size.

items.text: The morula is a solid ball of blastomeres that precedes the blastocyst.
items.explain: The morula forms before fluid accumulation produces a blastocyst.

items.text: Implantation usually begins about six to seven days after fertilisation.
items.explain: The blastocyst begins attaching to the endometrium near the end of the first week.

items.text: Spirometry measures the volume of air inhaled and exhaled as a function of time.
items.explain: Spirometry records airflow and volumes during respiratory manoeuvres.

items.text: The FEV1/FVC ratio is commonly reduced in obstructive ventilatory defects.
items.explain: Airflow limitation reduces FEV1 disproportionately to FVC.

items.text: Residual volume can be measured directly by simple spirometry.
items.explain: Residual volume requires methods such as gas dilution or body plethysmography.

items.text: Pulmonary function test results should be interpreted alongside clinical findings.
items.explain: PFTs quantify impairment but do not independently establish every diagnosis.

questions.q: About the endocrine functions of the pancreas:

items.text: Beta cells of pancreatic islets secrete insulin.
items.explain: Insulin is released by pancreatic beta cells.

items.text: Alpha cells secrete glucagon, which raises blood glucose partly through hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
items.explain: Glucagon acts mainly on the liver to increase glucose availability.

items.text: Somatostatin is secreted by pancreatic delta cells.
items.explain: Delta cells release somatostatin, which inhibits several pancreatic and gastrointestinal hormones.

items.text: Insulin secretion is normally suppressed by an increase in blood glucose.
items.explain: Rising blood glucose stimulates insulin release.

questions.q: About the renal mechanisms for concentrating urine:

items.text: The countercurrent multiplier mechanism depends on the loop of Henle.
items.explain: The loop establishes a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium.

items.text: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is highly permeable to water.
items.explain: It reabsorbs solutes but is relatively impermeable to water.

items.text: Antidiuretic hormone increases collecting-duct water permeability through aquaporin-2 insertion.
items.explain: ADH acts on V2 receptors to promote aquaporin-2 insertion.

items.text: Urea recycling contributes to the high osmolality of the inner renal medulla.
items.explain: Urea recycling helps maintain the medullary osmotic gradient.

questions.q: About the physiological regulation of arterial blood pressure:

items.text: Mean arterial pressure is determined largely by cardiac output and total peripheral resistance.
items.explain: MAP is approximately cardiac output multiplied by total peripheral resistance.

items.text: Arteriolar radius has a major influence on peripheral resistance.
items.explain: Small changes in arteriolar radius produce substantial changes in resistance.

items.text: Carotid sinus baroreceptors are located at the origin of the internal carotid artery.
items.explain: They detect stretch in the carotid sinus near the common carotid bifurcation.

items.text: An increase in arterial pressure normally increases sympathetic outflow through the baroreceptor reflex.
items.explain: Increased baroreceptor firing inhibits sympathetic outflow and increases parasympathetic influence.

items.text: Rods are more sensitive to low levels of illumination than cones.
items.explain: Rods mediate scotopic vision and are highly sensitive in dim light.

items.text: Cones are responsible for high-acuity colour vision in bright light.
items.explain: Cone photoreceptors support photopic vision and colour discrimination.

items.text: Photoreceptors depolarise when exposed to light.
items.explain: Light closes cGMP-gated channels, causing photoreceptor hyperpolarisation.

items.text: The fovea centralis has a high density of cones and is important for visual acuity.
items.explain: The fovea is specialised for detailed central vision.

questions.q: About the chemical properties of biological molecules:

items.text: Amino acids contain both an amino group and a carboxyl group.
items.explain: The basic amino acid structure includes both functional groups and a variable side chain.

items.text: At physiological pH, many amino acids exist predominantly as zwitterions.
items.explain: The amino and carboxyl groups commonly carry opposite charges.

items.text: Most naturally occurring unsaturated fatty acids in human tissues contain only trans double bonds.
items.explain: Naturally occurring unsaturated fatty acids in human tissues are predominantly cis.

items.text: A glycosidic bond links monosaccharide residues in oligo- and polysaccharides.
items.explain: Glycosidic linkages join sugar units.

items.text: Classical PKU most commonly results from deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase.
items.explain: Reduced conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine causes phenylalanine accumulation.

items.text: Untreated classical PKU can cause severe neurodevelopmental impairment.
items.explain: High phenylalanine concentrations are neurotoxic during brain development.

items.text: Tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid in untreated classical PKU.
items.explain: The metabolic block makes endogenous tyrosine production inadequate.

items.text: An unrestricted phenylalanine diet is recommended from infancy in classical PKU.
items.explain: Management requires phenylalanine restriction with adequate nutrition and monitoring.

items.text: Peptide hormones commonly act through cell-surface receptors.
items.explain: Their hydrophilic nature generally prevents free diffusion through lipid bilayers.

items.text: Steroid hormones commonly bind intracellular receptors that regulate gene transcription.
items.explain: Hormone-receptor complexes can alter transcription through DNA response elements.

items.text: Adenylyl cyclase generates cAMP from ATP.
items.explain: The enzyme catalyses conversion of ATP to cyclic AMP.

items.text: All hormones act exclusively through G-protein-coupled receptors.
items.explain: Hormones also signal through nuclear receptors, receptor tyrosine kinases and other receptor classes.

questions.q: About recombinant DNA technology and PCR:

items.text: Restriction endonucleases can cleave DNA at specific recognition sequences.
items.explain: These enzymes recognise defined DNA sequences and cut phosphodiester bonds.

items.text: DNA ligase can join compatible DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds.
items.explain: DNA ligase seals breaks in the sugar-phosphate backbone.

items.text: PCR requires a thermostable DNA polymerase for repeated high-temperature denaturation cycles.
items.explain: Thermostable polymerases remain functional through repeated heating cycles.

items.text: The annealing step of conventional PCR is performed at a higher temperature than denaturation.
items.explain: Primer annealing occurs at a lower temperature than the initial DNA denaturation step.

questions.q: About the biotransformation of drugs and other xenobiotics:

items.text: Phase I reactions may introduce or expose functional groups through oxidation, reduction or hydrolysis.
items.explain: These reactions commonly modify molecular structure and may increase polarity.

items.text: Cytochrome P450 enzymes are important in many oxidative Phase I reactions.
items.explain: The CYP enzyme family metabolises numerous drugs and xenobiotics.

items.text: Phase II reactions commonly involve conjugation with endogenous molecules such as glucuronic acid or sulfate.
items.explain: Conjugation generally increases water solubility and facilitates elimination.

items.text: Every drug metabolite is pharmacologically inactive and less toxic than its parent compound.
items.explain: Some metabolites remain active or are more toxic; bioactivation can produce reactive intermediates.

items.text: Osteoblasts synthesise new bone matrix.
items.explain: They produce osteoid and promote mineralisation.

items.text: Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells that resorb bone.
items.explain: They acidify and enzymatically digest bone.

items.text: Compact bone is organised into trabeculae separated by marrow spaces.
items.explain: That arrangement characterises cancellous bone; compact bone is organised mainly into osteons.

items.text: The periosteum covers external bone except at articular surfaces.
items.explain: Articular surfaces are covered by cartilage.

items.text: A skeletal muscle is typically surrounded by an epimysium.
items.explain: Epimysium encloses the whole muscle; perimysium surrounds fascicles and endomysium individual fibres.

items.text: Endomysium is the connective tissue sheath around a fascicle.
items.explain: Perimysium surrounds a fascicle; endomysium surrounds each muscle fibre.

items.text: A skeletal muscle fibre is a multinucleated cell formed by fusion of myoblasts.
items.explain: Myoblast fusion produces long syncytial fibres with peripheral nuclei.

items.text: The sarcolemma is the specialised plasma membrane of a muscle fibre.
items.explain: It encloses the fibre and conducts action potentials.

questions.q: About peripheral nerves and blood vessels:

items.text: The endoneurium surrounds individual nerve fibres within a peripheral nerve.
items.explain: It is connective tissue around individual axons and Schwann cells.

items.text: The perineurium encloses individual axons, while the epineurium encloses the entire nerve.
items.explain: Perineurium encloses fascicles; epineurium encloses the whole nerve.

items.text: Peripheral nerves contain blood vessels that supply their tissues.
items.explain: Nerves have an intrinsic vascular supply.

items.text: Arteries generally have a thicker tunica media than veins of comparable size.
items.explain: The thicker muscular and elastic layer supports higher-pressure flow.

questions.q: About surface anatomy of the thorax:

items.text: The sternal angle is a palpable landmark at the manubriosternal junction.
items.explain: The manubriosternal joint forms the sternal angle.

items.text: The second costal cartilage articulates with the sternum at the sternal angle.
items.explain: It helps identify rib and intercostal spaces.

items.text: The inferior angle of the scapula usually lies near T7 with the upper limb by the side.
items.explain: This is a commonly used surface landmark, though posture alters position.

items.text: The normal cardiac apex beat is usually palpated in the right fifth intercostal space.
items.explain: It is usually in the left fifth intercostal space near the midclavicular line.

items.text: Mitochondria contain enzymes involved in oxidative phosphorylation.
items.explain: The inner mitochondrial membrane contains the electron-transport chain and ATP synthase.

items.text: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is prominent in cells synthesising secreted proteins.
items.explain: Ribosome-studded rough ER synthesises proteins entering the secretory pathway.

items.text: Lysosomes are the principal site of ribosomal RNA transcription in human cells.
items.explain: rRNA is transcribed mainly in the nucleolus; lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes.

items.text: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids.
items.explain: Golgi cisternae process cargo from the ER.

items.text: Neutrophils are commonly prominent in acute bacterial infections.
items.explain: They are rapid responders that phagocytose and kill bacteria.

items.text: Eosinophils are associated with defence against helminths and allergic responses.
items.explain: They release granule proteins and inflammatory mediators.

items.text: Basophils are the most numerous leukocytes in normal peripheral blood.
items.explain: Neutrophils are most abundant; basophils are least abundant.

items.text: Monocytes can enter tissues and differentiate into macrophages.
items.explain: Monocytes can differentiate into tissue macrophages after leaving blood.

items.text: Anaemic hypoxia may occur despite a normal arterial oxygen tension.
items.explain: Low haemoglobin lowers arterial oxygen content even when PaO2 is normal.

items.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning reduces available haemoglobin for oxygen transport.
items.explain: CO binds haemoglobin with high affinity and impairs oxygen transport.

items.text: In stagnant hypoxia, tissue oxygen delivery is impaired because blood flow is reduced.
items.explain: Low perfusion limits oxygen delivery despite adequate arterial oxygenation.

items.text: Histotoxic hypoxia is caused by low haemoglobin concentration.
items.explain: It results from impaired cellular oxygen utilisation, classically due to cyanide.

items.text: The medullary respiratory network contributes to generation of the basic respiratory rhythm.
items.explain: Medullary networks generate and shape the respiratory pattern.

items.text: Central chemoreceptors respond mainly to hydrogen ion changes in brain extracellular fluid and CSF.
items.explain: CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier and generates hydrogen ions in CSF.

items.text: Peripheral chemoreceptors are located in the carotid and aortic bodies.
items.explain: These bodies detect changes in arterial blood gases and pH.

items.text: Central chemoreceptors directly detect a fall in arterial oxygen tension as their principal stimulus.
items.explain: Peripheral chemoreceptors, especially carotid bodies, sense reduced PaO2.

items.text: The myocardium receives most of its blood supply through the coronary arteries.
items.explain: Coronary arteries supply oxygen and metabolic substrates to myocardium.

items.text: The left ventricular myocardium extracts a relatively high proportion of delivered oxygen at rest.
items.explain: High resting extraction means increased demand is met largely by increasing flow.

items.text: Coronary blood flow to the left ventricular myocardium is greatest during systole.
items.explain: Contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels; perfusion is greatest during diastole.

items.text: Local metabolic vasodilation helps match coronary flow to myocardial oxygen demand.
items.explain: Increased myocardial work promotes resistance-vessel dilation and increased flow.

items.text: Carotid sinus baroreceptors send afferent signals through the glossopharyngeal nerve.
items.explain: Carotid sinus afferents travel in Hering's nerve, a branch of CN IX.

items.text: A rise in arterial pressure increases baroreceptor firing.
items.explain: Stretch of carotid sinus and aortic arch increases afferent discharge.

items.text: Increased baroreceptor firing normally increases sympathetic outflow to the heart.
items.explain: The reflex reduces sympathetic outflow and increases vagal influence.

items.text: Aortic arch baroreceptor afferents travel mainly in the vagus nerve.
items.explain: Aortic baroreceptor information reaches the medulla through vagal afferents.

items.text: Calcium binds to troponin C in skeletal and cardiac muscle.
items.explain: Calcium shifts troponin-tropomyosin and exposes actin binding sites.

items.text: ATP binding to myosin is required for detachment from actin.
items.explain: ATP binding lowers myosin's affinity for actin.

items.text: Smooth muscle contraction is regulated by troponin C as in skeletal muscle.
items.explain: Smooth muscle lacks troponin; calcium binds calmodulin and activates MLCK.

items.text: Myosin light-chain kinase phosphorylates myosin in smooth muscle.
items.explain: Calcium-calmodulin activates MLCK and promotes cross-bridge cycling.

items.text: A typical immunoglobulin monomer consists of two heavy chains and two light chains.
items.explain: The four chains are linked by disulphide bonds.

items.text: Variable regions of immunoglobulin chains contribute to antigen recognition.
items.explain: Variable domains form the antigen-binding site.

items.text: The Fc portion of an antibody is the principal region that binds the antigen epitope.
items.explain: Antigen binds Fab ends; Fc interacts with Fc receptors and complement.

items.text: IgM is commonly the first antibody class produced in a primary immune response.
items.explain: Naive B cells initially produce IgM before class switching.

items.text: The fluid mosaic model describes proteins embedded in or associated with a lipid bilayer.
items.explain: The membrane is a dynamic lipid bilayer containing integral and peripheral proteins.

items.text: Cholesterol can modulate membrane fluidity and permeability.
items.explain: Cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity and reduces permeability to some polar molecules.

items.text: All membrane proteins are freely mobile across the entire membrane.
items.explain: Some are anchored to cytoskeleton, extracellular matrix or membrane domains.

items.text: Carbohydrates of many membrane glycoproteins and glycolipids are exposed extracellularly.
items.explain: They contribute to glycocalyx and cell recognition.

questions.q: About genetic code and protein synthesis:

items.text: The genetic code is read in non-overlapping triplets during translation.
items.explain: Each codon consists of three nucleotides read in a fixed frame.

items.text: AUG commonly functions as the initiation codon and codes for methionine.
items.explain: AUG is the usual start codon; bacteria incorporate formylmethionine at initiation.

items.text: The genetic code is degenerate because an amino acid may be encoded by multiple codons.
items.explain: Several amino acids have multiple synonymous codons.

items.text: Ribosomes synthesise polypeptides by reading mRNA in the 3′ to 5′ direction.
items.explain: Ribosomes move along mRNA in the 5′ to 3′ direction.

items.text: Many peptide hormones act through receptors located on the cell surface.
items.explain: Peptide hormones are water-soluble and generally cannot diffuse through the lipid bilayer.

items.text: Activation of some Gs-coupled receptors stimulates adenylyl cyclase.
items.explain: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing intracellular cAMP.

items.text: cAMP can activate protein kinase A.
items.explain: cAMP binds regulatory subunits and activates PKA catalytic activity.

items.text: IP3 remains embedded in the plasma membrane and directly activates protein kinase C.
items.explain: IP3 diffuses through cytosol to trigger calcium release; DAG remains membrane-bound and activates PKC.

items.text: Astrocytes contribute to maintenance of the blood-brain barrier.
items.explain: Astrocytic end-feet support the neurovascular unit.

items.text: Oligodendrocytes myelinate peripheral nerve axons.
items.explain: Schwann cells myelinate PNS axons; oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons.

items.text: One oligodendrocyte can myelinate segments of several CNS axons.
items.explain: Its processes can form myelin internodes on multiple axons.

items.text: Microglia are resident immune cells of the CNS.
items.explain: They perform immune surveillance and phagocytosis.

items.text: The urinary bladder is lined by transitional epithelium.
items.explain: Urothelium accommodates stretching.

items.text: The glomerular filtration barrier includes fenestrated capillary endothelium.
items.explain: It also includes basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragms.

items.text: The proximal convoluted tubule is lined by simple squamous epithelium.
items.explain: It is simple cuboidal epithelium with a brush border.

items.text: Podocytes form part of the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule.
items.explain: Their foot processes surround glomerular capillaries.

items.text: The ovarian cortex contains follicles at different developmental stages.
items.explain: Follicles are located in the ovarian cortex.

items.text: The endometrium is the mucosal lining of the uterus.
items.explain: It undergoes cyclic changes under ovarian hormone influence.

items.text: The uterine myometrium is composed mainly of smooth muscle.
items.explain: It forms the thick muscular wall of the uterus.

items.text: The uterine tube is lined throughout by stratified squamous epithelium.
items.explain: It is mainly simple columnar epithelium with ciliated and secretory cells.

items.text: The thymus has a cortex and medulla within each lobule.
items.explain: The cortex is densely cellular and the medulla is paler.

items.text: Hassall corpuscles are found in the thymic medulla.
items.explain: They are formed by concentric epithelial reticular cells.

items.text: Lymph nodes receive lymph through afferent lymphatic vessels.
items.explain: Afferent vessels enter the node; efferent vessels leave at the hilum.

items.text: The spleen primarily filters lymph rather than blood.
items.explain: The spleen filters blood; lymph nodes filter lymph.

items.text: The fetal period begins at the start of the ninth week after fertilisation.
items.explain: It follows the embryonic period and is characterised by growth and maturation.

items.text: Organ systems continue to grow and mature during fetal life.
items.explain: Previously established organ systems enlarge and mature.

items.text: The fetal period ends at the beginning of the ninth week.
items.explain: The ninth week marks its beginning; it continues until birth.

items.text: Some teratogens can affect fetal growth and organ development.
items.explain: Effects depend on agent, dose, timing and developmental process.

items.text: GFR is an important overall indicator of glomerular function.
items.explain: It measures the rate at which plasma is filtered through glomeruli.

items.text: Creatinine clearance can be used to estimate GFR.
items.explain: It uses urine creatinine, urine flow and plasma creatinine.

items.text: Creatinine is filtered and completely unaffected by tubular secretion.
items.explain: Tubular secretion causes creatinine clearance to slightly overestimate GFR.

items.text: Increased serum creatinine may indicate reduced renal filtration.
items.explain: Reduced renal clearance commonly raises serum creatinine.

items.text: Haemodialysis removes solutes by diffusion across a semipermeable membrane.
items.explain: Solutes diffuse down concentration gradients between blood and dialysate.

items.text: Ultrafiltration during dialysis helps remove excess water.
items.explain: A transmembrane pressure gradient drives water removal.

items.text: Loop diuretics inhibit the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb.
items.explain: This reduces sodium, potassium and chloride reabsorption there.

items.text: Thiazide diuretics act primarily on the proximal convoluted tubule.
items.explain: They inhibit the Na-Cl cotransporter in the early distal convoluted tubule.

items.text: Sodium is the principal cation of extracellular fluid.
items.explain: It is the major determinant of extracellular fluid osmolality and volume.

items.text: Potassium is the principal cation of intracellular fluid.
items.explain: Most body potassium is located within cells.

items.text: Aldosterone promotes renal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.
items.explain: It acts on distal nephron segments.

items.text: ADH increases water permeability in collecting ducts.
items.explain: It promotes insertion of aquaporin-2 channels.

items.text: The skin contributes to regulation of body temperature.
items.explain: Cutaneous blood flow and sweating regulate heat exchange.

items.text: Eccrine sweat glands are important in evaporative cooling.
items.explain: Sweat evaporation removes heat from the body surface.

items.text: Cutaneous vasoconstriction increases heat loss from skin.
items.explain: It reduces skin blood flow and conserves heat.

items.text: The epidermis is avascular and receives nutrients by diffusion from dermis.
items.explain: It is nourished by diffusion from underlying dermal capillaries.

items.text: Parathyroid hormone increases serum calcium concentration.
items.explain: It increases renal calcium reabsorption and active vitamin D formation.

items.text: Calcitonin is secreted by thyroid parafollicular C cells.
items.explain: C cells produce calcitonin, which can inhibit osteoclast activity.

items.text: Atrial natriuretic peptide promotes renal sodium excretion.
items.explain: ANP increases natriuresis and opposes RAAS.

items.text: TSH is secreted by the posterior pituitary.
items.explain: TSH is secreted by anterior pituitary thyrotrophs.

questions.q: About body fluids and blood clotting:

items.text: Albumin is the major contributor to plasma colloid oncotic pressure.
items.explain: It is the most abundant plasma protein.

items.text: Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin during coagulation.
items.explain: Fibrin monomers polymerise and are stabilised into a clot.

items.text: Vitamin K is required for gamma-carboxylation of several clotting factors.
items.explain: Vitamin K-dependent factors include II, VII, IX and X, proteins C and S.

items.text: Serum normally contains more fibrinogen than plasma.
items.explain: Serum is obtained after clotting and contains little or no fibrinogen.

items.text: Haem consists of a porphyrin ring complexed with ferrous iron.
items.explain: Functional haem contains iron in the Fe2+ state.

items.text: Adult haemoglobin A contains two alpha and two beta globin chains.
items.explain: HbA is an alpha-2-beta-2 tetramer.

items.text: Iron released during haem breakdown is normally conserved and reused.
items.explain: Macrophages recover iron from senescent erythrocytes.

items.text: Bilirubin is produced directly from breakdown of globin chains.
items.explain: Haem becomes biliverdin then bilirubin; globin yields amino acids.

items.text: Vitamin D promotes intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate.
items.explain: Active vitamin D increases intestinal absorption of both minerals.

items.text: Vitamin C is required for normal collagen hydroxylation.
items.explain: Ascorbate supports prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases.

items.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause megaloblastic anaemia.
items.explain: Impaired DNA synthesis in marrow cells causes megaloblastic changes.

items.text: Vitamin K deficiency typically causes isolated microcytic anaemia.
items.explain: It impairs clotting factor activation and causes a bleeding tendency.

items.text: Purines include adenine and guanine.
items.explain: These are the two purine bases.

items.text: Pyrimidines include cytosine, thymine and uracil.
items.explain: Thymine is mainly in DNA and uracil mainly in RNA.

items.text: A nucleotide contains a base, pentose sugar and phosphate.
items.explain: A nucleoside plus phosphate group(s) forms a nucleotide.

items.text: RNA normally contains deoxyribose as its pentose sugar.
items.explain: RNA contains ribose; DNA contains deoxyribose.

items.text: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a coenzyme form of vitamin B1.
items.explain: It participates in oxidative decarboxylation and transketolase reactions.

items.text: FAD is derived from riboflavin (vitamin B2).
items.explain: Riboflavin is the precursor of FMN and FAD.

items.text: NAD+ is derived from niacin (vitamin B3).
items.explain: Niacin provides the nicotinamide component of NAD+ and NADP+.

items.text: Biotin functions primarily as a coenzyme for transaminase reactions.
items.explain: Biotin is used by carboxylases; pyridoxal phosphate is central to transamination.

items.text: Seminiferous tubules are the site of sperm production.
items.explain: Spermatogenesis occurs within the seminiferous epithelium.

items.text: Sertoli cells form part of the seminiferous epithelium.
items.explain: They support and regulate developing germ cells.

items.text: Leydig cells lie within seminiferous tubules and form the blood-testis barrier.
items.explain: Leydig cells are interstitial; Sertoli junctions form the barrier.

items.text: The epididymis is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia.
items.explain: Its epithelium supports sperm maturation and absorption.

items.text: The epidermis is keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
items.explain: It forms a keratinising protective barrier.

items.text: Melanocytes are located mainly in the stratum basale.
items.explain: Their processes transfer melanin to keratinocytes.

items.text: Eccrine sweat glands are holocrine glands.
items.explain: Eccrine glands are merocrine; sebaceous glands are holocrine.

items.text: The arrector pili muscle is composed of smooth muscle.
items.explain: It contracts under sympathetic stimulation.

items.text: The thyroid stores hormone precursor extracellularly in follicular colloid.
items.explain: Thyroglobulin-containing colloid is stored in follicular lumina.

items.text: Parafollicular C cells produce calcitonin.
items.explain: C cells are located between or adjacent to thyroid follicles.

items.text: The adrenal cortex is arranged into three zones.
items.explain: These are zona glomerulosa, fasciculata and reticularis.

items.text: The adrenal medulla is derived from mesoderm.
items.explain: Chromaffin cells are derived from neural crest.

items.text: The corneal epithelium is non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
items.explain: It forms a transparent protective surface.

items.text: The lens is avascular.
items.explain: It receives nutrients from aqueous and vitreous humour.

items.text: The organ of Corti is located in the cochlear duct.
items.explain: It contains sensory hair cells for hearing.

items.text: The retina contains photoreceptors but no supporting glial cells.
items.explain: The retina contains Müller glia and other supporting cells.

items.text: Cerebral cortical grey matter contains neuronal cell bodies and synapses.
items.explain: Grey matter is rich in neuronal somata, dendrites and synapses.

items.text: White matter consists largely of myelinated axons.
items.explain: Myelin contributes to its pale appearance.

items.text: The choroid plexus contributes to cerebrospinal fluid production.
items.explain: Choroid plexus epithelium secretes most CSF.

items.text: The blood-brain barrier is formed primarily by fenestrated capillary endothelium.
items.explain: It is associated with non-fenestrated endothelial cells joined by tight junctions.

items.text: Pulsatile GnRH secretion stimulates pituitary release of LH and FSH.
items.explain: GnRH pulses drive gonadotrophin secretion.

items.text: Adrenarche and gonadarche are distinct developmental processes.
items.explain: Adrenarche involves adrenal androgens; gonadarche reflects HPG-axis activation.

items.text: Leptin provides a permissive metabolic signal for normal pubertal development.
items.explain: Adequate energy stores and leptin signalling are associated with reproductive maturation.

items.text: Puberty in boys is initiated by a sustained rise in adrenal testosterone.
items.explain: Testosterone rises mainly from testicular Leydig cells under LH stimulation.

items.text: LH stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone.
items.explain: LH acts on Leydig cells in the testes.

items.text: FSH acts on Sertoli cells and supports spermatogenesis.
items.explain: Sertoli cells support and regulate germ cells.

items.text: Inhibin B from Sertoli cells selectively suppresses FSH secretion.
items.explain: It provides negative feedback on pituitary FSH.

items.text: The prostate is the principal source of fructose in seminal fluid.
items.explain: Seminal vesicles are the major source of seminal fructose.

questions.sub: Female reproductive physiology and ovarian cycle
questions.q: About female reproductive physiology and ovarian cycle:

items.text: The mid-cycle LH surge triggers ovulation.
items.explain: Sustained high oestradiol produces positive feedback leading to the LH surge.

items.text: The corpus luteum secretes progesterone during the luteal phase.
items.explain: Progesterone prepares the endometrium for implantation.

items.text: The proliferative phase of the endometrium is driven mainly by progesterone.
items.explain: Oestrogen drives proliferation; progesterone dominates the secretory phase.

items.text: FSH supports growth and development of ovarian follicles.
items.explain: FSH stimulates granulosa cells and follicular development.

items.text: hCG helps maintain the corpus luteum in early pregnancy.
items.explain: hCG acts on LH receptors to sustain early progesterone secretion.

items.text: The placenta becomes a major source of progesterone as pregnancy progresses.
items.explain: Placental steroidogenesis supports pregnancy maintenance.

items.text: Oxytocin promotes uterine contractions during labour.
items.explain: It stimulates myometrial contraction and positive feedback.

items.text: Prolactin is the principal hormone responsible for milk ejection.
items.explain: Oxytocin causes milk ejection; prolactin promotes milk synthesis.

items.text: Combined hormonal contraceptives suppress ovulation by inhibiting gonadotrophin secretion.
items.explain: Oestrogen and progestin suppress FSH and LH, preventing the mid-cycle surge.

items.text: Progestin-only methods can thicken cervical mucus.
items.explain: Thickened mucus impedes sperm penetration.

items.text: Copper intrauterine devices act by releasing systemic progesterone.
items.explain: Copper produces a local inflammatory environment; it is non-hormonal.

items.text: Condoms can reduce transmission of many sexually transmitted infections.
items.explain: Correct and consistent use reduces, but does not eliminate, STI risk.

questions.q: About recombinant dna and genetic diagnosis:

items.text: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific recognition sequences.
items.explain: Restriction enzymes recognise defined DNA sequences.

items.text: DNA ligase joins compatible DNA fragments.
items.explain: Ligase forms phosphodiester bonds between DNA ends.

items.text: PCR requires a thermostable DNA polymerase.
items.explain: Taq polymerase withstands repeated denaturation.

items.text: PCR amplification requires RNA primers.
items.explain: PCR uses short DNA primers.

items.text: Cytochrome P450 enzymes participate in many phase I drug reactions.
items.explain: CYP enzymes catalyse oxidation and other phase I reactions.

items.text: Phase II reactions commonly involve conjugation with endogenous molecules.
items.explain: Conjugation can increase water solubility and facilitate excretion.

items.text: Glucuronidation is a phase II conjugation reaction.
items.explain: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases add glucuronic acid to substrates.

items.text: All drug metabolites are less active than their parent compounds.
items.explain: Some metabolites remain active or are toxic.

items.text: Antibody-antigen binding is mediated by non-covalent interactions.
items.explain: Hydrogen bonds, electrostatic forces, hydrophobic interactions and van der Waals forces contribute.

items.text: A monoclonal antibody is produced by a single B-cell clone or its hybridoma derivative.
items.explain: Monoclonal antibodies share specificity for one epitope.

items.text: Agglutination involves visible clumping of particulate antigens by antibodies.
items.explain: Antibody cross-linking produces clumping.

items.text: Affinity and avidity describe exactly the same property.
items.explain: Affinity is strength at one binding site; avidity is overall binding strength.

items.text: Simple diffusion moves substances down their concentration gradient without direct energy input.
items.explain: Simple diffusion is passive transport.

items.text: Facilitated diffusion requires a membrane protein but does not directly use ATP.
items.explain: Channels and carriers permit passive movement down a gradient.

items.text: The sodium-potassium ATPase moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in per ATP hydrolysed.
items.explain: This electrogenic pump maintains ionic gradients.

items.text: Primary active transport moves solutes only down their electrochemical gradients.
items.explain: It uses energy to move at least one solute against its gradient.

items.text: Steroid hormones are synthesised from cholesterol.
items.explain: Cholesterol is the precursor for steroid hormones.

items.text: Catecholamines are derived from tyrosine.
items.explain: Tyrosine is converted through DOPA and dopamine to noradrenaline and adrenaline.

items.text: Peptide hormones are generally stored in secretory vesicles before release.
items.explain: They are stored for regulated exocytosis.

items.text: Thyroid hormones are stored as free T3 and T4 in secretory vesicles.
items.explain: They are stored extracellularly in follicular colloid bound to thyroglobulin.

items.text: The embryonic period extends from the beginning of the third week through the end of the eighth week after fertilisation.
items.explain: The embryonic period is conventionally described as weeks 3–8 post-fertilisation.

items.text: Organogenesis occurs predominantly during the embryonic period.
items.explain: Major organ systems are laid down during this period.

items.text: The neural tube gives rise to the brain and spinal cord.
items.explain: The cranial neural tube forms the brain and the caudal portion forms the spinal cord.

items.text: The fetal period is the principal period of initial organ formation.
items.explain: The fetal period is characterised mainly by growth and maturation.

items.text: The effect of a teratogen depends partly on the developmental stage at exposure.
items.explain: Timing, dose and agent influence the outcome of teratogenic exposure.

items.text: The embryonic period is particularly vulnerable to major structural malformations.
items.explain: Organogenesis is a critical period for structural development.

items.text: Monozygotic twins arise from fertilisation of two separate ova by two spermatozoa.
items.explain: Monozygotic twins arise when one zygote divides; separate fertilisations produce dizygotic twins.

items.text: Dizygotic twins are genetically similar to ordinary siblings rather than genetically identical.
items.explain: They share, on average, about half their segregating genetic variation.

questions.q: Regarding embryology of the respiratory system:

items.text: The respiratory diverticulum develops from the ventral wall of the foregut.
items.explain: The laryngotracheal diverticulum buds from the ventral foregut endoderm.

items.text: The epithelium of the lower respiratory tract is derived mainly from endoderm.
items.explain: Endoderm forms the epithelial lining and glands.

items.text: Cartilage and smooth muscle of the tracheobronchial tree are derived from splanchnic mesoderm.
items.explain: Visceral mesoderm contributes connective tissue, cartilage and smooth muscle.

items.text: The right lung normally develops three lobar buds and the left lung two.
items.explain: The secondary bronchial buds establish three right and two left lobes.

questions.q: Regarding embryology of the digestive system:

items.text: The epithelial lining of most of the gastrointestinal tract is derived from endoderm.
items.explain: Endoderm forms most of the gut epithelial lining and associated glands.

items.text: The stomach undergoes rotation during development.
items.explain: Differential growth and rotation establish its adult orientation.

items.text: The midgut undergoes temporary physiological herniation into the umbilical cord.
items.explain: Rapid midgut elongation produces temporary herniation during normal development.

items.text: The spleen develops from endoderm of the foregut.
items.explain: The spleen develops from mesenchyme in the dorsal mesogastrium.

questions.q: Regarding embryology of the genitourinary system:

items.text: The permanent kidney develops from the metanephros.
items.explain: The metanephros forms the definitive kidney.

items.text: The ureteric bud contributes to the collecting system of the kidney.
items.explain: It forms the ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts.

items.text: The metanephric mesenchyme gives rise to nephron components.
items.explain: It forms renal vesicles and nephron tubules.

items.text: The urinary bladder epithelium is derived entirely from mesoderm.
items.explain: Most bladder epithelium derives from endoderm of the urogenital sinus.

questions.q: Regarding energy expenditure and nutritional assessment:

items.text: Basal metabolic rate is measured under standardised resting, post-absorptive and thermoneutral conditions.
items.explain: These conditions minimise the effects of food, activity and ambient temperature.

items.text: The thermic effect of food is the increase in energy expenditure associated with eating and processing nutrients.
items.explain: It includes energy costs of digestion, absorption and metabolism.

items.text: Total daily energy expenditure includes resting expenditure, thermic effect of food and physical activity.
items.explain: These are the major components of total energy expenditure.
