items.text: Kwashiorkor is characterised by severe wasting without oedema.
items.explain: Oedema is a defining clinical feature of kwashiorkor; severe wasting is typical of marasmus.

questions.q: Regarding endocrine functions of the kidney:

items.text: Renal interstitial cells produce erythropoietin in response to reduced oxygen availability.
items.explain: Renal erythropoietin production increases with tissue hypoxia.

items.text: Renin is released by juxtaglomerular cells in response to reduced renal perfusion and other signals.
items.explain: Renin initiates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

items.text: The kidney converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
items.explain: Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase catalyses formation of calcitriol.

items.text: Erythropoietin directly stimulates platelet production in bone marrow.
items.explain: Erythropoietin primarily stimulates erythroid progenitors and red-cell production.

questions.q: Regarding sensory receptors and reflex arcs:

items.text: A reflex arc includes a receptor, afferent pathway, central integration and efferent pathway.
items.explain: These components connect a stimulus to an involuntary response.

items.text: Muscle spindles detect changes in muscle length.
items.explain: Muscle spindles are stretch receptors involved in proprioception.

items.text: Golgi tendon organs respond primarily to tension developed in tendons.
items.explain: They detect muscle-tendon tension.

items.text: The withdrawal reflex is normally a monosynaptic reflex.
items.explain: The withdrawal reflex is polysynaptic, involving interneurons.

questions.q: Regarding cerebral function, eeg and sleep:

items.text: Alpha waves are commonly recorded in relaxed, awake adults with eyes closed.
items.explain: Alpha activity is prominent during relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed.

items.text: REM sleep is associated with rapid eye movements and vivid dreaming.
items.explain: REM sleep has characteristic eye movements and low-voltage, mixed-frequency EEG.

items.text: Non-REM sleep includes stages N1, N2 and N3.
items.explain: Modern sleep staging recognises three NREM stages.

items.text: Sleep spindles are a characteristic feature of N3 sleep.
items.explain: Sleep spindles are characteristic of N2 sleep.

questions.q: Regarding postural control and motor pathways:

items.text: The vestibular apparatus contributes to the maintenance of balance and posture.
items.explain: Vestibular input informs postural reflexes and balance.

items.text: The vestibulo-ocular reflex helps stabilise gaze during head movement.
items.explain: It produces compensatory eye movement opposite to head movement.

items.text: The cerebellum contributes to coordination and error correction of movement.
items.explain: It compares intended and actual movement and adjusts motor output.

items.text: The cerebellum initiates voluntary movement by directly activating lower motor neurons.
items.explain: The cerebellum modulates movement; it does not directly initiate it.

items.text: Amino acids are amphoteric because they contain acidic and basic groups.
items.explain: Amino and carboxyl groups permit acid-base behaviour.

items.text: The isoelectric point is the pH at which a molecule has no net electrical charge.
items.explain: At the isoelectric point, positive and negative charges balance.

items.text: Peptide bonds link the amino group of one amino acid to the carboxyl group of another.
items.explain: Peptide bond formation links amino acids into polypeptides.

items.text: All monosaccharides are reducing sugars, including those with anomeric carbons locked in glycosidic bonds.
items.explain: A free anomeric carbon is required for a sugar to act as a reducing sugar.

questions.sub: Inborn errors of amino acid metabolism
questions.q: Regarding inborn errors of amino acid metabolism:

items.text: Phenylketonuria commonly results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase activity.
items.explain: Classical PKU is usually due to phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency.

items.text: Phenylalanine hydroxylase converts phenylalanine to tyrosine.
items.explain: The reaction requires tetrahydrobiopterin as a cofactor.

items.text: Untreated classic phenylketonuria can cause neurodevelopmental impairment.
items.explain: Accumulation of phenylalanine and related metabolites is neurotoxic.

items.text: A low-phenylalanine diet is unnecessary once a person with PKU reaches adulthood.
items.explain: Dietary treatment is generally lifelong, with ongoing phenylalanine monitoring.

questions.q: Regarding molecular basis of muscle contraction:

items.text: Calcium binds to troponin C in skeletal muscle.
items.explain: Calcium binding changes the troponin complex and moves tropomyosin.

items.text: ATP binding to myosin allows myosin to detach from actin.
items.explain: ATP binding breaks the actin-myosin cross-bridge.

items.text: Hydrolysis of ATP re-cocks the myosin head into a high-energy state.
items.explain: ATP hydrolysis energises the myosin head for another cycle.

items.text: In rigor mortis, myosin detaches from actin because ATP concentrations rise after death.
items.explain: ATP depletion prevents cross-bridge detachment, producing rigidity.

items.text: Thiamine pyrophosphate is the active coenzyme form of vitamin B1.
items.explain: TPP participates in oxidative decarboxylation and transketolase reactions.

items.text: FAD and FMN are derived from riboflavin.
items.explain: Vitamin B2 is the precursor of these flavin coenzymes.

items.text: NAD+ is derived from niacin.
items.explain: Vitamin B3 supplies the nicotinamide moiety of NAD and NADP.

items.text: Vitamin C is the precursor of coenzyme A.
items.explain: Coenzyme A contains pantothenic acid (vitamin B5).

questions.q: Regarding plasma proteins and haemostasis biochemistry:

items.text: Albumin contributes substantially to plasma colloid osmotic pressure.
items.explain: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and a major oncotic contributor.

items.text: Fibrin is formed from fibrinogen by the action of thrombin.
items.explain: Thrombin cleaves fibrinopeptides from fibrinogen, allowing fibrin polymerisation.

items.text: Vitamin K is required for gamma-carboxylation of several coagulation factors.
items.explain: Factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S are vitamin K dependent.

items.text: Plasmin promotes clot formation by converting fibrinogen into fibrin.
items.explain: Thrombin forms fibrin; plasmin degrades fibrin during fibrinolysis.

questions.q: About the classification and functions of epithelial tissue:

items.text: Simple epithelium consists of a single layer of cells.
items.explain: Simple epithelium has one cell layer, regardless of cell shape.

items.text: Pseudostratified epithelium is truly multilayered because every cell reaches the basement membrane.
items.explain: Pseudostratified epithelium appears multilayered, but all cells contact the basement membrane; not all reach the free surface.

items.text: Transitional epithelium can change its appearance as the urinary tract distends.
items.explain: Urothelium changes cell shape and surface appearance with filling and stretching.

items.text: Stratified squamous epithelium is specialised primarily for rapid diffusion.
items.explain: Its multiple layers primarily protect against abrasion; thin simple squamous epithelium is suited to diffusion.

questions.q: About connective tissue and its extracellular matrix:

items.text: The extracellular matrix of connective tissue includes fibres and ground substance.
items.explain: The matrix comprises protein fibres embedded in ground substance.

items.text: Fibroblasts are major cells responsible for producing connective tissue fibres and matrix.
items.explain: Fibroblasts synthesise collagen, elastic fibres and components of ground substance.

items.text: Hyaline cartilage normally contains abundant blood vessels within its matrix.
items.explain: Cartilage is avascular; nutrients diffuse through its matrix from surrounding tissues or synovial fluid.

items.text: Mature adipocytes are specialised connective-tissue cells that store triglyceride.
items.explain: Adipocytes store lipid and also have endocrine functions.

questions.q: About the microscopic structure of cardiac muscle:

items.text: Cardiac muscle fibres are striated and usually contain a centrally located nucleus.
items.explain: Cardiomyocytes are striated, branched cells, usually with one central nucleus.

items.text: Intercalated discs contain specialised junctions that mechanically and electrically connect cardiomyocytes.
items.explain: Desmosomes and fascia adherens provide mechanical coupling, while gap junctions permit electrical coupling.

items.text: Cardiac muscle fibres are long, unbranched and multinucleated like typical skeletal muscle fibres.
items.explain: Cardiomyocytes are generally short, branched and have one or occasionally two central nuclei.

items.text: Purkinje fibres are modified cardiac muscle cells specialised for rapid impulse conduction.
items.explain: Subendocardial Purkinje cells are large, glycogen-rich conducting cardiomyocytes.

questions.q: About fertilisation and early human development:

items.text: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube.
items.explain: The ampulla is the usual site where the sperm and secondary oocyte meet.

items.text: The secondary oocyte completes meiosis II before sperm penetration.
items.explain: Sperm penetration triggers completion of meiosis II; the ovulated cell is arrested in metaphase II.

items.text: Cleavage increases the number of blastomeres without a corresponding increase in the overall size of the conceptus.
items.explain: Early mitotic divisions partition the zygote into progressively smaller blastomeres within the zona pellucida.

items.text: The morula forms before the blastocyst.
items.explain: Compaction produces the morula, which subsequently develops a blastocyst cavity and distinct cell populations.

items.text: The first pharyngeal arch contributes to the maxilla, mandible and muscles of mastication.
items.explain: The first arch forms maxillary and mandibular prominences and is associated with muscles of mastication.

items.text: The second pharyngeal arch is associated with the facial nerve.
items.explain: The second arch musculature is supplied by cranial nerve VII.

items.text: The third pharyngeal arch is associated with the glossopharyngeal nerve.
items.explain: CN IX supplies third-arch derivatives, including stylopharyngeus.

items.text: The fourth and sixth arches are both supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.
items.explain: The fourth arch is associated with the superior laryngeal branch of CN X and the sixth with its recurrent laryngeal branch.

items.text: Interstitial cells of Cajal contribute to the generation and propagation of gastrointestinal slow waves.
items.explain: These pacemaker cells generate electrical slow waves that help organise smooth-muscle activity.

items.text: Slow waves are themselves equivalent to action potentials and always produce contractions.
items.explain: Slow waves set the timing of excitability; spike potentials and calcium entry are needed for stronger contractions.

items.text: The myenteric plexus is located between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers.
items.explain: Auerbach's plexus lies between the two main layers of the muscularis externa and regulates motility.

items.text: Peristalsis generally propels gastrointestinal contents aborally.
items.explain: Coordinated contraction behind and relaxation ahead of a bolus move contents along the tract.

questions.q: About digestion and absorption of nutrients:

items.text: Most digestion and absorption of macronutrients occur in the small intestine.
items.explain: Pancreatic, biliary and intestinal processes make the small intestine the principal site.

items.text: Pancreatic bicarbonate helps neutralise acidic chyme entering the duodenum.
items.explain: Bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion raises luminal pH to support intestinal and pancreatic enzymes.

items.text: Dietary long-chain fatty acids are transported from enterocytes mainly as free fatty acids directly into portal blood.
items.explain: They are re-esterified, packaged into chylomicrons and enter intestinal lymph before reaching systemic blood.

items.text: Vitamin B12 absorption requires intrinsic factor and occurs mainly in the terminal ileum.
items.explain: The intrinsic factor–B12 complex binds receptors in the terminal ileum for uptake.

questions.q: About the accessory organs of digestion:

items.text: Secretin stimulates bicarbonate-rich secretion from pancreatic duct cells.
items.explain: Acid in the duodenum stimulates S cells to release secretin, which promotes ductal bicarbonate secretion.

items.text: Cholecystokinin stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.
items.explain: CCK is released in response to fats and amino acids and coordinates pancreatic enzyme delivery with bile release.

items.text: Bile salts are digestive enzymes that hydrolyse triglycerides.
items.explain: Bile salts emulsify lipids and facilitate micelle formation; pancreatic lipase performs triglyceride hydrolysis.

items.text: The liver synthesises bile, while the gallbladder stores and concentrates it.
items.explain: Hepatocytes produce bile; the gallbladder concentrates and releases it in response to CCK.

items.text: Hypothalamic releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary through the hypophyseal portal circulation.
items.explain: The portal vessels deliver hypothalamic factors directly to the anterior pituitary.

items.text: Oxytocin is synthesised in the anterior pituitary and stored in the hypothalamus.
items.explain: Oxytocin is synthesised in hypothalamic neurons and transported for storage and release from the posterior pituitary.

items.text: Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin secretion.
items.explain: Hypothalamic dopamine acts on D2 receptors on lactotrophs to restrain prolactin release.

items.text: The posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin that are synthesised in hypothalamic nuclei.
items.explain: The neurohypophysis stores and releases hormones made by hypothalamic magnocellular neurons.

items.text: The zona glomerulosa is the principal source of aldosterone.
items.explain: The outer cortical zone produces mineralocorticoids, chiefly aldosterone.

items.text: The zona fasciculata is the main source of cortisol.
items.explain: The middle cortical zone produces glucocorticoids, predominantly cortisol.

items.text: Adrenal medullary chromaffin cells are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons.
items.explain: They are neural-crest-derived cells that release catecholamines into the circulation in response to preganglionic sympathetic stimulation.

items.text: ACTH is the main direct regulator of aldosterone secretion under normal physiological conditions.
items.explain: Angiotensin II and plasma potassium are the principal regulators of aldosterone; ACTH has a minor or transient influence.

items.text: Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol.
items.explain: The pathway's reactions occur in the cytosol of cells.

items.text: Phosphofructokinase-1 catalyses a major rate-limiting, irreversible step of glycolysis.
items.explain: PFK-1 converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and is tightly regulated.

items.text: Under anaerobic conditions, conversion of pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+.
items.explain: Lactate dehydrogenase oxidises NADH to NAD+, allowing glycolysis to continue.

items.text: Glycolysis can occur only when oxygen is available.
items.explain: Glycolysis does not directly require oxygen and can produce ATP under anaerobic conditions.

items.text: A competitive inhibitor typically increases the apparent Km without changing Vmax in the classical reversible model.
items.explain: Increasing substrate concentration can overcome competitive inhibition, so Vmax remains attainable.

items.text: A pure noncompetitive inhibitor decreases Vmax while leaving Km unchanged in the classical model.
items.explain: Pure noncompetitive inhibition reduces active enzyme capacity without changing substrate affinity.

items.text: A coenzyme is always a protein component of an enzyme.
items.explain: Coenzymes are non-protein organic cofactors, often derived from vitamins.

items.text: Apoenzyme combined with its required cofactor forms the active holoenzyme.
items.explain: The apoenzyme is the protein component; association with its cofactor yields the functional holoenzyme.

items.text: The fluid mosaic model describes membrane proteins embedded in or associated with a lipid bilayer.
items.explain: Membranes contain a dynamic lipid bilayer with integral and peripheral proteins.

items.text: Cholesterol can modulate membrane fluidity and permeability.
items.explain: Cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity, limiting excessive movement at higher temperatures and preventing tight packing at lower temperatures.

items.text: Simple diffusion across a membrane requires a specific carrier protein and ATP hydrolysis.
items.explain: Simple diffusion is passive and does not require a carrier or direct ATP expenditure.

items.text: The Na+/K+-ATPase is an example of primary active transport.
items.explain: It directly hydrolyses ATP to move sodium and potassium against their electrochemical gradients.

items.text: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble vitamins.
items.explain: These four vitamins are absorbed and transported with dietary lipids.

items.text: Fat-soluble vitamins are commonly incorporated into micelles during intestinal absorption.
items.explain: Bile salts support micelle formation, facilitating delivery of these hydrophobic vitamins to enterocytes.

items.text: Vitamin K is required for gamma-carboxylation of several coagulation proteins.
items.explain: Vitamin K-dependent carboxylation enables factors such as II, VII, IX and X to bind calcium.

items.text: Vitamin A deficiency typically causes night blindness rather than impaired dark adaptation being an early feature.
items.explain: Night blindness is a classic early manifestation because retinal is required for the visual cycle.

items.text: Thiamine pyrophosphate is the active coenzyme form of vitamin B1.
items.explain: TPP participates in oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids and transketolase reactions.

items.text: FAD and FMN are coenzyme forms derived from riboflavin.
items.explain: Vitamin B2 is converted to FMN and FAD, which function in oxidation-reduction reactions.

items.text: Niacin is a precursor of NAD+ and NADP+.
items.explain: Nicotinamide-containing coenzymes transfer reducing equivalents in many metabolic pathways.

items.text: Vitamin C is the coenzyme required for all transamination reactions.
items.explain: Pyridoxal phosphate, derived from vitamin B6, is the principal coenzyme for transamination.

questions.q: About the histology of the respiratory system:

items.text: The trachea is typically lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium.
items.explain: The respiratory epithelium of the trachea contains ciliated cells, goblet cells and basal cells.

items.text: Bronchioles normally contain cartilage plates in their walls.
items.explain: Cartilage supports the trachea and bronchi but is absent from bronchioles.

items.text: Type I pneumocytes form most of the thin alveolar gas-exchange surface.
items.explain: Flattened type I cells cover most of the alveolar surface and contribute to the air-blood barrier.

items.text: Type II pneumocytes secrete pulmonary surfactant.
items.explain: Type II cells contain lamellar bodies and release surfactant, reducing alveolar surface tension.

questions.q: About the histology of the urinary system:

items.text: The glomerular filtration barrier includes fenestrated capillary endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragms.
items.explain: These three components form the selective filtration barrier.

items.text: Podocytes are specialised epithelial cells whose foot processes surround glomerular capillaries.
items.explain: Podocyte pedicels interdigitate and form filtration slits bridged by slit diaphragms.

items.text: The proximal convoluted tubule is lined by simple squamous epithelium without a brush border.
items.explain: It is lined by cuboidal cells with a prominent brush border that increases absorptive surface area.

items.text: The macula densa is part of the distal nephron and senses tubular sodium chloride delivery.
items.explain: Macula densa cells participate in tubuloglomerular feedback and renin regulation.

questions.q: About the lower limb, particularly the femoral triangle and sciatic nerve:

items.text: The femoral triangle is bounded superiorly by the inguinal ligament.
items.explain: The inguinal ligament forms the base or superior boundary of the femoral triangle.

items.text: From lateral to medial, the major contents of the femoral triangle are femoral nerve, artery and vein.
items.explain: The familiar lateral-to-medial arrangement is nerve, artery, vein, and femoral canal.

items.text: The sciatic nerve usually leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen inferior to piriformis.
items.explain: The usual course is below piriformis, although anatomical variations occur.

items.text: The common fibular nerve is the principal motor supply to the posterior compartment of the leg.
items.explain: The tibial nerve supplies the posterior compartment; the common fibular nerve divides to supply the anterior and lateral compartments.

items.text: The portal vein is typically formed posterior to the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
items.explain: The two major tributaries usually unite behind the pancreatic neck.

items.text: The portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood from much of the gastrointestinal tract to the liver.
items.explain: It conveys absorbed nutrients and other substances for hepatic processing.

items.text: The greater omentum hangs from the lesser curvature of the stomach.
items.explain: The greater omentum descends from the greater curvature; the lesser omentum connects the liver to the lesser curvature and proximal duodenum.

items.text: The urinary bladder is an extraperitoneal organ in its empty state, with its superior surface related to peritoneum.
items.explain: The bladder lies subperitoneally; peritoneum covers part of its superior surface and reflects with distension.

questions.q: About the major tracts of the spinal cord:

items.text: The dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway carries vibration, conscious proprioception and discriminative touch.
items.explain: These modalities ascend ipsilaterally in the dorsal columns before decussating in the medulla.

items.text: The spinothalamic pathway usually crosses to the opposite side within the spinal cord shortly after entry.
items.explain: Second-order neurons cross through the anterior white commissure, typically within a few segments.

items.text: The lateral corticospinal tract decussates mainly in the spinal cord at the level where it terminates.
items.explain: Most fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla before descending in the lateral corticospinal tract.

items.text: A lesion of one dorsal column in the spinal cord causes ipsilateral loss of vibration and position sense below the lesion.
items.explain: Dorsal column fibres ascend on the same side until they decussate in the medulla.

items.text: The stretch reflex is mediated by muscle spindle afferents and alpha motor neurons.
items.explain: Ia afferents from muscle spindles monosynaptically excite alpha motor neurons supplying the same muscle.

items.text: The Golgi tendon organ primarily detects changes in muscle tension.
items.explain: Golgi tendon organs respond to tension transmitted through the tendon.

items.text: The withdrawal reflex is typically a monosynaptic reflex involving only one synapse.
items.explain: It is a polysynaptic protective reflex involving interneuronal circuits.

items.text: Reciprocal inhibition helps relax antagonist muscles during a stretch reflex.
items.explain: Inhibitory interneurons reduce activity in antagonist motor neurons while the agonist contracts.

questions.q: About red blood cells and oxygen transport:

items.text: Mature human erythrocytes lack a nucleus and mitochondria.
items.explain: Mature red cells lose their nucleus and organelles, relying on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP.

items.text: Haemoglobin is a tetramer with four heme groups, each capable of binding one oxygen molecule.
items.explain: Each globin subunit contains a heme group with ferrous iron that binds oxygen reversibly.

items.text: An increase in 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the left.
items.explain: 2,3-BPG decreases haemoglobin oxygen affinity and shifts the curve to the right.

items.text: Carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions and increased temperature in active tissues favour oxygen unloading.
items.explain: These factors promote a rightward shift of the dissociation curve, facilitating tissue oxygen delivery.

items.text: Platelets are anucleate cell fragments derived from megakaryocytes.
items.explain: Megakaryocytes in the bone marrow release circulating platelets.

items.text: Platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen is facilitated by von Willebrand factor binding to platelet GPIb.
items.explain: The vWF-GPIb interaction supports platelet tethering at sites of vascular injury.

items.text: Thromboxane A2 promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction.
items.explain: Activated platelets generate thromboxane A2, which recruits and activates additional platelets.

items.text: Aspirin promotes thromboxane A2 synthesis by irreversibly activating platelet cyclooxygenase-1.
items.explain: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1, reducing thromboxane A2 production and platelet aggregation.

questions.q: About ABO and Rh blood groups:

items.text: Group A red cells express A antigen on their surface and plasma normally contains anti-B antibodies.
items.explain: ABO antibodies are directed against the antigen absent from the individual's red cells.

items.text: Group O red cells lack both A and B antigens.
items.explain: Group O erythrocytes do not express A or B carbohydrate antigens.

items.text: An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus may become sensitised to the D antigen.
items.explain: Foetal red cells entering maternal circulation can induce anti-D formation in an unsensitised Rh-negative mother.

items.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin is used to treat established severe fetal anaemia after haemolytic disease has developed.
items.explain: Anti-D immunoglobulin prevents maternal sensitisation; it is not a treatment for established fetal anaemia.

items.text: Lung compliance is the change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure.
items.explain: Compliance describes the distensibility of the lungs.

items.text: Pulmonary surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension and increases lung compliance.
items.explain: Surfactant reduces the collapsing force at the air-liquid interface and makes lung expansion easier.

items.text: In quiet inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and moves inferiorly.
items.explain: Diaphragmatic contraction increases thoracic vertical dimension and contributes to negative intrathoracic pressure.

items.text: Airway resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of airway radius under laminar flow conditions.
items.explain: Poiseuille's relationship predicts a strong inverse fourth-power dependence on radius for laminar flow in a rigid tube.

questions.q: About the chemical properties of biomolecules:

items.text: Amino acids contain both an amino group and a carboxyl group.
items.explain: The common structure of an amino acid includes an amino group, carboxyl group and variable side chain.

items.text: At physiological pH, many amino acids exist predominantly as zwitterions.
items.explain: Their amino and carboxyl groups are commonly ionised, giving both positive and negative charges.

items.text: A peptide bond is formed by hydrolysis between two amino acids.
items.explain: A peptide bond is formed by a condensation reaction; hydrolysis breaks the bond.

items.text: Phospholipids are amphipathic molecules with hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions.
items.explain: Their polar head groups interact with water while their nonpolar tails avoid it.

questions.q: About selected inborn errors of metabolism:

items.text: Phenylketonuria commonly results from impaired conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine.
items.explain: Most classic PKU is caused by phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency; tetrahydrobiopterin defects can also impair phenylalanine metabolism.

items.text: Untreated classic phenylketonuria may cause neurodevelopmental impairment.
items.explain: Accumulation of phenylalanine and related metabolic disturbances can damage the developing brain.

items.text: Maple syrup urine disease is classically caused by deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase.
items.explain: Defective oxidative decarboxylation leads to accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, valine and their ketoacids.

items.text: Alkaptonuria results from deficiency of homogentisate oxidase and causes accumulation of homogentisic acid.
items.explain: Homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency leads to ochronosis and darkening of urine on standing.

questions.q: About the biochemistry of skeletal muscle contraction:

items.text: Calcium binds to troponin C in skeletal muscle.
items.explain: Calcium binding to troponin C shifts the troponin-tropomyosin complex and exposes actin's myosin-binding sites.

items.text: ATP binding to myosin causes myosin to detach from actin.
items.explain: ATP binding reduces myosin's affinity for actin, allowing cross-bridge detachment.

items.text: Hydrolysis of ATP by the myosin head helps re-cock the myosin head for another cross-bridge cycle.
items.explain: ATP hydrolysis energises the myosin head before it binds actin again.

items.text: In skeletal muscle, calcium initiates contraction by binding directly to tropomyosin.
items.explain: Calcium binds troponin C; tropomyosin moves as a consequence of the troponin conformational change.

items.text: Haem contains a porphyrin ring with a central ferrous iron atom.
items.explain: The iron in functional haem is in the Fe2+ state and binds oxygen reversibly in haemoglobin.

items.text: Each haemoglobin molecule can bind up to four oxygen molecules.
items.explain: Each of its four haem groups can bind one oxygen molecule.

items.text: The globin chains of adult haemoglobin A are composed of two alpha and two beta chains.
items.explain: HbA is the predominant adult haemoglobin, with an alpha2-beta2 structure.

items.text: Bilirubin is produced directly from the breakdown of the globin portion of haemoglobin.
items.explain: Haem is degraded to biliverdin and then bilirubin; globin is broken down into amino acids.

questions.q: About molecular biology and protein synthesis:

items.text: The genetic code is read in non-overlapping triplets called codons during translation.
items.explain: Ribosomes read mRNA in successive three-nucleotide codons.

items.text: AUG commonly serves as the initiation codon and encodes methionine.
items.explain: AUG is the usual start codon; in bacteria the initiating amino acid is formylmethionine.

items.text: The genetic code is degenerate, meaning that one codon can specify several different amino acids.
items.explain: Degeneracy means that several codons can encode the same amino acid.

items.text: Peptidyl transferase activity of the ribosome catalyses peptide bond formation.
items.explain: The ribosomal RNA of the large subunit catalyses peptide bond formation.

questions.q: About the structure and functions of the skin:

items.text: The epidermis is an avascular epithelial layer.
items.explain: The epidermis contains no blood vessels and receives nutrients by diffusion from the underlying dermis.

items.text: The dermis is composed primarily of keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
items.explain: The dermis is connective tissue containing collagen, elastic fibres, vessels, nerves and skin appendages; keratinised stratified squamous epithelium forms the epidermis.

items.text: The stratum lucidum is normally prominent in thick skin of the palms and soles.
items.explain: The stratum lucidum is a clear layer found in thick skin and is absent from typical thin skin.

items.text: Eccrine sweat glands usually release their secretion into hair follicles.
items.explain: Eccrine glands open directly onto the skin surface; apocrine glands commonly open into hair follicles.

questions.q: About the fascia and anatomical subdivisions of the neck:

items.text: The platysma lies in the superficial fascia of the neck.
items.explain: The platysma is a thin subcutaneous muscle within the superficial cervical fascia.

items.text: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia encloses the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
items.explain: The investing layer splits to surround both sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.

items.text: The carotid sheath normally contains the sympathetic trunk.
items.explain: The carotid sheath contains the carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus nerve; the sympathetic trunk lies posterior to it, outside the sheath.

items.text: The posterior triangle is bounded anteriorly by the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid.
items.explain: Its other principal boundaries are the anterior border of trapezius posteriorly and the middle third of the clavicle inferiorly.

questions.q: About the organisation of skeletal muscle:

items.text: The endomysium surrounds an individual muscle fibre.
items.explain: Endomysium is the delicate connective tissue around each muscle cell.

items.text: The perimysium surrounds a fascicle of muscle fibres.
items.explain: Perimysium groups muscle fibres into fascicles.

items.text: The epimysium surrounds each individual myofibril.
items.explain: Epimysium surrounds the whole muscle; myofibrils are intracellular contractile structures.

items.text: Skeletal muscle fibres are generally multinucleated, with nuclei located peripherally.
items.explain: Developing myoblasts fuse to form long multinucleated fibres whose nuclei usually lie beneath the sarcolemma.

questions.q: About the histology of endocrine glands:

items.text: The thyroid gland stores its hormone precursor extracellularly in follicular colloid.
items.explain: Thyroglobulin in the follicular lumen provides an extracellular store for thyroid hormone precursors.

items.text: Parafollicular C cells produce calcitonin.
items.explain: Thyroid C cells secrete calcitonin, which can reduce osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.

items.text: The adrenal cortex is arranged into zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata and zona reticularis.
items.explain: These three cortical zones have characteristic cellular arrangements and steroid products.

items.text: The adrenal medulla is derived embryologically from mesoderm.
items.explain: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla derive from neural crest cells, which are ectodermal in origin.

items.text: The primitive heart tube begins to develop during the third week of embryonic development.
items.explain: Cardiac progenitor cells form the cardiogenic region early in week three, and the paired tubes fuse into a primitive heart tube.

items.text: The truncus arteriosus contributes to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
items.explain: Conotruncal septation divides the outflow tract into the aortic and pulmonary channels.

items.text: The foramen ovale allows blood to pass from the left atrium to the right atrium in fetal life.
items.explain: The fetal foramen ovale directs blood from the right atrium into the left atrium, bypassing the pulmonary circulation.

items.text: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta.
items.explain: This fetal shunt diverts much of the right ventricular output away from the unexpanded lungs.

items.text: The first heart sound is associated principally with closure of the atrioventricular valves.
items.explain: S1 occurs at the beginning of ventricular systole when the mitral and tricuspid valves close.

items.text: The second heart sound is associated with closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves.
items.explain: S2 marks the end of ventricular ejection and the beginning of ventricular diastole.

items.text: During isovolumetric ventricular contraction, all four cardiac valves are closed.
items.explain: Ventricular pressure rises after AV valve closure but before semilunar valve opening, so ventricular volume remains constant.

items.text: Ventricular filling occurs only during atrial systole.
items.explain: Most ventricular filling is passive during early and middle diastole; atrial contraction contributes the final portion.

items.text: The P wave represents atrial depolarisation.
items.explain: Atrial depolarisation precedes atrial contraction and is represented by the P wave.

items.text: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation.
items.explain: The QRS complex reflects the spread of depolarisation through the ventricles; atrial repolarisation is usually obscured.

items.text: The T wave represents ventricular repolarisation.
items.explain: The T wave corresponds to ventricular recovery of membrane potential.

items.text: The PR interval is measured from the beginning of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave.
items.explain: The PR interval extends from the onset of the P wave to the onset of the QRS complex.

questions.q: About cardiac output and stroke volume:

items.text: Cardiac output is the product of heart rate and stroke volume.
items.explain: Cardiac output is calculated as heart rate multiplied by the volume ejected by a ventricle per beat.

items.text: Stroke volume is equal to end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume.
items.explain: The difference between ventricular volume before and after systole is the volume ejected per beat.

items.text: An increase in venous return can increase stroke volume through the Frank-Starling mechanism.
items.explain: Greater ventricular filling stretches myocardial fibres and, within physiological limits, increases force of contraction.

items.text: An increase in afterload always increases stroke volume in an otherwise unchanged ventricle.
items.explain: An increased afterload tends to oppose ejection and can reduce stroke volume if other factors remain unchanged.

questions.q: About renal regulation of acid-base balance:

items.text: Most filtered bicarbonate is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.
items.explain: The proximal tubule reclaims the majority of filtered bicarbonate, largely through hydrogen-ion secretion and carbonic anhydrase-dependent reactions.

items.text: The kidneys generate new bicarbonate when they excrete hydrogen ions as titratable acid or ammonium.
items.explain: Excretion of acid buffered by phosphate or as ammonium adds new bicarbonate to the extracellular fluid.

items.text: The collecting duct can contribute to acid secretion through alpha-intercalated cells.
items.explain: Alpha-intercalated cells secrete hydrogen ions and return bicarbonate to the blood.

items.text: In chronic respiratory acidosis, renal compensation consists of increased bicarbonate excretion.
items.explain: The kidneys compensate by increasing bicarbonate reabsorption and generation while increasing net acid excretion.

items.text: The detrusor muscle is composed predominantly of smooth muscle.
items.explain: The detrusor forms the muscular wall of the urinary bladder and contracts to expel urine.

items.text: Parasympathetic outflow from sacral spinal segments promotes detrusor contraction.
items.explain: Pelvic parasympathetic nerves from S2–S4 facilitate bladder emptying.

items.text: The external urethral sphincter is composed of skeletal muscle and is under voluntary control.
items.explain: The striated external sphincter is supplied by the pudendal nerve and permits voluntary continence.

items.text: Sympathetic activity generally promotes bladder emptying by contracting the detrusor.
items.explain: Sympathetic activity favours urine storage by relaxing the detrusor and increasing outlet resistance.

questions.q: About polymerase chain reaction and recombinant DNA technology:

items.text: PCR requires repeated cycles of DNA denaturation, primer annealing and extension.
items.explain: These three temperature-controlled stages separate DNA strands, allow primers to bind and permit DNA polymerase to extend them.

items.text: A thermostable DNA polymerase is used in conventional PCR.
items.explain: Thermostable enzymes such as Taq polymerase withstand repeated high-temperature denaturation steps.

items.text: PCR primers are designed to bind to the same DNA strand at the same end of the target sequence.
items.explain: The two primers anneal to opposite strands flanking the target, with their 3-prime ends oriented toward the region to be amplified.

items.text: Restriction endonucleases can generate DNA fragments with compatible ends for ligation into vectors.
items.explain: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific recognition sequences; compatible ends can be joined by DNA ligase.

questions.sub: Phase I and phase II biotransformation
questions.q: About the biotransformation of drugs and xenobiotics:

items.text: Cytochrome P450 enzymes catalyse many phase I oxidation reactions.
items.explain: The CYP enzyme family carries out numerous oxidative reactions that introduce or expose functional groups.

items.text: Phase II reactions commonly involve conjugation with endogenous molecules.
items.explain: Conjugation with glucuronic acid, sulfate, glutathione or other groups often increases polarity.

items.text: All phase I reactions necessarily make a compound less toxic.
items.explain: Biotransformation can detoxify compounds or bioactivate them to reactive or toxic metabolites.

items.text: Glucuronidation is a common conjugation reaction catalysed by UDP-glucuronosyltransferases.
items.explain: UGT enzymes transfer glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronic acid to suitable substrates.

items.text: A typical immunoglobulin monomer contains two heavy chains and two light chains.
items.explain: The four polypeptide chains are linked by disulphide bonds and non-covalent interactions.

items.text: The variable regions of heavy and light chains contribute to antigen binding.
items.explain: The paired variable domains form the antigen-binding site and determine much of antibody specificity.

items.text: IgM is usually the predominant immunoglobulin class in a secondary immune response.
items.explain: IgG is usually the predominant antibody class in secondary systemic responses; IgM is typically produced early in a primary response.

items.text: Secretory IgA is important in mucosal immune defence.
items.explain: Dimeric secretory IgA is transported across mucosal epithelium and helps neutralise pathogens at mucosal surfaces.

items.text: A nucleotide consists of a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and one or more phosphate groups.
items.explain: The base and sugar form a nucleoside; addition of phosphate produces a nucleotide.

items.text: Purine bases include adenine and guanine.
items.explain: Adenine and guanine are the two purines found in nucleic acids.

items.text: Pyrimidine bases include adenine, guanine and cytosine.
items.explain: Cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines; adenine and guanine are purines.

items.text: Ribonucleotides contain ribose, whereas deoxyribonucleotides contain 2-deoxyribose.
items.explain: The sugar at the 2-prime carbon distinguishes ribose from deoxyribose.

questions.q: About selected inborn errors of amino acid metabolism:

items.text: Classic phenylketonuria commonly results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase activity.
items.explain: Reduced conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine causes phenylalanine accumulation.

items.text: Untreated classic phenylketonuria may cause neurodevelopmental impairment.
items.explain: Persistently elevated phenylalanine is neurotoxic and can impair brain development.

items.text: Maple syrup urine disease is caused by impaired branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase activity.
items.explain: Deficiency of this enzyme complex impairs oxidative decarboxylation of leucine, isoleucine and valine ketoacids.

items.text: Alkaptonuria is caused by deficiency of homogentisate oxidase and typically produces dark urine on standing.
items.explain: Homogentisic acid accumulates and oxidises, causing urine to darken and contributing to ochronosis.

questions.q: About hormone receptors and intracellular signalling:

items.text: Steroid hormones commonly act through intracellular receptors that regulate gene transcription.
items.explain: Lipophilic steroid hormones cross the cell membrane and bind cytosolic or nuclear receptors that influence transcription.

items.text: Peptide hormones generally bind to receptors on the cell surface.
items.explain: Peptides are usually hydrophilic and signal through membrane receptors and intracellular second-messenger pathways.

items.text: The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase.
items.explain: Insulin binding activates receptor autophosphorylation and downstream signalling pathways.

items.text: All hormones act exclusively through cyclic AMP as their second messenger.
items.explain: Hormones use several signalling mechanisms, including cAMP, IP3/DAG, calcium, receptor tyrosine kinases and intracellular nuclear receptors.

questions.q: About the pleura and pleural cavities:

items.text: The parietal pleura receives its sensory innervation from somatic nerves.
items.explain: Intercostal and phrenic nerves supply the parietal pleura and make it pain-sensitive.

items.text: The visceral pleura is highly sensitive to pain from ordinary mechanical irritation.
items.explain: The visceral pleura has autonomic innervation and is relatively insensitive to pain.

items.text: The costodiaphragmatic recess is the lowest part of the pleural cavity in the upright position.
items.explain: The recess lies between costal and diaphragmatic pleura and can receive fluid when a patient is upright.

items.text: The phrenic nerve supplies the peripheral costal pleura.
items.explain: The peripheral costal pleura is supplied by intercostal nerves; the phrenic nerve supplies mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The lower oesophagus contains a portosystemic venous connection.
items.explain: Oesophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein communicate with systemic azygos tributaries.

items.text: The paraumbilical veins communicate with superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall.
items.explain: Paraumbilical portal tributaries communicate with superficial epigastric veins around the umbilicus.

items.text: The superior rectal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava.
items.explain: The superior rectal vein drains to the inferior mesenteric vein and portal system.

items.text: Portal hypertension may produce dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus.
items.explain: Recanalised paraumbilical channels can produce caput medusae.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula.
items.explain: Its superficial position at the fibular neck makes it vulnerable to trauma and compression.

items.text: The deep fibular nerve supplies the muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg.
items.explain: The superficial fibular nerve supplies the lateral compartment; the deep fibular nerve supplies the anterior compartment.

items.text: A common fibular nerve lesion may produce foot drop.
items.explain: Weakness of ankle dorsiflexors causes difficulty clearing the toes during swing phase.

items.text: The common fibular nerve carries fibres from the L2–L4 spinal nerve roots.
items.explain: Its root value is usually L4–S2, through the sciatic nerve.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: About the histology of the renal corpuscle:

items.text: The glomerular filtration barrier includes fenestrated endothelial cells.
items.explain: Fenestrated glomerular capillary endothelium forms the first layer of the filtration barrier.

items.text: Podocyte foot processes form filtration slits bridged by slit diaphragms.
items.explain: Interdigitating podocyte processes create filtration slits whose diaphragms contribute to selective filtration.

items.text: The parietal layer of Bowman's capsule is formed by simple cuboidal epithelium.
items.explain: The parietal layer is simple squamous epithelium; the visceral layer consists of podocytes.

items.text: Mesangial cells provide structural support and can contract.
items.explain: Mesangial cells support capillary loops, clear trapped material and influence filtration surface area by contraction.

questions.q: About embryological development of the urinary system:

items.text: The definitive kidney develops from the metanephros.
items.explain: The metanephros forms the permanent kidneys, beginning development during the fifth week.

items.text: The ureteric bud gives rise to the nephron loop and distal convoluted tubule.
items.explain: The metanephric mesenchyme forms nephron components; the ureteric bud forms the collecting system.

items.text: The ureteric bud forms the ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts.
items.explain: The ureteric bud branches repeatedly to form the drainage and collecting system of the kidney.

items.text: The kidneys initially develop in the pelvis and ascend to the lumbar region.
items.explain: The developing kidneys become positioned higher as the embryo grows and the caudal body region changes.

questions.sub: Neural and chemical control of breathing

items.text: Central chemoreceptors respond mainly to changes in hydrogen-ion concentration in brain extracellular fluid.
items.explain: Arterial carbon dioxide crosses the blood-brain barrier and generates hydrogen ions in cerebrospinal fluid and brain interstitial fluid.

items.text: Peripheral chemoreceptors are located in the carotid and aortic bodies.
items.explain: Carotid bodies lie at the carotid bifurcations and aortic bodies are near the aortic arch.

items.text: Carotid bodies respond only when arterial oxygen tension falls below normal by a small amount.
items.explain: Their ventilatory response becomes particularly strong when PaO2 falls substantially, especially below about 60 mmHg; they also detect carbon dioxide and pH.

items.text: The medullary respiratory network contributes to the basic rhythm of breathing.
items.explain: Medullary neuronal networks generate and shape respiratory motor output, with pontine centres modifying the pattern.
