questions.q: About spirometry and pulmonary function testing:

items.text: Forced vital capacity is the total volume forcibly expired after a maximal inspiration.
items.explain: FVC measures the volume expelled during a forced expiratory manoeuvre after full inspiration.

items.text: Residual volume can be measured directly by ordinary spirometry.
items.explain: Spirometry cannot measure residual volume or capacities that include it; gas-dilution or body-plethysmography methods are used.

items.text: An obstructive ventilatory defect commonly reduces the FEV1/FVC ratio.
items.explain: Airflow limitation reduces FEV1 disproportionately to FVC, lowering the ratio.

items.text: A restrictive ventilatory defect is confirmed by an increased total lung capacity.
items.explain: Restriction is characterised by reduced total lung capacity; spirometry may suggest it but lung-volume measurement confirms it.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Segmentation contractions mix intestinal contents with digestive secretions.
items.explain: Segmenting contractions repeatedly divide and remix chyme, promoting contact with the mucosa.

items.text: Peristalsis normally propels gastrointestinal contents aborally.
items.explain: Coordinated contraction behind and relaxation ahead of a bolus produce forward propulsion.

items.text: The migrating motor complex is most prominent during the fed state.
items.explain: The migrating motor complex occurs during fasting and is interrupted by feeding.

items.text: The ileocecal sphincter helps regulate the passage of contents from ileum to caecum.
items.explain: Its tone and coordinated relaxation regulate ileal emptying and limit reflux from the colon.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Insulin is secreted by pancreatic beta cells.
items.explain: Beta cells in the islets of Langerhans synthesise and release insulin.

items.text: Glucagon secretion is stimulated by a rise in blood glucose.
items.explain: High glucose suppresses glucagon secretion; hypoglycaemia and amino acids can stimulate it.

items.text: Insulin promotes glucose uptake in skeletal muscle partly by recruiting GLUT4 to the cell membrane.
items.explain: Insulin signalling promotes translocation of GLUT4-containing vesicles to the plasma membrane in muscle and adipose tissue.

items.text: Somatostatin from pancreatic delta cells inhibits secretion of several islet hormones.
items.explain: Somatostatin has paracrine inhibitory effects on both insulin and glucagon secretion.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Most coronary blood flow to the left ventricle occurs during diastole.
items.explain: Left ventricular contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels, so perfusion is greatest during diastole.

items.text: The cerebral circulation normally has a strong capacity for autoregulation.
items.explain: Cerebral arterioles adjust resistance to help maintain blood flow across a range of perfusion pressures.

items.text: The blood-brain barrier is formed principally by fenestrated cerebral capillary endothelium.
items.explain: It depends on tight junctions between non-fenestrated endothelial cells, supported by pericytes and astrocytic end-feet.

items.text: Increased arterial carbon dioxide generally causes cerebral vasoconstriction.
items.explain: Increased PaCO2 lowers perivascular pH and causes cerebral vasodilation, increasing cerebral blood flow.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Thiamine is required for the activity of transketolase.
items.explain: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a coenzyme for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway.

items.text: Pellagra is associated with deficiency of niacin.
items.explain: Niacin deficiency reduces NAD and NADP availability and classically causes dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.

items.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency typically causes microcytic anaemia.
items.explain: Vitamin B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and typically causes megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia.

items.text: Biotin functions as a coenzyme for carboxylation reactions.
items.explain: Biotin carries activated carbon dioxide in carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Transamination commonly requires pyridoxal phosphate as a coenzyme.
items.explain: Pyridoxal phosphate, derived from vitamin B6, transfers amino groups in aminotransferase reactions.

items.text: Glutamate can undergo oxidative deamination to release ammonium.
items.explain: Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyses oxidative deamination, linking amino acid metabolism with ammonia handling.

items.text: Urea is synthesised primarily in skeletal muscle.
items.explain: The urea cycle occurs mainly in hepatocytes, where toxic ammonia is converted to urea.

items.text: Essential amino acids must be supplied in the diet because human tissues cannot synthesise them in adequate amounts.
items.explain: Dietary intake is required for the essential amino acids because endogenous synthesis is absent or insufficient.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The fluid-mosaic model describes proteins embedded in or associated with a lipid bilayer.
items.explain: Membrane lipids and many proteins can move laterally, producing a dynamic mosaic structure.

items.text: Cholesterol generally reduces membrane permeability to small water-soluble molecules.
items.explain: Cholesterol modulates lipid packing and reduces permeability while also buffering membrane fluidity.

items.text: Integral membrane proteins can be removed from membranes by high-salt washing alone.
items.explain: High salt commonly removes peripheral proteins; integral proteins require disruption of hydrophobic interactions, often with detergents.

items.text: The carbohydrate portions of most plasma-membrane glycoproteins face the extracellular surface.
items.explain: Membrane carbohydrates are predominantly on the non-cytosolic surface, contributing to the glycocalyx.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Vitamin C enhances non-haem iron absorption in the intestine.
items.explain: Ascorbate reduces ferric iron to the more readily absorbed ferrous form and improves non-haem iron bioavailability.

items.text: Hepcidin increases intestinal iron absorption by promoting ferroportin activity.
items.explain: Hepcidin binds ferroportin and promotes its internalisation and degradation, reducing iron export into plasma.

items.text: Vitamin D promotes intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate.
items.explain: Active vitamin D increases expression of transport proteins involved in intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption.

items.text: Vitamin K is required for gamma-carboxylation of several coagulation factors.
items.explain: Vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation enables factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S to bind calcium.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: About molecular biology and gene expression:

items.text: RNA polymerase synthesises RNA in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction.
items.explain: RNA polymerase adds each incoming ribonucleotide to the 3-prime hydroxyl end of the growing RNA chain.

items.text: During translation, the ribosome reads mRNA in the 3-prime to 5-prime direction.
items.explain: The ribosome moves along mRNA in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction.

items.text: A codon consists of three nucleotides in the mRNA sequence.
items.explain: Each codon specifies an amino acid or a translation termination signal.

items.text: The anticodon of a tRNA base-pairs with a complementary codon on mRNA.
items.explain: Codon-anticodon pairing positions the aminoacyl-tRNA for addition of its amino acid to the growing polypeptide.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Skeletal muscle fibres are multinucleated cells with peripheral nuclei.
items.explain: Skeletal muscle fibres form by myoblast fusion and characteristically have multiple peripheral nuclei.

items.text: The A band becomes shorter during skeletal muscle contraction.
items.explain: The A band corresponds to the length of thick filaments and remains essentially constant; the I band and H zone shorten.

items.text: The sarcomere extends from one Z disc to the next.
items.explain: Z discs define the boundaries of a sarcomere, the basic contractile unit of striated muscle.

items.text: Satellite cells contribute to skeletal muscle repair and regeneration.
items.explain: Satellite cells are resident myogenic stem cells that can proliferate and contribute nuclei to damaged fibres.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Collagen fibres provide tensile strength to connective tissues.
items.explain: Collagen resists stretching forces and is a major structural component of connective tissue.

items.text: Elastic fibres allow tissues to recoil after stretching.
items.explain: Elastin-rich fibres provide extensibility and recoil in structures such as large arteries and elastic ligaments.

items.text: Fibroblasts are primarily responsible for producing connective tissue extracellular matrix.
items.explain: Fibroblasts synthesise collagen, elastin, proteoglycans and other matrix components.

items.text: Mast cells are the principal cells responsible for synthesising collagen fibres.
items.explain: Fibroblasts are the principal collagen-producing cells; mast cells participate in inflammatory and allergic responses.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Implantation normally begins approximately six to seven days after fertilisation.
items.explain: The blastocyst begins attaching to the endometrium near the end of the first week.

items.text: The trophoblast differentiates into cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast.
items.explain: These two trophoblastic layers participate in implantation and early placental development.

items.text: The embryoblast forms the trophoblast and the chorionic villi.
items.explain: The trophoblast contributes to chorionic and placental structures; the embryoblast forms the embryo proper and associated tissues.

items.text: The bilaminar embryonic disc consists of epiblast and hypoblast.
items.explain: During the second week, the embryoblast differentiates into these two cell layers.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells responsible for bone resorption.
items.explain: Osteoclasts dissolve mineral and degrade organic matrix during bone resorption.

items.text: Osteoblasts develop from osteoclast precursors.
items.explain: Osteoblasts arise from mesenchymal lineage cells, whereas osteoclasts arise from monocyte-macrophage lineage precursors.

items.text: Endochondral ossification involves replacement of a cartilage model by bone.
items.explain: A hyaline cartilage model is progressively replaced by bone during endochondral ossification.

items.text: The epiphyseal growth plate permits longitudinal growth of long bones.
items.explain: Chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy at the growth plate support lengthening before epiphyseal closure.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The first pharyngeal arch contributes to the maxilla and mandible.
items.explain: First-arch mesenchyme contributes to the maxillary and mandibular prominences and associated skeletal structures.

items.text: The second pharyngeal arch is associated with the facial nerve.
items.explain: The nerve of the second arch is the facial nerve, cranial nerve VII.

items.text: The third pharyngeal arch is associated with the glossopharyngeal nerve.
items.explain: The glossopharyngeal nerve, cranial nerve IX, is the nerve of the third arch.

items.text: The fourth and sixth arches are both supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.
items.explain: The vagus nerve supplies the fourth and sixth arches through its superior and recurrent laryngeal branches.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The glomerular filtration rate is influenced by the net filtration pressure and filtration coefficient.
items.explain: GFR depends on the balance of Starling forces across the glomerular membrane and the filtration coefficient.

items.text: Constriction of the afferent arteriole generally reduces glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure.
items.explain: Afferent constriction reduces renal blood flow and glomerular capillary pressure, lowering GFR.

items.text: Glucose is normally reabsorbed mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule.
items.explain: Sodium-glucose cotransporters in the proximal tubule reclaim filtered glucose under normal conditions.

items.text: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is highly permeable to water.
items.explain: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs solute but is relatively impermeable to water, helping dilute tubular fluid.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The loop of Henle contributes to the medullary osmotic gradient through countercurrent multiplication.
items.explain: Differential solute and water permeability along the loop establishes a corticomedullary osmotic gradient.

items.text: Antidiuretic hormone increases water permeability in the collecting ducts.
items.explain: ADH promotes insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane of collecting-duct principal cells.

items.text: The vasa recta help preserve the medullary osmotic gradient.
items.explain: Their countercurrent exchange arrangement limits washout of medullary solutes.

items.text: A person with complete absence of ADH action typically produces a small volume of highly concentrated urine.
items.explain: Loss of ADH action causes impaired water reabsorption and typically produces large volumes of dilute urine.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: About the regulation of body temperature:

items.text: The hypothalamus plays a central role in integrating thermoregulatory responses.
items.explain: Hypothalamic circuits integrate thermal information and coordinate autonomic, endocrine and behavioural responses.

items.text: Sweating promotes heat loss mainly through evaporation.
items.explain: Evaporation of sweat from the skin surface removes heat from the body.

items.text: Cutaneous vasoconstriction increases heat loss from the body.
items.explain: Cutaneous vasoconstriction reduces skin blood flow and conserves heat.

items.text: Shivering increases heat production through involuntary skeletal muscle activity.
items.explain: Rapid involuntary muscle contractions increase metabolic heat production.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: About the transport of respiratory gases:

items.text: Most oxygen in arterial blood is carried bound to haemoglobin.
items.explain: Only a small fraction of oxygen is physically dissolved in plasma; most is reversibly bound to haemoglobin.

items.text: The oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the right when carbon dioxide and hydrogen-ion concentrations rise.
items.explain: Increased CO2 and H+ reduce haemoglobin oxygen affinity, facilitating oxygen unloading in tissues.

items.text: Carbon dioxide is transported mainly as carbaminohaemoglobin.
items.explain: Most carbon dioxide is transported as bicarbonate ions, with smaller fractions dissolved or bound to proteins.

items.text: The chloride shift facilitates transport of carbon dioxide from tissues in red blood cells.
items.explain: Bicarbonate exits red cells in exchange for chloride, maintaining electrical neutrality during CO2 carriage.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The rapid upstroke of a typical neuronal action potential is primarily due to voltage-gated sodium-channel opening.
items.explain: Sodium influx produces the rapid depolarising phase of the neuronal action potential.

items.text: The absolute refractory period is mainly associated with inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels.
items.explain: Inactivated sodium channels cannot reopen immediately, preventing another action potential during this period.

items.text: Increasing stimulus strength normally increases the amplitude of an individual action potential.
items.explain: Action potentials are all-or-none; stronger stimuli generally increase firing frequency rather than action-potential amplitude.

items.text: Myelination increases conduction velocity partly by enabling saltatory conduction.
items.explain: Action potentials are regenerated at nodes of Ranvier, allowing rapid conduction between nodes.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The Michaelis constant is the substrate concentration at which reaction velocity is half the maximum velocity in simple Michaelis-Menten kinetics.
items.explain: For a Michaelis-Menten enzyme, Km corresponds to the substrate concentration at one-half Vmax.

items.text: A competitive inhibitor typically increases the apparent Km without changing Vmax.
items.explain: Competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration, leaving Vmax unchanged.

items.text: A pure noncompetitive inhibitor increases Vmax.
items.explain: Pure noncompetitive inhibition reduces Vmax while leaving Km unchanged.

items.text: Enzymes alter the equilibrium constant of the reactions they catalyse.
items.explain: Enzymes lower activation energy and accelerate attainment of equilibrium but do not change the reaction equilibrium constant.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Beta-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids occurs mainly in the mitochondrial matrix.
items.explain: Fatty acyl-CoA undergoes repeated beta-oxidation cycles in the mitochondrial matrix after transport into mitochondria.

items.text: Carnitine is involved in transporting long-chain fatty acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
items.explain: The carnitine shuttle transfers long-chain acyl groups into the mitochondrial matrix.

items.text: Malonyl-CoA activates carnitine palmitoyltransferase I.
items.explain: Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT I, limiting fatty acid entry into mitochondria during fatty acid synthesis.

items.text: Each cycle of beta-oxidation of a saturated even-chain fatty acyl-CoA generally yields one acetyl-CoA, one NADH and one FADH2.
items.explain: The four-step cycle produces reducing equivalents and removes a two-carbon acetyl-CoA unit.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The first step of haem synthesis occurs in mitochondria.
items.explain: ALA synthase catalyses the condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA in mitochondria.

items.text: Lead poisoning can inhibit aminolevulinate dehydratase and ferrochelatase.
items.explain: Lead inhibits key enzymes in haem synthesis, including ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase.

items.text: Bilirubin is produced from haem degradation.
items.explain: Haem oxygenase converts haem to biliverdin, which is subsequently reduced to bilirubin.

items.text: Unconjugated bilirubin is highly water-soluble and is freely excreted in urine.
items.explain: Unconjugated bilirubin is poorly water-soluble, circulates bound to albumin and is not normally filtered into urine.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: DNA polymerases generally require a primer with a free 3-prime hydroxyl group.
items.explain: DNA polymerases extend an existing primer by adding nucleotides to its 3-prime end.

items.text: The leading strand is synthesised discontinuously as Okazaki fragments.
items.explain: The leading strand is synthesised continuously toward the replication fork; the lagging strand forms Okazaki fragments.

items.text: DNA ligase seals nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone.
items.explain: DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds to join adjacent DNA fragments.

items.text: Mismatch repair helps correct errors that escape DNA polymerase proofreading.
items.explain: Mismatch repair recognises and removes incorrectly paired bases remaining after replication.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: The antigen-binding site of an antibody is formed by variable regions of its heavy and light chains.
items.explain: Variable domains of both chains contribute to the antigen-binding surface.

items.text: The Fc region is primarily responsible for antigen recognition specificity.
items.explain: Antigen specificity is determined by the Fab variable regions; the Fc region mediates effector functions and receptor interactions.

items.text: Affinity describes the strength of binding between one antigenic epitope and one antibody-binding site.
items.explain: Affinity refers to the strength of an individual antigen-antibody binding interaction.

items.text: Avidity reflects the combined strength of multiple antigen-antibody interactions.
items.explain: Avidity is the overall functional binding strength arising from multiple binding interactions.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding the cervical fascia and deep neck spaces:

items.text: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia encloses the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
items.explain: The investing layer splits to enclose both sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, and contributes to the roof of the posterior triangle.

items.text: The pretracheal fascia surrounds the carotid sheath and its contents.
items.explain: The carotid sheath is a distinct fascial condensation; the pretracheal layer encloses the visceral compartment and is related to the infrahyoid muscles.

items.text: The retropharyngeal space can provide a route for infection to descend into the mediastinum.
items.explain: Potential spaces posterior to the pharynx communicate inferiorly with the mediastinum, allowing spread of deep neck infection.

items.text: The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia forms the anterior boundary of the retropharyngeal space.
items.explain: The prevertebral fascia forms its posterior boundary; the buccopharyngeal fascia covers the pharynx anteriorly.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.sub: Internal capsule and cerebral blood supply
questions.q: Regarding the internal capsule and its vascular supply:

items.text: The posterior limb of the internal capsule contains corticospinal fibres.
items.explain: Corticospinal fibres descend through the posterior limb before entering the cerebral peduncle and brainstem.

items.text: The genu of the internal capsule is associated with corticobulbar fibres.
items.explain: Corticobulbar fibres predominantly pass through the genu to reach motor nuclei of cranial nerves.

items.text: The lenticulostriate arteries usually arise from the anterior cerebral artery.
items.explain: The lenticulostriate (lateral striate) arteries usually arise from the middle cerebral artery and supply deep structures including parts of the internal capsule.

items.text: A lesion of the posterior limb may produce contralateral motor weakness because many descending motor fibres are concentrated there.
items.explain: Compact arrangement of corticospinal fibres means a relatively small lesion can cause marked contralateral weakness.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding the histology of the uterine tube and ovary:

items.text: Ciliated cells of the uterine tube help propel the oocyte toward the uterus.
items.explain: Ciliary beating, together with smooth-muscle contractions and tubal fluid, assists transport toward the uterine cavity.

items.text: The ampulla is the narrowest part of the uterine tube.
items.explain: The ampulla is the widest and longest segment and is the usual site of fertilisation; the intramural part is narrow.

items.text: Ovarian follicles are found predominantly in the ovarian cortex.
items.explain: The cortex contains follicles at different developmental stages within a stromal framework; the medulla is more vascular.

items.text: The corpus luteum is formed from the remnants of the ruptured follicle after ovulation.
items.explain: After ovulation, granulosa and theca interna cells luteinise to form the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding neuroglia and myelination in the nervous system:

items.text: One oligodendrocyte can contribute myelin to segments of several axons in the central nervous system.
items.explain: Oligodendrocytes extend processes to myelinate segments on multiple CNS axons.

items.text: A Schwann cell normally myelinates segments of several different axons simultaneously.
items.explain: A single myelinating Schwann cell forms one internode on one axon in the peripheral nervous system.

items.text: Microglia act as resident immune and phagocytic cells of the central nervous system.
items.explain: Microglia survey neural tissue and become activated to clear debris and participate in immune responses.

items.text: Ependymal cells line the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord.
items.explain: Ependymal cells form the epithelial-like lining of the ventricular system and central canal; specialised ependymal cells participate in the choroid plexus.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding the anatomy and lymphatic drainage of the breast:

items.text: Most lymph from the breast drains initially to the axillary lymph nodes, especially the anterior (pectoral) group.
items.explain: The majority of breast lymph, particularly from the lateral quadrants, drains to axillary nodes, commonly via the pectoral group.

items.text: The suspensory ligaments of the breast are fibrous septa extending from the dermis toward the deep fascia.
items.explain: Cooper's suspensory ligaments traverse the breast and help support its shape.

items.text: The medial quadrants of the breast have no lymphatic communication with the opposite breast.
items.explain: Medial breast lymphatics may drain to parasternal nodes and can communicate across the midline with the opposite breast.

items.text: The retromammary space permits some movement of the breast over the pectoral fascia.
items.explain: Loose connective tissue in the retromammary space allows mobility of the breast over the underlying deep fascia.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding leucocytes and innate immune defence:

items.text: Neutrophils are usually the most abundant circulating leucocytes in a healthy adult.
items.explain: Neutrophils commonly constitute the largest proportion of the circulating white blood cell differential.

items.text: Eosinophils are particularly associated with defence against helminths and allergic responses.
items.explain: Eosinophils release granule proteins involved in parasite defence and contribute to allergic inflammation.

items.text: Monocytes differentiate into tissue macrophages after leaving the circulation in many tissues.
items.explain: Circulating monocytes can migrate into tissues and differentiate into macrophages or related mononuclear phagocytes.

items.text: Basophils are the principal cells responsible for antibody production.
items.explain: Antibodies are secreted by plasma cells derived from B lymphocytes; basophils participate in inflammatory and allergic responses.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Arrival of an action potential at a presynaptic terminal opens voltage-gated calcium channels.
items.explain: Terminal depolarisation opens voltage-gated calcium channels, allowing calcium influx that triggers vesicle fusion.

items.text: Neurotransmitter release from a typical chemical synapse is independent of extracellular calcium.
items.explain: Calcium entry is the key trigger for synaptic vesicle exocytosis at most conventional chemical synapses.

items.text: An excitatory postsynaptic potential is a graded change that increases the likelihood of postsynaptic firing.
items.explain: An EPSP is usually a local depolarisation; summation may bring the postsynaptic membrane to threshold.

items.text: Chemical synaptic transmission is generally slower than electrical transmission through gap junctions.
items.explain: Neurotransmitter release, diffusion and receptor activation introduce a synaptic delay absent or much smaller in electrical synapses.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding short-term neural regulation of arterial pressure:

items.text: Carotid sinus baroreceptor afferents travel mainly in the glossopharyngeal nerve.
items.explain: Afferents from the carotid sinus travel through the carotid sinus nerve, a branch of glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

items.text: Aortic arch baroreceptor afferents travel mainly in the vagus nerve.
items.explain: Aortic baroreceptor signals are conveyed centrally through vagal afferents.

items.text: An acute rise in arterial pressure increases baroreceptor firing and reduces sympathetic outflow.
items.explain: Increased stretch raises afferent firing to the medullary cardiovascular centres, increasing vagal and reducing sympathetic activity.

items.text: Baroreceptors are the principal long-term mechanism for controlling blood volume over weeks.
items.explain: Baroreceptors are important for rapid pressure buffering; renal-body fluid mechanisms dominate long-term regulation of arterial pressure.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding the visual pathway and pupillary light reflex:

items.text: Nasal retinal fibres cross in the optic chiasm, while temporal retinal fibres remain uncrossed.
items.explain: Partial decussation at the optic chiasm allows each optic tract to carry information from the contralateral visual field.

items.text: The lateral geniculate body of the thalamus is a major relay in the conscious visual pathway.
items.explain: Retinal ganglion cell axons synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus before visual information reaches the primary visual cortex.

items.text: The afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex is carried by the oculomotor nerve.
items.explain: The optic nerve (CN II) is the afferent limb; parasympathetic fibres in the oculomotor nerve (CN III) form the efferent limb.

items.text: Light directed into one eye normally causes constriction of both pupils.
items.explain: Bilateral pretectal projections activate both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, producing direct and consensual pupillary constriction.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding digestion and absorption in the small intestine:

items.text: Bile salts facilitate lipid absorption by forming mixed micelles.
items.explain: Mixed micelles carry products of lipid digestion through the unstirred water layer to the enterocyte surface.

items.text: Most dietary iron is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
items.explain: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum; the terminal ileum is important for vitamin B12-bile salt absorption.

items.text: Glucose and galactose enter enterocytes across the apical membrane largely through sodium-dependent cotransport.
items.explain: SGLT1 couples glucose or galactose uptake to the inward sodium gradient maintained by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase.

items.text: Long-chain fatty acids are generally re-esterified within enterocytes and exported in chylomicrons.
items.explain: Long-chain fatty acids are reassembled into triacylglycerols, packaged with other lipids and apoproteins into chylomicrons, and enter lymphatic lacteals.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.sub: Amino acids, peptides and protein structure
questions.q: Regarding the chemical properties and organisation of proteins:

items.text: A peptide bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance.
items.explain: Resonance restricts rotation around the peptide C-N bond, making the peptide group relatively planar.

items.text: At its isoelectric point, an amino acid has a net electrical charge of zero.
items.explain: At the isoelectric point, positive and negative charges balance, although charged groups may still be present.

items.text: Disulphide bonds form between the side chains of two cysteine residues.
items.explain: Oxidation of two cysteine thiol groups forms a covalent disulphide bond that can stabilise protein structure.

items.text: Primary protein structure refers to the three-dimensional folding of a polypeptide into its native conformation.
items.explain: Primary structure is the amino-acid sequence; secondary, tertiary and quaternary levels describe higher-order organisation.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding selected inherited disorders of intermediary metabolism:

items.text: Classic phenylketonuria most commonly results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase activity.
items.explain: Reduced conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine causes phenylalanine accumulation; defects in tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism can produce related forms.

items.text: Untreated classic phenylketonuria may cause neurodevelopmental impairment.
items.explain: Persistently elevated phenylalanine is neurotoxic during development; early dietary treatment greatly reduces this risk.

items.text: Classic galactosaemia is commonly caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase.
items.explain: GALT deficiency leads to accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate and other metabolites after lactose exposure.

items.text: In classic galactosaemia, unrestricted milk feeding is recommended to prevent hypoglycaemia.
items.explain: Management requires prompt restriction of dietary galactose and lactose, including removal of ordinary milk.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding thyroid hormone synthesis, transport and action:

items.text: Thyroid peroxidase catalyses iodide oxidation and iodination of tyrosyl residues in thyroglobulin.
items.explain: At the apical surface, thyroid peroxidase supports iodide oxidation, organification and coupling reactions.

items.text: Most circulating T3 is secreted directly by the thyroid gland rather than formed in peripheral tissues.
items.explain: The thyroid secretes predominantly T4; much circulating T3 is generated by peripheral deiodination of T4.

items.text: Thyroid hormones circulate largely bound to plasma proteins, including thyroxine-binding globulin.
items.explain: Protein binding creates a circulating reservoir; only the small free fraction is biologically available to tissues.

items.text: Thyroid hormone receptors act mainly as intracellular nuclear receptors that regulate gene transcription.
items.explain: T3 binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors, which interact with DNA response elements and transcriptional coregulators.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding the biotransformation of drugs and xenobiotics:

items.text: Phase I reactions include oxidation, reduction and hydrolysis.
items.explain: Phase I reactions introduce or expose functional groups and commonly involve cytochrome P450 enzymes.

items.text: Phase II reactions commonly conjugate compounds with groups such as glucuronate, sulphate or glutathione.
items.explain: Conjugation generally increases polarity and often facilitates excretion, although exceptions occur.

items.text: Cytochrome P450 enzymes are located exclusively in the cytosol.
items.explain: Many clinically important microsomal CYP enzymes are associated with the smooth endoplasmic reticulum; others occur in mitochondria.

items.text: Biotransformation always converts a pharmacologically active compound into an inactive metabolite.
items.explain: Metabolism can inactivate drugs, activate prodrugs, or generate active or toxic metabolites.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

questions.q: Regarding polymerase chain reaction and molecular diagnosis:

items.text: PCR amplification requires template DNA, primers, nucleotides and a thermostable DNA polymerase.
items.explain: These components are required for repeated cycles of denaturation, primer annealing and extension.

items.text: The denaturation step of conventional PCR separates the two DNA strands by heating.
items.explain: High temperature disrupts hydrogen bonding between complementary strands, producing single-stranded templates.

items.text: Primers in conventional PCR are designed to bind to the same DNA strand at the same end of the target region.
items.explain: The two primers anneal to opposite strands flanking the target, with their 3-prime ends oriented toward the region to be amplified.

items.text: Real-time quantitative PCR can monitor amplification during cycling using a fluorescent signal.
items.explain: Fluorescence measured during amplification permits estimation of starting nucleic acid quantity within the assay's validated range.

questions.referenceScope: topic-level supporting references; individual claims still require review

items.text: Folding converts the flat embryonic disc into a more cylindrical body form.
items.explain: Cephalocaudal and lateral folding reshape the disc and incorporate part of the yolk sac into the primitive gut.

items.text: Lateral folding contributes to closure of the ventral body wall.
items.explain: The right and left body folds move ventrally and fuse in the midline, except at the umbilical region.

items.text: The intraembryonic coelom forms within extraembryonic mesoderm.
items.explain: It develops within lateral plate mesoderm, which separates into somatic and splanchnic layers.

items.text: The pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities arise from subdivisions of the intraembryonic coelom.
items.explain: The initially continuous coelomic space is partitioned during development.

items.text: Dizygotic twins arise from fertilisation of two separate oocytes.
items.explain: Two ova are fertilised by separate spermatozoa; dizygotic twins are genetically like ordinary siblings.

items.text: Monozygotic twins arise from division of a single fertilised conceptus.
items.explain: The timing of separation influences chorionicity and amnionicity.

items.text: All monozygotic twins have separate chorions and amniotic sacs.
items.explain: They may be dichorionic or monochorionic and may share an amniotic sac depending on timing.

items.text: Conjoined twins are associated with incomplete embryonic separation.
items.explain: Incomplete division of the embryonic primordium is the classic embryological explanation.

items.text: The ductus venosus allows umbilical venous blood to partly bypass hepatic sinusoids.
items.explain: It directs a substantial proportion of oxygenated blood toward the inferior vena cava.

items.text: The foramen ovale shunts blood from the right atrium to the left atrium.
items.explain: This directs relatively oxygen-rich blood toward the left ventricle and systemic circulation.

items.text: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta.
items.explain: It diverts much right ventricular output away from the high-resistance fetal lungs.

items.text: Umbilical arteries carry oxygenated blood from placenta to fetus.
items.explain: Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the placenta; the umbilical vein returns oxygenated blood.

items.text: Ribosomes on rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesise many secreted and membrane proteins.
items.explain: These proteins enter the secretory pathway for processing and sorting.

items.text: The Golgi apparatus modifies and sorts proteins for delivery to cellular destinations.
items.explain: Golgi cisternae process cargo and package it into transport vesicles.

items.text: Lysosomal hydrolases function optimally at neutral cytosolic pH.
items.explain: Lysosomal enzymes are adapted to the acidic lumen maintained by proton pumps.

items.text: Mitochondria contain their own DNA and ribosomes.
items.explain: They encode some proteins and retain a specialised protein-synthesis apparatus.

items.text: The endoneurium surrounds individual nerve fibres and associated Schwann cells.
items.explain: It is delicate connective tissue around individual fibres within a fascicle.

items.text: The perineurium encloses a bundle of nerve fibres to form a fascicle.
items.explain: Perineurial layers surround fascicles and contribute to the blood-nerve barrier.

items.text: The epineurium surrounds the entire peripheral nerve.
items.explain: It encloses fascicles and contains larger vessels and connective tissue.

items.text: Peripheral nerves lack a dedicated vascular supply.
items.explain: Vasa nervorum supply peripheral nerves through an intraneural vascular network.

items.text: The renal corpuscle consists of a glomerular tuft enclosed by Bowman's capsule.
items.explain: The corpuscle is the filtration component of the nephron.

items.text: The macula densa senses sodium chloride delivery in tubular fluid.
items.explain: It participates in tubuloglomerular feedback and signalling to juxtaglomerular cells.

items.text: Juxtaglomerular granular cells secrete renin.
items.explain: These modified smooth muscle cells are located mainly in the afferent arteriole wall.

items.text: All cortical nephrons lack a loop of Henle.
items.explain: Cortical nephrons have shorter loops; juxtamedullary nephrons have longer loops extending deep into the medulla.

questions.sub: Renal function and acute kidney injury
questions.q: Regarding renal function and acute kidney injury:

items.text: Serum creatinine may rise after a delay following an abrupt fall in GFR.
items.explain: Creatinine kinetics mean the serum concentration may lag behind acute changes in filtration.

items.text: Blood urea nitrogen is specific for intrinsic renal parenchymal disease.
items.explain: Urea is influenced by hydration, protein intake, catabolism and gastrointestinal bleeding.

items.text: Urine microscopy can help distinguish causes of acute kidney injury.
items.explain: Casts and cellular elements can suggest tubular, glomerular or interstitial pathology.

items.text: Common eGFR equations are reliable during rapidly changing serum creatinine.
items.explain: They assume approximate steady state and are unreliable during evolving acute kidney injury.

items.text: Low ionised plasma calcium stimulates parathyroid hormone secretion.
items.explain: Reduced activation of calcium-sensing receptors on chief cells promotes PTH release.

items.text: PTH increases renal tubular calcium reabsorption.
items.explain: It conserves calcium, particularly in the distal nephron.

items.text: PTH increases proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption.
items.explain: PTH reduces phosphate reabsorption, causing phosphaturia.

items.text: PTH stimulates renal production of active vitamin D.
items.explain: It stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase, increasing calcitriol formation.

items.text: Muscle spindles detect muscle length and changes in length.
items.explain: Intrafusal fibres and sensory endings signal static and dynamic stretch.

items.text: Primary muscle spindle afferents are group Ia fibres.
items.explain: Ia afferents arise from primary spindle endings.

items.text: The principal excitatory connection in the stretch reflex is polysynaptic.
items.explain: The classic Ia excitation of the homonymous alpha motor neuron is monosynaptic.

items.text: Golgi tendon organs respond to tension in the muscle-tendon unit.
items.explain: Ib afferents signal tension, particularly during active contraction.

items.text: Cutaneous vasodilation increases transfer of core heat to the skin surface.
items.explain: Increased skin blood flow facilitates heat loss to the environment.

items.text: Evaporation of sweat is an important route of heat loss.
items.explain: Evaporation removes latent heat from the skin; high humidity reduces its effectiveness.

items.text: Cutaneous vasoconstriction generally increases heat loss.
items.explain: It reduces skin blood flow and conserves heat.

items.text: Skin thermoreceptors contribute information to central thermoregulatory pathways.
items.explain: Peripheral temperature signals contribute to autonomic and behavioural responses.

items.text: The insulin receptor has intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity.
items.explain: Ligand binding triggers receptor autophosphorylation and downstream signalling.

items.text: Insulin promotes GLUT4 translocation in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.
items.explain: More GLUT4 at the cell surface increases insulin-stimulated glucose uptake.

items.text: Insulin stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis in the fed state.
items.explain: Insulin promotes glycogen synthesis and suppresses hepatic glucose output.

items.text: Insulin promotes lipogenesis and suppresses adipose lipolysis.
items.explain: It favours energy storage and inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase activity.

items.text: Adult haemoglobin A contains two alpha and two beta chains.
items.explain: HbA is an alpha2-beta2 tetramer.

items.text: Cooperative oxygen binding contributes to haemoglobin's sigmoidal dissociation curve.
items.explain: Oxygen binding increases the affinity of remaining subunits through allosteric transitions.

items.text: A rightward shift of the oxygen dissociation curve indicates increased oxygen affinity.
items.explain: A right shift means reduced affinity and facilitates unloading.

items.text: Fetal haemoglobin has greater oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin.
items.explain: HbF binds 2,3-BPG less strongly, supporting placental oxygen transfer.

items.text: The liver converts vitamin D to 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
items.explain: This is the major circulating storage form measured clinically.

items.text: Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol.
items.explain: The kidney produces the hormonally active 1,25-dihydroxy form.

items.text: Calcitriol reduces intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate.
items.explain: It increases absorption of both minerals.

items.text: Severe vitamin D deficiency in children can cause rickets.
items.explain: Defective mineralisation of growing bone and growth plates causes rickets.

items.text: Promoter CpG methylation is commonly associated with transcriptional repression.
items.explain: Methylation can reduce transcription factor binding and recruit repressive chromatin proteins.

items.text: Histone acetylation is generally associated with more accessible chromatin.
items.explain: Acetylation of lysine residues often favours transcriptionally active chromatin.

items.text: Epigenetic regulation necessarily changes the DNA nucleotide sequence.
items.explain: Epigenetic mechanisms alter gene expression without changing the underlying sequence.

items.text: Some epigenetic marks can be maintained through cell division.
items.explain: Maintenance systems preserve certain methylation and chromatin patterns in daughter cells.

items.text: Allosteric enzymes may show sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic substrate-velocity curves.
items.explain: Cooperative interactions between subunits can produce sigmoidal kinetics.

items.text: An allosteric regulator binds at a site distinct from the enzyme's active site.
items.explain: Binding at a regulatory site changes enzyme conformation and activity.

items.text: Allosteric inhibition is always overcome by increasing substrate concentration.
items.explain: Allosteric regulation is not simply competitive inhibition; increasing substrate does not necessarily reverse it.

items.text: Feedback inhibition commonly involves an end product inhibiting an earlier enzyme in its biosynthetic pathway.
items.explain: This mechanism helps match pathway flux to cellular demand and product availability.

questions.sub: Histology of the retina and organ of Corti
questions.q: Regarding the histology of the retina and organ of Corti:

items.text: The retina contains a pigmented layer and a neural layer.
items.explain: The retinal pigment epithelium lies externally, while the neural retina contains photoreceptors and associated neuronal layers.

items.text: Rods are primarily responsible for colour vision in bright light.
items.explain: Cones mediate colour vision and high-acuity photopic vision; rods are more sensitive in dim light and do not mediate colour discrimination.

items.text: The fovea centralis is specialised for high visual acuity.
items.explain: Its cone-rich arrangement and displacement of inner retinal layers reduce light scattering and support detailed vision.

items.text: Hair cells of the organ of Corti are mechanoreceptors involved in hearing.
items.explain: Deflection of their stereocilia converts mechanical vibration into receptor potentials that drive auditory signalling.

references: Ross and Pawlina, Histology: A Text and Atlas, 8th ed.
Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas, 16th ed.

questions.sub: Histology of skin and cutaneous appendages
questions.q: Regarding the histology of skin and its appendages:

items.text: The epidermis is a keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
items.explain: The epidermis forms a protective epithelial barrier and is avascular.

items.text: The dermis is composed mainly of connective tissue.
items.explain: The dermis contains collagen and elastic fibres, vessels, nerves and skin appendages.

items.text: Eccrine sweat glands usually open into hair follicles.
items.explain: Eccrine glands generally open directly onto the skin surface; apocrine glands commonly open into hair follicles.

items.text: The stratum lucidum is a prominent layer in thick skin.
items.explain: It is present in thick skin such as the palms and soles and is located between the stratum granulosum and corneum.

references: Ross and Pawlina, Histology: A Text and Atlas, 8th ed.
Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas, 16th ed.

questions.sub: Histology of testes and excurrent ducts
questions.q: Regarding the histology of the male reproductive tract:

items.text: Seminiferous tubules contain developing germ cells and Sertoli cells.
items.explain: Sertoli cells support spermatogenesis and form the blood-testis barrier.

items.text: Leydig cells are located within the seminiferous epithelium.
items.explain: Leydig cells lie in the interstitial tissue between seminiferous tubules and produce testosterone.

items.text: The epididymis is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia.
items.explain: Stereocilia increase surface area for absorption and contribute to sperm maturation.

items.text: The ductus deferens has a prominent muscular wall.
items.explain: Its thick smooth-muscle layers generate peristaltic contractions during ejaculation.

references: Ross and Pawlina, Histology: A Text and Atlas, 8th ed.
Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas, 16th ed.

questions.q: Regarding the general histological organisation of the gastrointestinal tract:

items.text: The mucosa consists of epithelium, lamina propria and muscularis mucosae.
items.explain: These three components form the innermost tunic of most of the gastrointestinal tract.

items.text: The submucosa contains the myenteric plexus.
items.explain: The submucosa contains the submucosal (Meissner) plexus; the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus lies between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers.

items.text: The stomach has gastric pits and glands but no villi.
items.explain: Its mucosal surface contains pits leading into gastric glands; villi are characteristic of the small intestine.

items.text: Brunner glands are found in the submucosa of the duodenum.
items.explain: These glands secrete alkaline mucus that helps neutralise acidic chyme.

references: Ross and Pawlina, Histology: A Text and Atlas, 8th ed.

questions.sub: Histology of lymph nodes and spleen
questions.q: Regarding the histology of lymphoid organs:

items.text: A lymph node has an outer cortex and an inner medulla.
items.explain: The cortex contains lymphoid follicles, while the medulla contains cords and sinuses.

items.text: The spleen filters blood rather than lymph.
items.explain: Splenic red pulp removes aged erythrocytes and blood-borne particles; white pulp participates in immune responses.

items.text: The thymus normally contains lymphoid follicles with germinal centres.
items.explain: The thymus has a cortex and medulla but lacks typical lymphoid follicles and germinal centres.

items.text: High endothelial venules are important sites of lymphocyte entry into lymph nodes.
items.explain: These specialised postcapillary venules allow circulating lymphocytes to enter lymph node tissue.

questions.sub: Gonadal hormones and reproductive endocrine control
questions.q: Regarding gonadal hormones and their regulation:

items.text: LH stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone.
items.explain: LH acts on Leydig cells in the testes to promote androgen synthesis.

items.text: FSH acts on Sertoli cells and supports spermatogenesis.
items.explain: Sertoli cells respond to FSH and provide support for developing germ cells.

items.text: In ovarian follicles, LH is the principal stimulus for granulosa-cell aromatase throughout the follicular phase.
items.explain: FSH stimulates granulosa-cell aromatase; theca cells respond to LH and provide androgen substrate for oestrogen synthesis.

items.text: Inhibin selectively suppresses pituitary FSH secretion.
items.explain: Inhibin from gonadal cells provides negative feedback, particularly on FSH.

references: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 15th ed.
Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, 27th ed.

items.text: The mid-cycle LH surge is the immediate hormonal trigger for ovulation.
items.explain: Sustained high oestradiol from the dominant follicle produces positive feedback that triggers the LH surge.

items.text: The corpus luteum secretes progesterone after ovulation.
items.explain: Luteinised granulosa and theca cells produce progesterone, preparing and maintaining the endometrium.

items.text: The proliferative phase of the endometrium is driven mainly by progesterone.
items.explain: Oestrogen drives the proliferative phase; progesterone predominates during the secretory phase.

items.text: If pregnancy does not occur, regression of the corpus luteum contributes to a fall in progesterone.
items.explain: Withdrawal of luteal progesterone contributes to endometrial breakdown and menstruation.

references: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 15th ed.
Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, 27th ed.

items.text: Human chorionic gonadotropin helps maintain the corpus luteum in early pregnancy.
items.explain: hCG acts on LH receptors and sustains progesterone secretion before placental steroid production is established.

items.text: Prolactin stimulates milk synthesis by the mammary alveolar cells.
items.explain: Prolactin supports milk production, with suckling promoting prolactin release.

items.text: Oxytocin is the principal hormone responsible for milk synthesis.
items.explain: Oxytocin causes milk ejection by contracting myoepithelial cells; prolactin is responsible for milk synthesis.

items.text: Placental progesterone contributes to maintenance of the uterine lining during pregnancy.
items.explain: Progesterone supports the decidualised endometrium and helps maintain uterine quiescence.

Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, 27th ed.

questions.sub: EEG patterns and stages of sleep

items.text: Alpha rhythm is commonly recorded in a relaxed, awake person with eyes closed.
items.explain: The posterior dominant alpha rhythm is prominent during relaxed wakefulness and attenuates with eye opening or attention.

items.text: NREM sleep includes stages N1, N2 and N3.
items.explain: These stages represent progressively deeper non-rapid-eye-movement sleep.

items.text: Rapid eye movement sleep is typically associated with prominent skeletal muscle atonia.
items.explain: Pontine and medullary pathways inhibit spinal motor neurons, producing marked reduction in skeletal muscle tone.

items.text: Delta waves are characteristic of relaxed alert wakefulness in a healthy adult.
items.explain: High-amplitude delta activity is characteristic of deep NREM sleep; relaxed wakefulness is commonly associated with alpha activity.

references: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 15th ed.
Boron and Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, 4th ed.

questions.q: Regarding postural control and motor pathways:

items.text: The vestibular system contributes to balance and postural adjustments.
items.explain: Vestibular inputs signal head position and movement and influence vestibulospinal pathways.

items.text: The cerebellum contributes to coordination and error correction of movement.
items.explain: It compares intended and actual movement and helps adjust timing, force and coordination.

items.text: The corticospinal tract is the only descending pathway involved in posture.
items.explain: Reticulospinal, vestibulospinal and other descending pathways also contribute importantly to posture and tone.

items.text: Proprioceptive input from muscles and joints contributes to postural stability.
items.explain: Proprioceptors provide information about body position and movement used in spinal and supraspinal control.

Boron and Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, 4th ed.

questions.sub: Citric acid cycle and metabolic integration

items.text: The citric acid cycle occurs mainly in the mitochondrial matrix.
items.explain: Most cycle enzymes are in the matrix, although succinate dehydrogenase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

items.text: Each acetyl-CoA oxidised in one turn of the cycle yields two carbon dioxide molecules.
items.explain: The cycle releases two CO2 molecules per acetyl-CoA, while regenerating oxaloacetate.

items.text: The cycle directly consumes molecular oxygen at the citrate synthase step.
items.explain: Oxygen is not a direct substrate of the cycle; the cycle depends indirectly on oxidative phosphorylation to reoxidise NADH and FADH2.

items.text: Succinyl-CoA synthetase generates GTP or ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.
items.explain: The conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinate conserves energy in a high-energy nucleotide triphosphate.

questions.referenceScope: Textbook-level references; individual claims require academic review.

items.text: The urea cycle converts toxic ammonia into urea for excretion.
items.explain: Hepatic urea synthesis is a major pathway for disposal of nitrogen from amino acid catabolism.

items.text: The first two reactions of the urea cycle occur in the mitochondrial matrix.
items.explain: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamylase are mitochondrial enzymes.

items.text: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is activated by N-acetylglutamate.
items.explain: N-acetylglutamate is an essential allosteric activator of CPS I.

items.text: Both nitrogen atoms in urea are derived directly from free ammonia.
items.explain: One nitrogen comes from free ammonia via carbamoyl phosphate; the other is donated by aspartate.

questions.referenceScope: Textbook-level references; individual claims require academic review.

items.text: Ketone bodies are synthesised mainly in the liver mitochondria during increased fatty acid oxidation.
items.explain: Fasting and low-insulin states increase hepatic acetyl-CoA availability and ketogenesis.

items.text: The principal ketone bodies are acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone.
items.explain: Acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are major circulating fuels; acetone is largely exhaled.

items.text: The liver readily utilises ketone bodies because it expresses high levels of thiophorase.
items.explain: The liver lacks significant succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase), so it exports ketone bodies rather than consuming them.

items.text: Red blood cells can use ketone bodies as a major energy source.
items.explain: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and rely on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP.

questions.q: Regarding haem degradation and bilirubin metabolism:

items.text: Haem oxygenase converts haem to biliverdin while releasing iron and carbon monoxide.
items.explain: Haem oxygenase catalyses oxidative ring opening, producing biliverdin, iron and carbon monoxide.

items.text: Biliverdin is reduced to unconjugated bilirubin by biliverdin reductase.
items.explain: Biliverdin reductase produces bilirubin, which circulates bound to albumin.

items.text: Unconjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and is freely filtered by the kidney.
items.explain: Unconjugated bilirubin is poorly water-soluble and albumin-bound; conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and may appear in urine.

items.text: Conjugation of bilirubin in hepatocytes involves UDP-glucuronosyltransferase.
items.explain: UGT1A1 conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid, facilitating biliary excretion.

items.text: Albumin is the major contributor to plasma colloid osmotic pressure.
items.explain: Its high concentration and relative abundance make albumin the principal determinant of plasma oncotic pressure.

items.text: Most plasma albumin is synthesised by hepatocytes.
items.explain: The liver is the principal site of albumin synthesis.

items.text: Immunoglobulins are normally synthesised by hepatocytes.
items.explain: Immunoglobulins are produced by differentiated B lymphocytes (plasma cells).

items.text: Albumin contributes to transport of substances such as unconjugated bilirubin, fatty acids and some drugs.
items.explain: Albumin has multiple binding sites and serves as an important plasma carrier protein.

items.text: A typical vertebra has a vertebral body and a vertebral arch enclosing the vertebral foramen.
items.explain: The body lies anteriorly; the arch is formed by pedicles and laminae and encloses the vertebral foramen.

items.text: The vertebral canal is formed by the alignment of vertebral foramina.
items.explain: Successive vertebral foramina form the vertebral canal, which contains the spinal cord and its coverings.

items.text: The dens is a feature of the seventh cervical vertebra.
items.explain: The dens (odontoid process) projects superiorly from the body of the axis, C2.

items.text: The atlas has a large vertebral body and a prominent spinous process.
items.explain: The atlas (C1) is ring-shaped, lacks a body and has no typical spinous process.

items.text: The pelvic diaphragm is formed principally by the levator ani and coccygeus muscles.
items.explain: These paired muscles form the muscular floor of the pelvis.

items.text: The puborectalis part of levator ani contributes to the anorectal angle.
items.explain: Its sling around the anorectal junction helps maintain faecal continence.

items.text: The pelvic diaphragm separates the pelvic cavity from the perineum.
items.explain: It forms the inferior boundary of the pelvic cavity and the roof of the perineum.

items.text: The pudendal nerve is the motor supply to all parts of levator ani.
items.explain: Levator ani receives direct branches from sacral ventral rami (typically S3–S4); pudendal branches supply perineal muscles and sensation.

items.text: The dura mater is the outermost meningeal layer surrounding the brain.
items.explain: The cranial meninges comprise dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater from superficial to deep.

items.text: The subarachnoid space contains cerebrospinal fluid.
items.explain: CSF circulates in the space between arachnoid and pia and around the brain and spinal cord.

items.text: The falx cerebri separates the two cerebral hemispheres.
items.explain: This dural fold occupies the longitudinal fissure between the cerebral hemispheres.

items.text: The superior sagittal sinus lies between the arachnoid mater and pia mater.
items.explain: It is a dural venous sinus situated within the attached superior margin of the falx cerebri.

questions.q: Regarding embryological septation of the heart:

items.text: The interatrial septum develops through coordinated formation of septum primum and septum secundum.
items.explain: The two septa develop sequentially and leave the foramen ovale for fetal right-to-left atrial shunting.

items.text: The foramen ovale normally permits blood to pass from the left atrium to the right atrium in fetal life.
items.explain: Fetal right atrial pressure exceeds left atrial pressure, directing blood through the foramen ovale to the left atrium.

items.text: The membranous part of the interventricular septum forms later than much of its muscular part.
items.explain: The membranous component forms through contributions involving endocardial cushions and conotruncal ridges.

items.text: Failure of closure of the foramen ovale after birth always produces a large haemodynamically significant shunt.
items.explain: A patent foramen ovale is often functionally silent; shunting depends on pressure relationships and other factors.

references: Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR. Clinically Oriented Anatomy. 9th ed.
Standring S, ed. Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd ed.

items.text: Hyaline cartilage contains type II collagen as its principal collagen type.
items.explain: Type II collagen fibrils are characteristic of hyaline cartilage, although they may be difficult to distinguish in routine sections.

items.text: Cartilage is normally richly supplied by blood vessels.
items.explain: Cartilage is avascular; nutrients diffuse through the matrix from surrounding tissues or synovial fluid.

items.text: Chondrocytes may be found in lacunae, sometimes grouped as isogenous groups.
items.explain: Isogenous groups arise when a chondrocyte divides within the matrix.

items.text: The perichondrium is present around articular cartilage at synovial joint surfaces.
items.explain: Articular cartilage lacks a perichondrium and receives nutrients mainly from synovial fluid.

items.text: Sound-induced movement of the stapes footplate produces pressure waves in the cochlear fluids.
items.explain: The stapes transmits vibrations through the oval window into the scala vestibuli.

items.text: Inner hair-cell stereocilia deflection toward the tallest stereocilium generally depolarises the hair cell.
items.explain: Tip-link tension opens mechanically gated channels, allowing potassium-rich endolymph to enter.

items.text: The round window helps accommodate pressure displacement within the cochlea.
items.explain: Its compliant membrane moves in response to cochlear fluid displacement, allowing travelling waves.

items.text: The auditory nerve is formed by axons of outer hair cells.
items.explain: Most afferent auditory fibres arise from spiral ganglion neurons that receive input predominantly from inner hair cells.

items.text: Light activation of rhodopsin ultimately reduces the concentration of cyclic GMP in rod photoreceptors.
items.explain: Activated rhodopsin stimulates transducin and phosphodiesterase, which hydrolyses cGMP.

items.text: In darkness, rod photoreceptors are relatively depolarised compared with their response to light.
items.explain: High cGMP keeps cation channels open in darkness, sustaining the dark current and glutamate release.

items.text: The optic chiasm contains crossing fibres from the nasal halves of the retinas.
items.explain: Nasal retinal fibres decussate, while temporal retinal fibres remain ipsilateral.

items.text: A lesion of the right optic tract typically causes loss of vision in the right eye only.
items.explain: A right optic tract lesion causes left homonymous visual-field loss because each tract carries information from the contralateral visual field.

items.explain: Thyroid peroxidase participates in oxidation, organification and coupling reactions at the follicular-colloid interface.

items.text: Most circulating thyroid hormone is transported bound to plasma proteins.
items.explain: Thyroxine-binding globulin, transthyretin and albumin carry most circulating T4 and T3.

items.text: T3 generally has greater biological activity at nuclear thyroid hormone receptors than T4.
items.explain: T4 acts largely as a prohormone and is converted in tissues to the more active T3.

items.text: Thyroid-stimulating hormone secretion is increased by sustained high circulating free T3 and T4.
items.explain: Free thyroid hormones exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, reducing TRH and TSH.

items.text: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
items.explain: Parietal cells produce gastric acid and intrinsic factor, which is required for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

items.text: Histamine stimulates acid secretion by activating H2 receptors on parietal cells.
items.explain: H2 receptor activation increases intracellular cAMP and stimulates the acid-secretory machinery.

items.text: Somatostatin generally inhibits gastric acid secretion.
items.explain: Somatostatin suppresses gastrin release and directly inhibits acid secretion.

items.text: Chief cells are the principal source of intrinsic factor.
items.explain: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen; intrinsic factor is secreted by parietal cells.

items.text: Arterioles are major resistance vessels that regulate tissue blood flow.
items.explain: Changes in arteriolar smooth-muscle tone produce substantial changes in vascular resistance.

items.text: Capillary walls are generally composed of a single endothelial layer with a basement membrane.
items.explain: This thin barrier facilitates exchange; specialised capillaries may have additional structural features.

items.text: An increase in plasma colloid osmotic pressure favours movement of fluid into capillaries.
items.explain: Plasma proteins generate oncotic pressure that opposes filtration and favours reabsorption.

items.text: Lymphatic vessels normally return excess interstitial fluid and proteins to the circulation.
items.explain: Lymphatic drainage helps maintain interstitial fluid balance and returns escaped proteins to the blood.

items.text: Glycogen synthase catalyses formation of alpha-1,4 glycosidic linkages during glycogen synthesis.
items.explain: Glycogen synthase extends glycogen chains using UDP-glucose; the branching enzyme forms alpha-1,6 linkages.

items.text: Glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose-1-phosphate from glycogen.
items.explain: It cleaves alpha-1,4 bonds by phosphorolysis but cannot pass branch points unaided.

items.text: Liver glycogen helps maintain blood glucose between meals.
items.explain: Hepatic glycogen can be mobilised and the liver can release free glucose because it expresses glucose-6-phosphatase.

items.text: Skeletal muscle glycogen is a major direct source of free glucose released into the bloodstream.
items.explain: Skeletal muscle lacks significant glucose-6-phosphatase activity and uses glycogen-derived glucose-6-phosphate locally.

items.text: The electron transport chain is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
items.explain: Its complexes and mobile electron carriers are embedded in or associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane.

items.text: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the mitochondrial electron transport chain.
items.explain: Oxygen accepts electrons and protons to form water at complex IV.

items.text: The proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane drives ATP synthesis by ATP synthase.
items.explain: The proton-motive force powers rotation and conformational changes in the F0F1 ATP synthase complex.

items.text: Complex II pumps protons from the mitochondrial matrix into the intermembrane space.
items.explain: Complex II transfers electrons from succinate to ubiquinone but does not pump protons.

items.text: Chylomicrons transport dietary triacylglycerol from the intestine to peripheral tissues.
items.explain: Nascent chylomicrons enter lymph and then blood, where they acquire apolipoproteins and deliver dietary lipid.

items.text: Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses triacylglycerol in circulating chylomicrons and VLDL.
items.explain: Endothelial-bound lipoprotein lipase releases fatty acids for uptake by muscle and adipose tissue.

items.text: LDL is a major carrier of cholesterol from the liver to peripheral tissues.
items.explain: LDL delivers cholesterol to cells through receptor-mediated uptake, including via the LDL receptor.

items.text: HDL is the principal lipoprotein responsible for transporting dietary triacylglycerol from the intestine.
items.explain: Chylomicrons perform that function; HDL participates in reverse cholesterol transport and apolipoprotein exchange.

items.text: Uric acid is the final product of purine degradation in humans.
items.explain: Humans lack functional uricase, so uric acid is the terminal product of purine catabolism.

items.text: Xanthine oxidase catalyses conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid.
items.explain: These sequential oxidation reactions generate uric acid and are inhibited by drugs such as allopurinol.

items.text: A deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase can cause Lesch–Nyhan syndrome.
items.explain: HGPRT deficiency impairs purine salvage and is associated with hyperuricaemia and characteristic neurological and behavioural manifestations.

items.text: Allopurinol lowers uric acid by directly increasing renal urate reabsorption.
items.explain: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, reducing uric acid production.

items.text: The pyrimidine ring is assembled before attachment to ribose phosphate in de novo synthesis.
items.explain: The ring is synthesised from carbamoyl phosphate and aspartate, then attached to PRPP at the orotate stage.

items.text: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane.
items.explain: This enzyme catalyses oxidation of dihydroorotate to orotate and links pyrimidine synthesis to mitochondrial electron transfer.

items.text: Thymidylate synthase converts dUMP to dTMP using a folate-derived one-carbon donor.
items.explain: The reaction uses 5,10-methylene tetrahydrofolate, which is oxidised to dihydrofolate.

items.text: A deficiency of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase has no effect on fluoropyrimidine toxicity.
items.explain: Reduced degradation of 5-fluorouracil can cause severe or potentially fatal fluoropyrimidine toxicity.

questions.q: Regarding the axilla and its contents:

items.text: The axilla is a pyramidal space between the upper limb and thoracic wall.
items.explain: Its apex, base and four walls define a passageway for major neurovascular structures between the neck and upper limb.

items.text: The axillary artery is divided into three parts by the pectoralis minor muscle.
items.explain: The muscle crosses anterior to the artery; the parts are named according to their relationship to it.

items.text: The cords of the brachial plexus are named in relation to the second part of the axillary artery.
items.explain: The lateral, medial and posterior cords are arranged around the second part of the artery.

items.text: The axillary vein lies posterior to the axillary artery throughout its course.
items.explain: The axillary vein is generally medial and anterior to the artery and receives the basilic and brachial veins.

items.text: The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity between the pleural sacs.
items.explain: It contains most thoracic viscera apart from the lungs.

items.text: The transverse thoracic plane passing through the sternal angle and T4/T5 intervertebral disc separates superior and inferior mediastina.
items.explain: This plane is a key landmark for mediastinal subdivision.

items.text: The heart and pericardium occupy the middle mediastinum.
items.explain: The middle mediastinum contains the pericardium, heart and roots of the great vessels.

items.text: The oesophagus is a content of the anterior mediastinum.
items.explain: The oesophagus lies in the superior and posterior mediastina; the anterior mediastinum is mainly connective tissue, fat and lymph nodes.

items.text: The greater omentum descends from the greater curvature of the stomach and is related to the transverse colon.
items.explain: It is a double-layered peritoneal fold that hangs anterior to the intestinal coils and attaches to the transverse colon.

items.text: The lesser sac communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen.
items.explain: The omental foramen provides the normal communication between the two peritoneal compartments.

items.text: The hepatoduodenal ligament contains the portal triad.
items.explain: The portal vein, proper hepatic artery and bile duct run within its free edge.

items.text: The kidneys are intraperitoneal organs.
items.explain: The kidneys are primarily retroperitoneal organs, lying posterior to the parietal peritoneum.

items.text: The hip is a synovial ball-and-socket joint.
items.explain: The spherical femoral head articulates with the acetabulum, allowing movement in multiple axes.

items.text: The acetabular labrum deepens the acetabular socket.
items.explain: This fibrocartilaginous rim increases socket depth and contributes to joint stability.

items.text: The ligament of the head of the femur is the principal structure preventing hip dislocation in adults.
items.explain: The strong capsule and its reinforcing ligaments are major stabilisers; the ligament of the head carries a small artery and has limited mechanical importance in adults.

items.text: The iliofemoral ligament resists excessive extension of the hip.
items.explain: Its strong Y-shaped fibres become taut in extension and help maintain upright posture.
