items.text: Osteocytes occupy lacunae within the bone matrix.
items.explain: Osteocytes are mature bone cells residing in lacunae and communicate through canaliculi.

items.text: In compact bone, concentric lamellae are arranged around central (Haversian) canals in osteons.
items.explain: Central canals contain vessels and nerves; perforating canals connect them.

items.text: Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells derived from the monocyte-macrophage lineage.
items.explain: They resorb bone using acid and proteolytic enzymes at specialised resorption surfaces.

items.text: Osteoblasts are primarily responsible for resorbing mineralised bone.
items.explain: Osteoblasts form bone by synthesising osteoid and promoting its mineralisation; osteoclasts resorb bone.

questions.q: Regarding transmission at the neuromuscular junction:

items.text: Acetylcholine is released from motor nerve terminals by calcium-dependent exocytosis.
items.explain: Arrival of an action potential opens presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, triggering vesicle fusion.

items.text: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the motor end plate is a ligand-gated cation channel.
items.explain: Binding of acetylcholine opens the channel, producing a net inward current and end-plate depolarisation.

items.text: Acetylcholinesterase terminates the action of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft.
items.explain: It rapidly hydrolyses acetylcholine to acetate and choline; choline is taken up for resynthesis.

items.text: Curare produces neuromuscular blockade by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase.
items.explain: Non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers such as curare competitively antagonise nicotinic receptors.

items.text: The sinoatrial node is normally the dominant pacemaker of the heart.
items.explain: Its spontaneous depolarisation rate is usually faster than that of subsidiary pacemaker tissues.

items.text: The atrioventricular nodal delay allows time for ventricular filling before ventricular contraction.
items.explain: Slow conduction through the AV node helps coordinate atrial and ventricular systole.

items.text: The Purkinje system conducts impulses rapidly through the ventricular myocardium.
items.explain: Purkinje fibres have specialised properties that allow rapid distribution of excitation.

items.text: The bundle of His normally conducts impulses from the ventricles back to the atria.
items.explain: The AV bundle conducts impulses from the AV node into the interventricular septum and bundle branches.

items.text: The lungs regulate blood pH partly by altering the rate of carbon dioxide elimination.
items.explain: Changes in alveolar ventilation alter arterial PCO2 and therefore the carbonic acid-bicarbonate equilibrium.

items.text: The kidneys contribute to acid-base balance by reabsorbing filtered bicarbonate and generating new bicarbonate.
items.explain: Renal mechanisms include bicarbonate reclamation and acid excretion as titratable acid and ammonium.

items.text: In metabolic acidosis, respiratory compensation generally involves hypoventilation.
items.explain: The compensatory response is increased alveolar ventilation, which lowers PCO2.

items.text: The Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship links pH to the ratio of bicarbonate concentration to dissolved carbon dioxide.
items.explain: For the bicarbonate buffer system, pH depends on the ratio of [HCO3−] to 0.03 × PCO2.

items.text: Glucose and galactose are absorbed across the apical membrane of enterocytes mainly by sodium-dependent cotransport.
items.explain: SGLT1 uses the sodium gradient maintained by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase.

items.text: Fructose enters enterocytes primarily through facilitated diffusion via GLUT5.
items.explain: GLUT5 is an apical fructose transporter; fructose exits basolaterally mainly via GLUT2.

items.text: Long-chain fatty acids are commonly re-esterified and packaged into chylomicrons in enterocytes.
items.explain: Chylomicrons enter intestinal lacteals and reach the systemic circulation through lymph.

items.text: Most vitamin B12 is absorbed in the duodenum independently of intrinsic factor.
items.explain: The intrinsic factor-vitamin B12 complex is absorbed by receptor-mediated uptake in the terminal ileum.

questions.q: Regarding physiological responses to dynamic exercise:

items.text: Cardiac output increases during dynamic exercise through increases in heart rate and stroke volume.
items.explain: Sympathetic activation, increased venous return and enhanced contractility contribute to the rise in cardiac output.

items.text: Blood flow to active skeletal muscle increases through local metabolic vasodilation.
items.explain: Metabolites and endothelial signals reduce arteriolar resistance in exercising muscle.

items.text: Systolic arterial pressure usually rises during moderate-to-heavy dynamic exercise.
items.explain: Increased cardiac output raises systolic pressure, while diastolic pressure often changes relatively little.

items.text: Oxygen extraction by active skeletal muscle decreases during strenuous exercise.
items.explain: The arteriovenous oxygen difference generally increases as active tissues extract more oxygen.

items.text: HMG-CoA reductase catalyses the rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis.
items.explain: It converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate and is a major regulatory point in the pathway.

items.text: Statins lower cholesterol synthesis by competitively inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase.
items.explain: Reduced hepatic cholesterol synthesis also promotes increased expression of LDL receptors.

items.text: Cholesterol is a precursor for steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D.
items.explain: These products are synthesised from cholesterol in specialised tissues.

items.text: The liver obtains all of its cholesterol exclusively through de novo synthesis.
items.explain: Hepatic cholesterol also comes from uptake of circulating lipoproteins and dietary cholesterol delivered in remnants.

items.text: Von Gierke disease is classically caused by deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase activity or its transport system.
items.explain: The defect impairs release of free glucose from hepatic glucose-6-phosphate.

items.text: McArdle disease is associated with deficiency of skeletal-muscle glycogen phosphorylase.
items.explain: Impaired muscle glycogenolysis causes exercise intolerance and may produce myoglobinuria.

items.text: Pompe disease results from lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency.
items.explain: Glycogen accumulates in lysosomes, particularly affecting cardiac and skeletal muscle.

items.text: In McArdle disease, fasting hypoglycaemia is usually the dominant presentation because hepatic glycogenolysis is defective.
items.explain: McArdle disease primarily affects skeletal muscle; hepatic glucose release is generally preserved.

items.text: Reduced glutathione contains a gamma-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine tripeptide.
items.explain: Its unusual gamma-glutamyl linkage involves the gamma-carboxyl group of glutamate.

items.text: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione to reduce hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides.
items.explain: The reaction oxidises glutathione to its disulphide form, GSSG.

items.text: Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione from GSSG.
items.explain: NADPH supplies reducing equivalents to maintain the intracellular GSH pool.

items.text: Erythrocytes are protected from oxidative damage by a mitochondrial source of NADPH.
items.explain: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria; the pentose phosphate pathway is a key source of NADPH.

items.text: Tetrahydrofolate carries one-carbon units in several oxidation states.
items.explain: THF derivatives participate in purine synthesis, thymidylate synthesis and amino acid metabolism.

items.text: Folate deficiency can impair DNA synthesis and cause megaloblastic anaemia.
items.explain: Reduced thymidylate and purine synthesis disrupts DNA replication in rapidly dividing cells.

items.text: Vitamin B12 is required for the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA.
items.explain: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is an adenosylcobalamin-dependent enzyme.

items.text: Folate deficiency typically causes increased methylmalonic acid concentrations.
items.explain: Methylmalonic acid rises in vitamin B12 deficiency; folate deficiency typically does not cause this change.

items.text: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues occurs in the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
items.explain: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases modify procollagen chains in the ER and require vitamin C.

items.text: Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen maturation and can cause scurvy.
items.explain: Defective hydroxylation weakens collagen stability and connective tissue integrity.

items.text: Triple-helix formation occurs before procollagen is secreted from the cell.
items.explain: Pro-alpha chains align and form a triple helix in the ER before secretion.

items.text: Mature collagen fibrils are formed entirely within the Golgi apparatus.
items.explain: After secretion, procollagen propeptides are cleaved extracellularly and collagen molecules assemble into fibrils.

items.explain: Unlike the other laryngeal cartilages, the cricoid forms a complete ring.

items.text: The posterior cricoarytenoid muscles abduct the vocal folds.
items.explain: They are the only intrinsic laryngeal muscles that abduct the vocal folds.

items.text: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid.
items.explain: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid.

items.text: The internal laryngeal nerve provides the motor supply to cricothyroid.
items.explain: It is primarily sensory above the vocal folds; cricothyroid is supplied by the external branch.

questions.q: Regarding the anatomy of the liver:

items.text: The bare area of the liver is not covered by peritoneum.
items.explain: It contacts the diaphragm and is bounded by the coronary ligament.

items.text: The porta hepatis transmits hepatic ducts, hepatic arterial branches and portal venous branches.
items.explain: These structures pass through the transverse fissure with lymphatics and nerves.

items.text: The falciform ligament attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm.
items.explain: It is a peritoneal fold connecting the liver to the anterior wall and inferior diaphragm.

items.text: The falciform ligament separates the functional right and left lobes of the liver.
items.explain: Functional division follows a plane from the gallbladder fossa towards the inferior vena cava.

questions.q: Regarding the arches of the foot:

items.text: The medial longitudinal arch is higher and more elastic than the lateral longitudinal arch.
items.explain: The medial arch is more mobile and is supported by the spring ligament and muscles including tibialis posterior.

items.text: The calcaneus, cuboid and fourth and fifth metatarsals contribute to the lateral longitudinal arch.
items.explain: These bones form the principal bony components of the lateral arch.

items.text: The plantar aponeurosis contributes to maintenance of the longitudinal arches.
items.explain: Its tension supports the arches, including through the windlass mechanism.

items.text: The transverse arch is maintained solely by plantar ligaments.
items.explain: Bone shape, interosseous ligaments and muscular/tendinous supports also contribute.

questions.q: Regarding embryological development of the pancreas:

items.text: The pancreas develops from dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds arising from foregut endoderm.
items.explain: The buds rotate and fuse as the duodenum changes position.

items.text: The ventral pancreatic bud contributes to the uncinate process and inferior part of the pancreatic head.
items.explain: The ventral bud rotates posteriorly with the bile duct and fuses with the dorsal bud.

items.text: The main pancreatic duct usually forms from the ventral duct and distal part of the dorsal duct.
items.explain: The proximal dorsal duct may persist as the accessory pancreatic duct.

items.text: Annular pancreas is caused by failure of the dorsal pancreatic bud to develop.
items.explain: It is associated with abnormal migration or configuration of the ventral pancreatic bud.

questions.q: Regarding the histology of the pituitary gland:

items.text: The adenohypophysis is derived embryologically from oral ectoderm.
items.explain: It develops from Rathke's pouch, an upgrowth of the primitive oral cavity.

items.text: The neurohypophysis contains axons whose cell bodies lie in hypothalamic nuclei.
items.explain: Axons from supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei terminate in the posterior pituitary.

items.text: Acidophils of the anterior pituitary include somatotrophs and lactotrophs.
items.explain: These cells secrete growth hormone and prolactin, respectively.

items.text: The posterior pituitary synthesises oxytocin and vasopressin in pituicytes.
items.explain: These hormones are synthesised in hypothalamic neurons and stored and released posteriorly.

items.text: Renal clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per unit time.
items.explain: It is urinary concentration multiplied by urine flow, divided by plasma concentration.

items.text: Inulin clearance measures GFR because inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted.
items.explain: Under steady-state conditions, inulin clearance approximates GFR.

items.text: Glucose appears in urine when its filtered load exceeds tubular reabsorptive capacity.
items.explain: Once transport capacity is exceeded, glucose is excreted.

items.text: Para-aminohippurate clearance at low plasma concentrations measures renal plasma flow exactly.
items.explain: It estimates effective renal plasma flow because extraction is high but incomplete.

items.explain: Channel closure depolarises the membrane and opens voltage-gated calcium channels.

items.text: Insulin promotes GLUT4 translocation in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.
items.explain: Insulin signalling recruits GLUT4 vesicles to the plasma membrane.

items.text: Insulin promotes hepatic glycogen synthesis and inhibits gluconeogenesis.
items.explain: It favours glucose storage and suppresses hepatic glucose output.

items.text: A fall in plasma glucose normally stimulates insulin secretion.
items.explain: Low glucose suppresses insulin release; rising glucose stimulates beta cells.

items.text: Lung compliance is the change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure.
items.explain: It describes distensibility and is the slope of the pressure-volume relationship.

items.text: Pulmonary surfactant reduces surface tension at the alveolar air-liquid interface.
items.explain: Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant, which reduces inflation work and stabilises alveoli.

items.text: Lung compliance is generally reduced in pulmonary fibrosis.
items.explain: Fibrotic lungs are stiff and require greater pressure to achieve a given volume.

items.text: Emphysema typically reduces compliance because elastic recoil is increased.
items.explain: Loss of elastic tissue reduces recoil and typically increases compliance.

items.text: Fast, sharp pain is commonly transmitted by thinly myelinated A-delta fibres.
items.explain: A-delta fibres conduct relatively rapidly and convey well-localised pricking pain.

items.text: Slow, dull pain is commonly transmitted by unmyelinated C fibres.
items.explain: C fibres conduct slowly and convey aching, burning and poorly localised pain.

items.text: Many second-order anterolateral system neurons cross near their spinal level of entry.
items.explain: Pain and temperature fibres commonly decussate through the anterior white commissure.

items.text: The periaqueductal grey participates in descending modulation of nociception.
items.explain: It engages brainstem pathways that influence dorsal horn transmission.

items.text: At steady state, venous return to the heart equals cardiac output.
items.explain: In a closed circulation, inflow and outflow must be equal over time.

items.text: The skeletal muscle pump assists venous return from the limbs.
items.explain: Muscle contraction compresses veins and valves direct blood centrally.

items.text: An increase in mean systemic filling pressure, with other factors unchanged, tends to increase venous return.
items.explain: It increases the pressure gradient driving blood towards the right atrium.

items.text: An increase in right atrial pressure increases the pressure gradient for venous return.
items.explain: Higher right atrial pressure reduces the gradient driving venous return.

items.text: The first step of haem synthesis occurs in mitochondria and is catalysed by aminolevulinate synthase.
items.explain: ALAS condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA to form delta-aminolevulinate.

items.text: Aminolevulinate synthase requires pyridoxal phosphate.
items.explain: Vitamin B6 in its active PLP form is a required cofactor.

items.text: Hepatic haem synthesis is regulated by feedback effects of haem on ALAS1.
items.explain: Haem suppresses ALAS1 expression and mitochondrial import.

items.text: Lead inhibits ferrochelatase and thereby increases haem synthesis.
items.explain: Lead inhibits ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase, impairing haem synthesis.

questions.q: Regarding reciprocal regulation of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis:

items.text: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activates phosphofructokinase-1.
items.explain: It is a potent allosteric activator of PFK-1 and promotes glycolysis.

items.text: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.
items.explain: It suppresses a key gluconeogenic step.

items.text: Glucagon signalling in the liver generally lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate concentration.
items.explain: cAMP-dependent phosphorylation favours the phosphatase activity of the bifunctional enzyme.

items.text: Pyruvate kinase converts pyruvate to phosphoenolpyruvate during gluconeogenesis.
items.explain: Pyruvate kinase catalyses the glycolytic conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate.

questions.sub: Bile acid synthesis and enterohepatic circulation

items.text: Cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase is a key rate-limiting enzyme in the classic bile acid synthesis pathway.
items.explain: CYP7A1 catalyses the initial rate-limiting hydroxylation.

items.text: Conjugation with glycine or taurine increases bile acid water solubility.
items.explain: Conjugated bile salts are more ionised and aid micelle formation.

items.text: Most bile acids are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver through portal blood.
items.explain: This enterohepatic circulation conserves the bile acid pool.

items.text: Bile salts are normally absorbed mainly in the stomach.
items.explain: Active reabsorption occurs principally in the terminal ileum.

items.text: Most aminotransferases require pyridoxal phosphate.
items.explain: PLP is a coenzyme for transfer of amino groups.

items.text: Alanine aminotransferase transfers an amino group between alanine and alpha-ketoglutarate.
items.explain: The reaction produces pyruvate and glutamate.

items.text: Glutamate dehydrogenase can release ammonium from glutamate by oxidative deamination.
items.explain: This mitochondrial enzyme links nitrogen handling with alpha-ketoglutarate metabolism.

items.text: Transamination reactions normally release free ammonia directly as their principal product.
items.explain: Transamination transfers amino groups to alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate.

items.text: Lactate dehydrogenase catalyses the reversible conversion of pyruvate to lactate.
items.explain: The reaction interconverts pyruvate and lactate with NADH/NAD+.

items.text: The Cori cycle transports lactate from peripheral tissues to the liver for gluconeogenesis.
items.explain: Lactate can be converted to glucose in the liver.

items.text: Conversion of pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+ needed to sustain glycolysis.
items.explain: This allows glycolytic ATP production to continue when oxidative NADH reoxidation is limited.

items.text: Conversion of lactate to glucose in the liver produces net ATP for the body as a whole.
items.explain: Hepatic gluconeogenesis consumes energy; the Cori cycle shifts an energetic cost to the liver.

questions.q: Regarding the inguinal canal and its boundaries:

items.text: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in the transversalis fascia.
items.explain: The deep ring is an evagination of transversalis fascia lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

items.text: The superficial inguinal ring is an opening in the external oblique aponeurosis.
items.explain: The superficial ring is a triangular gap in the external oblique aponeurosis.

items.text: The inferior epigastric vessels lie medial to the deep inguinal ring.
items.explain: The deep ring is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; indirect hernias enter lateral to them.

items.text: A direct inguinal hernia passes through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
items.explain: A direct hernia protrudes through the posterior wall in Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

questions.q: Regarding the lymphatic drainage and clinical anatomy of the breast:

items.text: Most lymph from the breast drains initially to axillary lymph nodes.
items.explain: The majority, especially from the lateral quadrants, drains to the pectoral (anterior) axillary group.

items.text: The medial quadrants of the breast may drain to parasternal nodes.
items.explain: Medial breast lymphatics commonly follow perforating vessels to parasternal nodes.

items.text: Subareolar lymphatics communicate across the midline with the opposite breast.
items.explain: The subareolar plexus provides pathways for cross-midline lymphatic communication.

items.text: The posterior intercostal nodes are the sole destination for lymph from the medial breast.
items.explain: Medial drainage commonly reaches parasternal nodes; other pathways can also occur.

questions.q: Regarding embryological rotation of the midgut:

items.text: Physiological umbilical herniation occurs because the rapidly growing midgut temporarily outgrows the abdominal cavity.
items.explain: The midgut temporarily herniates into the proximal umbilical cord during early development.

items.text: The midgut normally rotates a total of 270 degrees counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery when viewed from the front.
items.explain: Rotation occurs in stages around the superior mesenteric artery axis.

items.text: The caecum initially returns to the abdomen in a position near the left upper quadrant before descending.
items.explain: The caecal bud returns high in the abdomen and later descends to the right iliac fossa.

items.text: Failure of normal midgut rotation can never predispose to volvulus.
items.explain: Malrotation can leave an abnormal mesenteric attachment and predispose to midgut volvulus.

questions.sub: Spinal cord and peripheral nerve histology
questions.q: Regarding the microscopic organisation of nervous tissue:

items.text: The grey matter of the spinal cord contains neuronal cell bodies, dendrites and synapses.
items.explain: Grey matter is rich in neuronal somata, dendrites, synapses and supporting glia.

items.text: The white matter of the spinal cord consists predominantly of myelinated axons arranged in tracts.
items.explain: Ascending and descending axonal pathways account for the pale appearance of white matter.

items.text: A peripheral nerve fascicle is surrounded by perineurium.
items.explain: Perineurium encloses each fascicle and contributes to the blood-nerve barrier.

items.text: The endoneurium surrounds the entire peripheral nerve trunk external to the epineurium.
items.explain: Endoneurium surrounds individual nerve fibres; epineurium encloses the whole nerve.

questions.q: Regarding the major ascending and descending spinal cord pathways:

items.text: The dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway carries vibration, conscious proprioception and discriminative touch.
items.explain: These modalities ascend ipsilaterally in the dorsal columns before decussating in the medulla.

items.text: Spinothalamic fibres usually cross to the opposite side within a few spinal segments of entry.
items.explain: Second-order neurons cross through the anterior white commissure, often after a short ascent or descent.

items.text: The lateral corticospinal tract decussates predominantly at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla.
items.explain: Most corticospinal fibres cross in the caudal medulla before descending in the lateral corticospinal tract.

items.text: A hemisection of the spinal cord produces loss of pain and temperature on the same side below the lesion as its defining sensory finding.
items.explain: Pain and temperature are typically lost contralaterally below the lesion, while dorsal-column modalities are lost ipsilaterally.

items.text: Platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen is facilitated by von Willebrand factor.
items.explain: Von Willebrand factor bridges platelet glycoprotein Ib receptors to exposed subendothelial structures.

items.text: Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
items.explain: Thrombin cleaves fibrinopeptides from fibrinogen, allowing fibrin monomers to polymerise.

items.text: Activated factor XIII stabilises the fibrin clot by cross-linking fibrin strands.
items.explain: Factor XIIIa forms covalent cross-links that strengthen the fibrin network.

items.text: Aspirin increases platelet thromboxane A2 synthesis by activating cyclo-oxygenase-1.
items.explain: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclo-oxygenase-1 and reduces thromboxane A2 production.

questions.q: Regarding ABO and Rh blood-group physiology:

items.text: Group A red cells express A antigen on their surface.
items.explain: ABO phenotype is determined by the carbohydrate antigen expressed on red-cell membranes.

items.text: A person with group O blood normally has both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma.
items.explain: Group O individuals lack A and B antigens and typically possess both corresponding antibodies.

items.text: The RhD antigen is a carbohydrate expressed on the red-cell membrane.
items.explain: RhD is a transmembrane protein antigen, not a carbohydrate antigen.

items.text: Maternal anti-D IgG can cross the placenta and cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.
items.explain: In an RhD-negative sensitised mother, anti-D IgG can cross the placenta and destroy RhD-positive fetal erythrocytes.

questions.q: Regarding cerebrospinal fluid formation and circulation:

items.text: Most cerebrospinal fluid is produced by the choroid plexuses.
items.explain: Choroid plexus epithelial cells actively secrete most CSF.

items.text: Cerebrospinal fluid flows from the lateral ventricles through the interventricular foramina into the third ventricle.
items.explain: The foramina of Monro connect each lateral ventricle with the third ventricle.

items.text: Arachnoid granulations provide an important route for CSF absorption into dural venous sinuses.
items.explain: Arachnoid villi and granulations allow CSF to pass into venous blood.

items.text: Cerebrospinal fluid is normally produced only when a person is asleep.
items.explain: CSF production is continuous rather than restricted to sleep.

items.text: Central chemoreceptors respond primarily to changes in hydrogen ion concentration in brain extracellular fluid generated from arterial carbon dioxide.
items.explain: Carbon dioxide crosses the blood-brain barrier and generates hydrogen ions in CSF and brain extracellular fluid.

items.text: Peripheral chemoreceptors include carotid and aortic bodies.
items.explain: Carotid bodies and aortic bodies detect arterial chemical changes.

items.text: A fall in arterial oxygen tension strongly stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors, particularly when PaO2 falls below about 60 mmHg.
items.explain: The ventilatory response to hypoxaemia becomes marked at low arterial oxygen tensions.

items.text: Central chemoreceptors directly detect arterial oxygen tension as their principal stimulus.
items.explain: Central chemoreceptors primarily mediate the response to CO2-related changes in CSF hydrogen ion concentration.

questions.q: Regarding the short-term baroreceptor regulation of arterial pressure:

items.text: Baroreceptors are located in the carotid sinus and aortic arch.
items.explain: Stretch-sensitive endings in these regions detect changes in arterial wall distension.

items.text: Increased arterial pressure increases baroreceptor afferent firing.
items.explain: Greater stretch increases discharge through glossopharyngeal and vagal afferents.

items.text: Increased baroreceptor firing tends to reduce sympathetic outflow and increase parasympathetic influence on the heart.
items.explain: The reflex reduces heart rate, contractility and peripheral vascular resistance.

items.text: The baroreceptor reflex is the principal long-term controller of arterial pressure through direct regulation of total body sodium.
items.explain: Renal-body fluid mechanisms are central to long-term pressure regulation; baroreceptors reset and are more important short term.

questions.q: Regarding buffer systems and acid-base chemistry:

items.text: A buffer consists of a weak acid and its conjugate base, or a weak base and its conjugate acid.
items.explain: A buffer limits pH change by reversibly binding or releasing hydrogen ions.

items.text: The bicarbonate buffer system is an open system because carbon dioxide can be eliminated by the lungs.
items.explain: Ventilation regulates the carbon dioxide component while the kidneys regulate bicarbonate.

items.text: At pH equal to the pKa of a weak acid, the concentrations of the acid and its conjugate base are equal.
items.explain: This follows from the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship.

items.text: A buffer has its greatest capacity when the solution pH is many units away from its pKa.
items.explain: Buffering is most effective near the pKa, where acid and conjugate base concentrations are comparable.

questions.q: Regarding selected inherited disorders of amino acid metabolism:

items.text: Phenylketonuria commonly results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase activity.
items.explain: Reduced conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine causes phenylalanine accumulation in classic PKU.

items.text: Alkaptonuria is associated with deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase.
items.explain: Homogentisic acid accumulates and can darken urine and deposit in connective tissues.

items.text: Maple syrup urine disease is caused by impaired branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase activity.
items.explain: The enzyme complex is required for oxidative decarboxylation of branched-chain amino-acid ketoacids.

items.text: Classic phenylketonuria is treated by deliberately increasing dietary phenylalanine intake.
items.explain: Treatment restricts phenylalanine while ensuring adequate amounts for protein synthesis; tyrosine becomes conditionally essential.

questions.q: Regarding the biochemical metabolism of drugs and other xenobiotics:

items.text: Cytochrome P450 enzymes are important catalysts of many phase I oxidation reactions.
items.explain: The microsomal CYP system introduces or exposes functional groups in many compounds.

items.text: Phase II reactions commonly involve conjugation with molecules such as glucuronic acid, sulfate or glutathione.
items.explain: Conjugation often increases water solubility and facilitates excretion.

items.text: All phase I reactions invariably make a xenobiotic less toxic.
items.explain: Some phase I reactions generate reactive or toxic metabolites, including bioactivation products.

items.text: Glutathione conjugation can contribute to detoxification of electrophilic compounds.
items.explain: Glutathione S-transferases catalyse conjugation of glutathione to many electrophiles.

questions.q: Regarding the principles of the polymerase chain reaction (PCR):

items.text: PCR uses repeated cycles of denaturation, primer annealing and extension.
items.explain: Thermal cycling separates DNA strands, permits primer binding and allows polymerase-mediated synthesis.

items.text: A thermostable DNA polymerase is used to withstand repeated high-temperature denaturation steps.
items.explain: Taq and other thermostable polymerases remain active after repeated heating.

items.text: The primers determine the boundaries of the DNA region amplified.
items.explain: Primers bind to sequences flanking the target and define the amplicon.

items.text: PCR amplification can proceed without primers if sufficient deoxyribonucleotides are present.
items.explain: DNA polymerase requires a primer-template junction with a free 3-prime hydroxyl group.

questions.q: Regarding the major plasma protein fractions:

items.text: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and contributes substantially to plasma colloid osmotic pressure.
items.explain: Its concentration and molecular properties make albumin a major determinant of oncotic pressure.

items.text: Most immunoglobulins migrate in the gamma-globulin region on serum protein electrophoresis.
items.explain: Immunoglobulins, particularly IgG, contribute to the gamma fraction.

items.text: Fibrinogen is normally present in serum after blood has clotted.
items.explain: Serum is plasma after clotting and therefore has had most fibrinogen removed.

items.text: Alpha- and beta-globulin fractions include proteins involved in transport and acute-phase responses.
items.explain: These fractions contain diverse transport proteins, complement components and acute-phase proteins.

questions.q: Regarding the cavernous sinus and structures related to it:

items.text: The internal carotid artery passes through the cavernous sinus.
items.explain: The cavernous segment of the internal carotid artery traverses the venous sinus.

items.text: The abducens nerve runs within the cavernous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery.
items.explain: CN VI lies within the sinus proper, close to the internal carotid artery.

items.text: The oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic and maxillary nerves are embedded in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus.
items.explain: CN III, IV, V1 and V2 course in the lateral wall, whereas CN VI and the artery lie within the sinus.

items.text: An infection from the danger area of the face can never spread to the cavernous sinus because venous flow is exclusively away from the cranial cavity.
items.explain: Valveless facial and ophthalmic venous communications can permit retrograde spread of infection.

questions.q: Regarding the course and clinically important relations of the ureter in the pelvis:

items.text: The ureter enters the pelvis by crossing the bifurcation of the common iliac artery or the external iliac artery near it.
items.explain: The pelvic ureter commonly crosses the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim.

items.text: In the female pelvis, the uterine artery passes superior to the ureter near the cervix.
items.explain: The uterine artery crosses above the ureter, remembered clinically as water under the bridge.

items.text: In the male pelvis, the ductus deferens crosses superior to the ureter near the bladder.
items.explain: The ductus deferens passes over the ureter before reaching the posterior aspect of the bladder.

items.text: The ureter is normally situated anterior to the uterine artery at the point where the artery crosses it.
items.explain: The ureter passes inferior to the uterine artery; this relationship is important during hysterectomy.

questions.sub: Histology of the kidney and nephron
questions.q: Regarding the microscopic structure of the kidney:

items.text: The parietal layer of Bowman's capsule is lined by simple squamous epithelium.
items.explain: The parietal layer is predominantly simple squamous epithelium, transitioning near the urinary pole.

items.text: Podocytes form the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule.
items.explain: Podocyte cell bodies and foot processes cover the glomerular capillaries.

items.text: The proximal convoluted tubule has a prominent brush border formed by microvilli.
items.explain: The brush border increases surface area for extensive reabsorption.

items.text: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is freely permeable to water under normal conditions.
items.explain: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs solutes but is essentially impermeable to water, helping dilute tubular fluid.

questions.q: Regarding embryological development of the thyroid gland:

items.text: The thyroid primordium begins as an endodermal thickening in the floor of the primitive pharynx near the foramen caecum.
items.explain: The median thyroid diverticulum arises from endoderm at the foramen caecum region.

items.text: The thyroid descends in the midline anterior to the hyoid bone and laryngeal cartilages.
items.explain: It migrates from the tongue region to its definitive pretracheal position.

items.text: The thyroglossal duct normally obliterates during development.
items.explain: The duct usually disappears, leaving the foramen caecum as a landmark.

items.text: A pyramidal lobe of the thyroid is evidence that the thyroid gland failed to develop from mesoderm.
items.explain: A pyramidal lobe is a common remnant of the thyroglossal duct, not evidence of mesodermal origin.

questions.q: Regarding the organisation and major branches of the brachial plexus:

items.text: The roots of the brachial plexus are the anterior rami of spinal nerves C5 to T1 in the typical pattern.
items.explain: The plexus is usually formed by the anterior rami of C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1.

items.text: The musculocutaneous nerve is a terminal branch of the lateral cord.
items.explain: The lateral cord gives rise to the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve.

items.text: The radial nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.
items.explain: The posterior cord terminates as the axillary and radial nerves.

items.text: The ulnar nerve is normally formed directly from the superior trunk.
items.explain: The ulnar nerve is a terminal branch of the medial cord, carrying mainly C8 and T1 fibres.

questions.q: Regarding the hormones of the adrenal cortex:

items.text: The zona glomerulosa primarily secretes mineralocorticoids, particularly aldosterone.
items.explain: The outer cortical zone expresses the enzymatic machinery for aldosterone synthesis.

items.text: The zona fasciculata is the principal source of cortisol.
items.explain: The middle cortical zone produces glucocorticoids, with cortisol being the major human glucocorticoid.

items.text: Adrenocorticotropic hormone is the principal long-term regulator of aldosterone secretion.
items.explain: Angiotensin II and plasma potassium are the major regulators of aldosterone; ACTH has a lesser, generally transient influence.

items.text: Cortisol secretion is regulated by hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH in a negative-feedback system.
items.explain: Cortisol inhibits CRH and ACTH release through hypothalamic and pituitary feedback.

questions.q: Regarding antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and renal water conservation:

items.text: ADH is synthesised in hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary.
items.explain: It is synthesised mainly in supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and transported to the neurohypophysis.

items.text: ADH increases water permeability in collecting-duct principal cells by promoting insertion of aquaporin-2 channels.
items.explain: V2 receptor activation promotes aquaporin-2 insertion into the apical membrane.

items.text: Increased plasma osmolality is an important stimulus for ADH secretion.
items.explain: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect increases in effective plasma osmolality.

items.text: ADH acts mainly through V1 receptors on collecting-duct principal cells to insert aquaporin-2.
items.explain: Aquaporin-2 insertion is mediated by V2 receptors; V1 receptors primarily mediate vasoconstrictor effects.

questions.q: Regarding excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle:

items.text: An action potential in the muscle fibre propagates along the sarcolemma and into the transverse tubules.
items.explain: T-tubules carry depolarisation into the fibre interior.

items.text: Calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to troponin C.
items.explain: Calcium binding changes the troponin-tropomyosin complex and exposes myosin-binding sites on actin.

items.text: ATP binding to myosin is required for detachment of myosin from actin.
items.explain: ATP binding reduces myosin's affinity for actin, allowing cross-bridge detachment.

items.text: Relaxation occurs because calcium is pumped out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol.
items.explain: SERCA pumps return calcium from cytosol into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, lowering cytosolic calcium.

questions.q: Regarding the regulation of exocrine pancreatic secretion:

items.text: Secretin stimulates pancreatic duct cells to secrete a bicarbonate-rich fluid.
items.explain: Secretin is released in response to acidic chyme and promotes bicarbonate secretion.

items.text: Cholecystokinin stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic acinar secretion.
items.explain: CCK released from the small intestine promotes enzyme secretion from acinar cells.

items.text: Vagal cholinergic activity can stimulate pancreatic exocrine secretion.
items.explain: Parasympathetic activity contributes to pancreatic secretion, especially during cephalic and gastric phases.

items.text: The P wave represents atrial depolarisation.
items.explain: Atrial depolarisation precedes atrial contraction.

items.text: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation.
items.explain: Ventricular depolarisation produces the QRS complex; atrial repolarisation is usually obscured.

items.text: The PR interval extends from the beginning of atrial depolarisation to the beginning of ventricular depolarisation.
items.explain: It includes conduction through the atria, AV node and His-Purkinje system up to ventricular activation.

items.text: The QT interval is normally independent of heart rate.
items.explain: QT duration varies with heart rate and is commonly interpreted using a rate-corrected QT interval.

items.text: Chylomicrons transport dietary triacylglycerol from the intestine to peripheral tissues.

items.text: Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses triacylglycerol in circulating chylomicrons and VLDL.

items.text: Apolipoprotein B-100 is the principal structural apolipoprotein of VLDL, IDL and LDL.
items.explain: ApoB-100 is retained as VLDL is metabolised through IDL to LDL.

items.text: HDL is the main lipoprotein that carries newly absorbed dietary triacylglycerol from the intestine.
items.explain: Chylomicrons carry dietary triacylglycerol; HDL participates in reverse cholesterol transport and apolipoprotein exchange.

questions.q: Regarding electrophoresis as a biochemical laboratory technique:

items.text: Electrophoresis separates charged molecules according to their migration in an electric field.
items.explain: Migration depends on charge, size, shape, gel properties and applied field conditions.

items.text: At a fixed pH, a protein's net charge influences its direction and rate of migration.
items.explain: The relationship between pH and isoelectric point determines the protein's net charge.

items.text: In SDS-PAGE, sodium dodecyl sulfate denatures proteins and gives them a broadly similar charge-to-mass ratio.
items.explain: SDS masks much of the proteins' intrinsic charge, allowing separation mainly by molecular mass.

items.text: In isoelectric focusing, proteins are separated primarily by their native molecular mass.
items.explain: Isoelectric focusing separates proteins according to their isoelectric points in a pH gradient.

items.text: Alanine aminotransferase is relatively more specific for hepatocellular injury than alkaline phosphatase.
items.explain: ALT is concentrated in hepatocytes, whereas ALP may arise from liver, bone and other tissues.

items.text: A raised alkaline phosphatase with a raised gamma-glutamyl transferase can support a hepatobiliary source of ALP.

items.text: Serum albumin concentration can reflect hepatic synthetic function, although it is affected by other conditions and changes relatively slowly.
items.explain: Albumin has a long half-life and can also be reduced by renal loss, inflammation and malnutrition.

items.text: An isolated increase in serum bilirubin always proves hepatocellular necrosis.
items.explain: Hyperbilirubinaemia has multiple causes, including haemolysis, impaired conjugation and cholestasis.

items.text: The neural plate develops from ectoderm under inductive signals from underlying tissues.
items.explain: Dorsal ectoderm is induced to form neuroectoderm.

items.text: The neural tube gives rise to the brain and spinal cord.

items.text: Failure of caudal neuropore closure is associated with open spinal neural tube defects.

items.text: The first heart sound is associated mainly with closure of atrioventricular valves.
items.explain: S1 occurs near the beginning of ventricular systole.

items.text: The second heart sound is associated with closure of aortic and pulmonary valves.
items.explain: S2 marks the end of ventricular ejection.

items.text: During isovolumetric ventricular contraction all four valves are closed.
items.explain: Pressure rises while ventricular volume remains constant.

items.text: Semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure falls below great-artery pressure.
items.explain: They open when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure.

items.explain: Renal oxygen sensing increases erythropoietin production.

items.text: Erythropoietin acts mainly on erythroid progenitors in bone marrow.
items.explain: It supports survival and differentiation of erythroid precursors.

items.text: Mature human erythrocytes normally retain a nucleus and mitochondria.

items.text: At the apex of an upright lung, V/Q is generally higher than at the base.
items.explain: Perfusion falls more markedly towards the apex than ventilation.

items.text: Pulmonary embolism can create ventilated but poorly perfused alveoli.
items.explain: High-V/Q units increase physiological dead space.

items.text: Complete airway obstruction with preserved perfusion produces a high V/Q ratio.
items.explain: Perfusion without ventilation creates low V/Q, approaching shunt.

items.text: The gallbladder concentrates bile by absorbing water and electrolytes.
items.explain: Its mucosa removes water and electrolytes.

items.text: Cholecystokinin promotes gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi.

items.text: An oral glucose tolerance test assesses handling of a standardised oral glucose load.
items.explain: Serial glucose measurements assess glucose tolerance.

items.text: HbA1c reflects glycaemic exposure over roughly the preceding two to three months.
items.explain: Red-cell lifespan integrates glycaemia over weeks to months.

items.text: Altered red-cell lifespan can affect HbA1c interpretation.
items.explain: Haemolysis, blood loss and transfusion may distort HbA1c.

items.text: A single normal fasting glucose excludes diabetes in every clinical circumstance.

items.text: Acute intermittent porphyria is associated with deficient porphobilinogen deaminase (HMBS).

items.text: Lead can inhibit ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase.
items.explain: Lead disrupts haem synthesis.

items.text: Sodium is a major determinant of extracellular fluid osmolality.
items.explain: Sodium and accompanying anions account for most effective extracellular osmoles.

items.text: Potassium is the principal intracellular cation.
items.explain: Most body potassium is inside cells, especially skeletal muscle.

items.text: Severe hyperkalaemia can alter cardiac conduction and cause life-threatening arrhythmias.
items.explain: Raised extracellular potassium changes cardiac membrane excitability.

items.text: Low serum sodium always means total body sodium content is reduced.

items.text: The elbow joint includes humeroulnar and humeroradial articulations.
items.explain: These articulations permit flexion and extension; the proximal radioulnar joint shares the capsule.

items.text: The annular ligament encircles the head of the ulna.
items.explain: It encircles the radial head and holds it against the radial notch of the ulna.

items.text: The median nerve normally lies medial to the brachial artery in the cubital fossa.
items.explain: The principal contents from lateral to medial are biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve.

items.text: The radial nerve divides into superficial and deep branches near the lateral elbow.

items.text: The right gastro-omental artery usually arises from the splenic artery.
items.explain: It usually arises from the gastroduodenal artery; the left gastro-omental arises from the splenic artery.

items.text: The pancreas and left kidney contribute to the stomach bed.

items.text: Gastric lymph drains exclusively to inferior mesenteric nodes.
items.explain: Lymph follows arterial routes to gastric, pyloric and pancreaticosplenic nodes, then coeliac nodes.

items.text: The ulnar nerve normally traverses the carpal tunnel alongside the median nerve.

items.text: Median nerve compression may cause thenar weakness and sensory symptoms in the lateral three and a half digits.

items.text: The paramesonephric ducts contribute to the uterine tubes, uterus and upper vagina.

items.text: In the absence of anti-Müllerian hormone, the paramesonephric ducts normally regress.

items.text: The ovaries develop from the mesonephric ducts.

items.text: The functional layer of the endometrium is shed during menstruation.
items.explain: The basal layer remains and regenerates the functional layer.

items.text: The ovarian cortex contains most developing follicles, while the medulla is more vascular.

items.text: The uterine endocervix is normally lined by keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.

items.text: Stretch of the afferent arteriole during increased pressure can trigger myogenic constriction.
items.explain: This intrinsic response buffers changes in renal blood flow and filtration.

items.text: Increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa generally promotes afferent arteriolar constriction.

items.text: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis involves increased ventilation and reduced PaCO2.
items.explain: Lowering carbon dioxide partially offsets the reduction in bicarbonate.

items.text: Renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis includes increased net acid excretion and bicarbonate retention.
items.explain: Renal adaptation develops over hours to days.

items.text: Compensation normally overshoots and produces the opposite primary acid-base disorder.
items.explain: Compensation limits the pH change but ordinarily does not overshoot.

items.text: Hypoventilation can partially compensate for metabolic alkalosis by raising PaCO2.
items.explain: This response is limited by the need to maintain adequate oxygenation.

questions.sub: Types and physiological effects of hypoxia

items.text: In anaemic hypoxia, PaO2 may be normal despite reduced blood oxygen content.
items.explain: Dissolved oxygen tension may be preserved while reduced haemoglobin lowers oxygen-carrying capacity.

items.text: In circulatory hypoxia, tissue oxygen delivery is impaired by reduced blood flow.
items.explain: Arterial oxygen content may be normal, but perfusion is inadequate.

items.text: In histotoxic hypoxia, tissues cannot utilise delivered oxygen effectively.
items.explain: Cyanide inhibits cellular oxidative metabolism; venous oxygen extraction is impaired.

items.text: A rightward shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve increases haemoglobin affinity for oxygen.
items.explain: A right shift reduces affinity and facilitates oxygen unloading in tissues.

items.text: Uncouplers can increase oxygen consumption while decreasing ATP synthesis efficiency.
items.explain: They dissipate the proton gradient, uncoupling electron transport from ATP production.

items.text: Acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are the principal circulating ketone bodies.

items.text: Unconjugated bilirubin circulates bound to albumin and is poorly water-soluble.
items.explain: Albumin transports it to the liver; it is not normally filtered into urine.

items.text: Hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid.
items.explain: Conjugation forms water-soluble bilirubin glucuronides for biliary excretion.

items.text: Conjugated bilirubin may appear in urine when its plasma concentration is increased.
items.explain: Its water solubility permits renal filtration in cholestasis or hepatocellular disease.

items.text: Intestinal bacteria convert bilirubin into biliverdin, the main pigment responsible for normal stool colour.
items.explain: Bacteria form urobilinogen; oxidation to stercobilin contributes to stool's brown colour.

questions.q: Regarding amino-group transfer in amino acid metabolism:

items.text: Most aminotransferases require pyridoxal phosphate derived from vitamin B6.
items.explain: PLP acts as a coenzyme in reversible transfer of amino groups.

items.text: Alanine aminotransferase transfers alanine's amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate, producing pyruvate and glutamate.
items.explain: This links amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism.

items.text: Transamination reactions generally release free ammonia directly as their main product.
items.explain: They transfer amino groups to alpha-keto acids; ammonia release occurs through other processes, including oxidative deamination.

items.text: Aspartate aminotransferase catalyses a reaction involving oxaloacetate and glutamate.
items.explain: AST catalyses aspartate + alpha-ketoglutarate ⇌ oxaloacetate + glutamate.

items.text: The pyrimidine ring is synthesised before it is attached to PRPP.
items.explain: The ring is assembled first, then linked to PRPP to form orotidine monophosphate.

items.text: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II is a cytosolic enzyme involved in de novo pyrimidine synthesis.
items.explain: Mammalian CPS II uses glutamine, bicarbonate and ATP as part of the CAD complex.

items.text: Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and orotidylate decarboxylase participate in UMP synthesis.
items.explain: These catalytic activities are present in the bifunctional UMP synthase enzyme.

items.text: UMP synthase deficiency causes Lesch–Nyhan syndrome.
items.explain: It causes hereditary orotic aciduria; Lesch–Nyhan syndrome results from HGPRT deficiency.

questions.sub: Posterior abdominal wall and lumbar plexus

items.text: Psoas major arises from the sides of the bodies and transverse processes of T12–L5 vertebrae.
items.explain: It descends through the pelvis to join iliacus in forming iliopsoas.

items.text: The femoral nerve emerges from the medial border of psoas major.
items.explain: It emerges from the lateral border; the obturator nerve emerges from the medial border.

items.text: The sympathetic trunks lie anterior to the psoas muscles in the abdomen.
items.explain: They descend on the anterolateral aspects of the vertebral bodies.

items.text: Quadratus lumborum attaches to the 12th rib and contributes to the posterior abdominal wall.
items.explain: It extends between the iliac crest, 12th rib and lumbar transverse processes.

questions.q: Regarding the perineum and its fascial spaces:

items.text: The perineal membrane separates the superficial and deep perineal pouches.
items.explain: It forms an important boundary between these spaces in the urogenital triangle.

items.text: The bulb and crura of the penis are located in the superficial perineal pouch.
items.explain: They are erectile tissues associated with the superficial pouch.

items.text: The membranous urethra passes through the perineal membrane.
items.explain: It traverses the deep perineal region and external urethral sphincter complex.

items.text: The ischioanal fossae are located in the urogenital triangle.
items.explain: They lie in the anal triangle, lateral to the anal canal.

questions.sub: Development of the heart and aortic arches
questions.q: Regarding embryological development of the heart:

items.text: The primitive heart tube forms from cardiogenic mesoderm and begins to beat during the fourth week.
items.explain: Contractions begin at approximately day 22.

items.text: The truncus arteriosus is divided into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk by the aorticopulmonary septum.
items.explain: Conotruncal ridges contribute to the spiral septum.

items.text: The left sixth aortic arch contributes to the ductus arteriosus.
items.explain: Its distal portion persists as the ductus arteriosus and later becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

items.text: The foramen ovale is formed by complete fusion of septum primum and septum secundum before birth.
items.explain: Their overlapping arrangement creates a flap-like fetal communication; functional closure follows birth.

questions.q: Regarding development of the respiratory system:

items.text: The respiratory diverticulum arises from the ventral wall of the foregut.
items.explain: It appears during the fourth week and gives rise to the lower respiratory tract.

items.text: The epithelium of the lower respiratory tract is derived mainly from endoderm.
items.explain: Cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue derive from surrounding splanchnic mesoderm.

items.text: Type II pneumocytes produce pulmonary surfactant.
items.explain: Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension and helps prevent collapse.

items.text: The pleura and lung connective tissue are derived entirely from endoderm.
items.explain: Pleura and supporting connective tissues are mesodermal in origin.

questions.sub: Inguinal canal: walls and deep ring

items.text: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in the transversalis fascia.
items.explain: It lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

items.text: The conjoint tendon contributes to the posterior wall of the medial inguinal canal.
items.explain: It is formed by fused aponeurotic fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

items.text: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the canal medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
items.explain: It enters lateral to these vessels through the deep ring.

items.text: The ilioinguinal nerve enters the inguinal canal through the deep ring.
items.explain: It usually pierces internal oblique and exits through the superficial ring.

items.text: Neutrophils are commonly the first circulating leukocytes recruited in acute bacterial inflammation.
items.explain: They rapidly migrate into tissues in response to chemotactic signals.

items.text: Eosinophils are associated with helminth infection and allergic responses.
items.explain: Their granule proteins contribute to parasite defence and allergic inflammation.

items.text: Mature erythrocytes are the principal antigen-presenting cells of adaptive immunity.
items.explain: Professional antigen-presenting cells include dendritic cells, macrophages and B lymphocytes.

items.text: Natural killer cells can destroy some virus-infected and tumour cells without prior antigen-specific sensitisation.
items.explain: They respond to altered MHC class I expression and activating signals.

items.text: Tissue factor initiates the extrinsic pathway by forming a complex with factor VIIa.
items.explain: The complex activates factor X and can also activate factor IX.

items.text: Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
items.explain: It cleaves fibrinopeptides, allowing fibrin monomers to polymerise.

items.text: Factor XIII stabilises the fibrin clot by cross-linking fibrin strands.
items.explain: Activated factor XIII forms covalent cross-links in the fibrin network.

items.text: Plasmin promotes clot dissolution by degrading fibrin.
items.explain: Plasmin is generated from plasminogen, notably through tissue plasminogen activator.

items.text: The mid-cycle LH surge is the principal trigger for ovulation.
items.explain: Sustained high oestradiol switches to positive feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

items.text: The corpus luteum secretes progesterone during the luteal phase.
items.explain: Progesterone prepares the endometrium for possible implantation.

items.text: FSH stimulates granulosa cells, including their aromatase activity.
items.explain: Granulosa-cell aromatase converts theca-derived androgens to oestrogens.

items.text: Theca interna cells are the principal source of aromatase that converts androgens to oestradiol.
items.explain: Granulosa cells express aromatase; theca cells produce androgen precursors under LH stimulation.

questions.sub: Calcium homeostasis: PTH, vitamin D and calcitonin

items.text: Parathyroid hormone increases renal calcium reabsorption, particularly in the distal nephron.
items.explain: PTH conserves calcium while promoting phosphate excretion in the proximal tubule.

items.text: PTH stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, increasing formation of active vitamin D.
items.explain: This increases intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate.

items.text: Calcitonin is the dominant long-term regulator of plasma calcium in healthy adults.
items.explain: PTH and vitamin D are the major regulators; calcitonin has a more limited role.

items.text: PTH generally increases serum calcium while reducing serum phosphate.
items.explain: Its renal phosphaturic effect reduces serum phosphate.

references: Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology, 15th ed.
Boron and Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, 4th ed.

items.text: Most cerebrospinal fluid is produced by the choroid plexuses of the ventricles.
items.explain: Choroid plexus epithelial cells actively secrete CSF.

items.text: CSF flows from the lateral ventricles through the foramina of Monro into the third ventricle.
items.explain: The interventricular foramina connect the lateral ventricles with the third ventricle.

items.text: CSF is absorbed mainly through arachnoid granulations into dural venous sinuses.
items.explain: These structures permit CSF to enter the venous circulation.

items.text: Obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct typically causes communicating hydrocephalus.
items.explain: Aqueductal obstruction causes non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus.

items.text: Lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids can serve as substrates for gluconeogenesis.
items.explain: They enter through pyruvate, dihydroxyacetone phosphate or citric-acid-cycle intermediates.

items.text: The liver is the principal site of gluconeogenesis during fasting, with the renal cortex also contributing.
items.explain: Renal gluconeogenesis becomes more important during prolonged fasting and acidosis.

items.text: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate stimulates fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.
items.explain: It inhibits this enzyme and activates phosphofructokinase-1, favouring glycolysis.

items.text: Glucagon promotes hepatic gluconeogenesis partly by lowering fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.
items.explain: Phosphorylation of the bifunctional enzyme reduces its kinase activity and favours its phosphatase activity.

items.text: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is an X-linked urea-cycle disorder.
items.explain: It commonly causes hyperammonaemia and increased urinary orotic acid.

items.text: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I requires N-acetylglutamate as an essential activator.
items.explain: N-acetylglutamate activates mitochondrial CPS I.

items.text: A urea-cycle defect may cause hyperammonaemia with neurological manifestations.
items.explain: Ammonia is neurotoxic and can cause encephalopathy and cerebral oedema.

items.text: Increased urinary orotic acid is characteristic of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency.
items.explain: It is classically increased in OTC deficiency because excess carbamoyl phosphate enters pyrimidine synthesis.

items.text: Dietary non-haem iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C.
items.explain: Vitamin C helps reduce ferric iron to the more readily absorbed ferrous form.

items.text: Ferroportin exports iron from enterocytes and macrophages into plasma.
items.explain: It is the principal known cellular iron exporter.

items.text: Hepcidin increases intestinal iron absorption by promoting ferroportin expression.
items.explain: Hepcidin binds ferroportin and causes its internalisation and degradation.

items.text: Transferrin transports iron in plasma, while ferritin stores intracellular iron.
items.explain: Transferrin is the major plasma carrier; ferritin provides a soluble storage form.

items.text: Alanine aminotransferase is generally more liver-specific than aspartate aminotransferase.
items.explain: AST is also present in cardiac and skeletal muscle and other tissues.

items.text: Raised alkaline phosphatase with raised gamma-glutamyl transferase supports a hepatobiliary source.
items.explain: GGT helps distinguish hepatobiliary ALP elevation from many bone-related causes.

items.text: Serum amylase is more specific for acute pancreatitis than serum lipase.
items.explain: Lipase is generally more specific and remains elevated longer.

items.text: Creatine kinase may be increased following skeletal-muscle injury.
items.explain: CK is released from damaged muscle, particularly the CK-MM fraction.

items.text: Vitamin D increases intestinal absorption of both calcium and phosphate.
items.explain: Active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D increases intestinal transport of both minerals.

items.text: PTH increases renal phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule.
items.explain: PTH reduces proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption, causing phosphaturia.

items.text: Chronic kidney disease can cause phosphate retention and reduced calcitriol production.
items.explain: These changes contribute to hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

items.text: Most of the body's calcium is stored in extracellular fluid.
items.explain: Approximately 99% is present in bone and teeth, predominantly as hydroxyapatite.
